What is the Blessed One's intention here? It is the Blessed One's intention that those who wish to seek the Deathless will live heedfully. This is the intention (adhippāya).

Among those (four), what is the origin (nidāna)? Just as the herdsman Dhaniya said to the Blessed One:

“One with sons rejoices in sons; likewise, one with cattle rejoices in cattle. For acquisitions (upadhi) are a man’s joy; one without acquisitions does not rejoice.”

The Blessed One replied:

“One with sons sorrows because of sons; likewise, one with cattle sorrows because of cattle. For acquisitions are a man’s sorrow; one without acquisitions does not sorrow.”
31:
By this story and this origin, it is to be understood: “In this Dispensation, the Blessed One spoke of external possessions (pariggaha) as acquisitions (upadhi).” And when Māra the Evil One dropped a large rock from the Gijjhakūṭa mountain, the Blessed One said:

“Even if you were to move the whole of Gijjhakūṭa, there is no trembling for the Buddhas who are perfectly liberated. Even if the sky were to crack, the earth to shake, and all beings to be terrified, and even if a spike were to pierce and shake their breast, the Buddhas do not seek protection in acquisitions.”

By this story and this origin, it is to be understood: “In this Dispensation, the Blessed One spoke of the physical body as acquisitions.” As he also said:

“That bond is not strong, say the wise—that which is made of iron, wood, or hemp. But that attachment to jeweled earrings, and the longing for sons and wives (is a strong bond).”

By this story and this origin, it is to be understood: “In this Dispensation, the Blessed One spoke of craving for external objects as acquisitions.” As he also said:

“This bond is strong, say the wise—it drags one down, is loose yet hard to untie. Having cut even this, they wander forth, regardless of sensual pleasures, having abandoned them.”

By this story and this origin, it is to be understood: “In this Dispensation, the Blessed One spoke of the abandonment of craving for external objects.” As he also said:

“Behold this body—afflicted, impure, putrid, foul-smelling, dependent on the frame, oozing day and night, and greatly delighted in by fools.”

By this story and this origin, it is to be understood: “In this Dispensation, the Blessed One spoke of the abandonment of craving for internal objects.” As he also said:
32:
“Cut out your self-love as one would pluck an autumn lotus with the hand. Cherish only the path to peace, the Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.”

By this story and this origin, it is to be understood: “In this Dispensation, the Blessed One spoke of the abandonment of craving for internal objects.” This is the origin (nidāna).

Among those four, what is the sequence of connection (pubbāparasaṅdhi)? As the Blessed One said:

“Blinded by sensual lust, covered by the net of craving, shrouded by the canopy of craving, bound by the bond of heedlessness, like fish in the mouth of a trap, they follow after aging and death, just as a suckling calf follows its mother.”

This is the teaching on craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā). With what sequence of connection is that craving for sensual pleasures associated? As the Blessed One said:

“One who is lustful does not know the meaning; one who is lustful does not see the Dhamma. When lust overcomes a man, then there is utter darkness.”

Thus, that very craving is described in terms of blindness and being covered. By the phrase “blinded by sensual lust, covered by the net of craving, shrouded by the canopy of craving,” and by the phrase “one who is lustful does not know the meaning, one who is lustful does not see the Dhamma,” that very craving is described in terms of its outbursts (pariyuṭṭhāna). That which is darkness is the origin of suffering (dukkha-samudaya); that which is craving leads to renewed existence. What are called “sensual pleasures” (kāma) are the defilements of sensuality (kilesa-kāma). By saying “covered by the net of craving,” he shows the outburst through the repeated practice of those sensual pleasures. Therefore, the bond of craving is spoken of by way of defilement and by way of outburst. Those who are of such a nature follow after aging and death; this was shown by the Blessed One through the power of the verse as it was laid down: “they follow after aging and death.”

“For that sage (muni) in whom there is no proliferation (papañca) nor persistence (ṭhiti), who has transcended the bond and the bolt, that sage who wanders free from craving, the world with its devas does not know him.”

“Proliferation” (papañca) refers to craving, views, and conceit, and the formations (saṅkhāra) conditioned by them. “Persistence” (ṭhiti) refers to the underlying tendencies (anusaya). “Bond” (sandāna) refers to the outburst of craving, those thirty-six types of craving...
33:
These are the wanderings (vicārita) of the net of craving. Delusion (moha) is called the bolt (paligha). Whoever overcomes all these—the mental formations (saṅkhāra) that proliferate in saṃsāra, the persistence (ṭhiti), the bond (sandāna), and the bolt (paligha)—is called one free from craving. In that context, the formations known as obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna) have results to be experienced in the present life, the next life, or in subsequent lives. Thus, craving gives three types of results: in the present life, the next life, or in other subsequent lives. Thus the Blessed One said: "Whatever action one performs through greed, whether by body, speech, or mind, one experiences its result in the present life, the next life, or in other subsequent lives." This is consistent with the Blessed One's previous and subsequent statements. In that context, obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) is karma to be experienced in the present life, the next life, or in subsequent lives; thus karma ripens in three ways: in the present life, the next life, or in other subsequent lives. As the Blessed One said: "If a fool in this world is a killer of living beings... (p)... has wrong view, he experiences the result of that karma in the present life, the next life, or in other subsequent lives." This is consistent with the Blessed One's previous and subsequent statements. In that context, obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) should be abandoned by the power of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānabala); formations (saṅkhāra) by the power of vision (dassanabala); and the thirty-six wanderings of craving by the power of cultivation (bhāvanābala). Thus, craving is also abandoned in three ways. That state of being free from craving is the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu). This peace due to the breaking up of the body is the Nibbāna element without residue remaining (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Following along without being released from the burden is called proliferation (papañca). The Blessed One said: "One proliferates based on forms cognizable by the eye, whether past, future, or present." The Blessed One said: "Rādha, be without regard for past forms; do not delight in future forms; practice for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment of present forms." This is consistent with the Blessed One's previous and subsequent statements. Proliferation (papañca), formations (saṅkhāra), and the delighting in the past, future, and present—these have the same meaning. However, the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma in immeasurable ways through different terms, different letters, and different phrasings. Thus, by comparing sutta with sutta and connecting the previous with the subsequent, the sutta is explained. 

This connection (sandhi) between the previous and the subsequent is of four types: connection of meaning (attha-sandhi), connection of phrasing (byañjana-sandhi), connection of teaching (desanā-sandhi), and connection of explanation (niddesa-sandhi).
34:
Among those four, the connection of meaning (attha-sandhi) has six aspects: brief indication (saṅkāsanā), initial showing (pakāsanā), opening (vivaraṇā), analysis (vibhajanā), making clear (uttānīkammata), and designation (paññatti).

The connection of phrasing (byañjana-sandhi) has six aspects: letter (akkhara), term (pada), phrasing (byañjana), mode (ākāra), language (nirutti), and detailed analysis (niddesa).

The connection of teaching (desanā-sandhi) is as follows: A meditator who has entered meditative absorption (jhāna) does not meditate depending on the object of earth, yet he meditates. He does not meditate depending on the object of water, yet he meditates. He does not meditate depending on the object of fire, yet he meditates. He does not meditate depending on the object of air, yet he meditates. He does not meditate depending on the sphere of infinite space... (and so on)... the sphere of infinite consciousness... the sphere of nothingness... the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... this world... the world beyond, yet he meditates. Whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, thought, reflected upon, and repeatedly pondered by the mind in between these two worlds—he does not meditate depending on that either, yet he meditates. In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, such an Arahant meditating with a mind that is independent of any object cannot be known.

Just as the Evil Māra, searching for the consciousness of the clansman Godhika, could not know or see it. For he had transcended proliferation (papañca), and by abandoning craving, he no longer had the support of views (diṭṭhi). Just like the Elder Godhika, the Elder Vakkali meditating with an independent mind cannot be known in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans. This is the connection of teaching (desanā-sandhi).

Among those four, what is the connection of explanation (niddesa-sandhi)? Those with a dependent mind should be explained by way of the unwholesome side; those with an independent mind should be explained by way of the wholesome side. Those with a dependent mind should be explained by way of defilements (kilesa); those with an independent mind by way of purification (vodāna). Those with a dependent mind by way of the continuation of saṃsāra; those with an independent mind by way of the cessation of saṃsāra. Those with a dependent mind by way of craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā); those with an independent mind by way of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Those with a dependent mind by way of lack of shame (ahirika) and lack of moral dread (anottappa); those with an independent mind by way of shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa). Those with a dependent mind by way of lack of mindfulness (asati) and lack of clear comprehension (asampajañña); those with an independent mind by way of mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña). Those with a dependent mind
35:
Persons with a dependent mind should be indicated by improper cause and improper attention. Persons with an independent mind should be indicated by proper cause and proper attention.

Persons with a dependent mind should be indicated by laziness and being difficult to admonish. Persons with an independent mind should be indicated by the arousal of effort and being easy to admonish.

Persons with a dependent mind should be indicated by lack of faith and negligence. Persons with an independent mind should be indicated by faith and heedfulness.

Persons with a dependent mind should be indicated by hearing false teachings and lack of restraint. Persons with an independent mind should be indicated by hearing the true Dhamma and restraint.

Persons with a dependent mind should be indicated by covetousness and ill-will. Persons with an independent mind should be indicated by non-covetousness and non-ill-will.

Persons with a dependent mind should be indicated by the hindrances and things that lead to fetters. Persons with an independent mind should be indicated by the liberation of mind through dispassion from lust and the liberation by wisdom through dispassion from ignorance.

Persons with a dependent mind should be indicated by the view of annihilationism and the view of eternalism. Persons with an independent mind should be indicated by the Nibbāna element with residue of clinging and the Nibbāna element without residue of clinging. This is the junction of the indication (Niddesasanthi). Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "Neruttama-adhippāya" (The intention of the linguistic expression).

## The Mode of Conveying a Combined Formulation (Catubyūha Hāra) has been presented and applied.

## 7. Analysis of the Mode of Conveying a Reversal (Āvaṭṭahāra-vibhaṅga)

Among those sixteen modes, what is the Mode of Reversal? It is the statement: "In a single state (padaṭṭhāna)".

"Arouse yourselves, go forth,
Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching;
Destroy the army of Death,
As an elephant destroys a reed hut."

"Arouse yourselves, go forth" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of effort (viriya). "Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching" is the proximate cause of concentration (samādhi). "Destroy the army of Death, as an elephant destroys a reed hut" is the proximate cause of wisdom (paññā). "Arouse yourselves, go forth" is the proximate cause of the faculty of effort (viriyindriya). "Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching" is the proximate cause of the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya). "Destroy the army of Death, as an elephant destroys a reed hut" is the proximate cause of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). These proximate causes are called the teaching (desanā).

It occurs in the application of beings who do not apply themselves, and in the effort of beings who do apply themselves.

Among those beings, those who do not apply themselves do so because of negligence. That negligence is of two kinds: rooted in craving and rooted in ignorance. Among those two, the negligence rooted in ignorance...
36:
That which is veiled and obstructed by ignorance, such that one does not know what should be known—that "the five aggregates are of the nature of arising and passing away"—is negligence rooted in ignorance. Negligence rooted in craving is of three kinds: seeking unarisen wealth, and because of guarding arisen wealth and because of enjoying wealth, one falls into negligence. Thus, in the world, negligence is of four kinds: one kind due to ignorance and three kinds due to craving.

Among those types of negligence, the proximate cause of ignorance is the mental body (nāmakāya). The proximate cause of craving is the physical body (rūpakāya). Why is that? Because there is attachment to material existences and delusion regarding immaterial existences. Between those two, the physical body is the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). The four mental aggregates are the mental body (nāmakāya). By what clinging (upādāna) do these five aggregates become associated with clinging? They become associated with clinging through craving and ignorance.

Between those two, craving constitutes two types of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna) and clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna). Ignorance constitutes two types of clinging: clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna) and clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). The aggregates clung to by these four types of clinging are called Suffering (dukkha). The four types of clinging are called the Origin (samudaya). The five aggregates are Suffering (dukkha). The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding and abandoning of those five aggregates; for the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of the origin.

Those three kinds of craving-rooted negligence are: seeking unarisen wealth, guarding arisen wealth, and enjoying it. The restraint of the mind through the thorough penetration of that negligence and the suppression of negligence is called Calm (samatha).

How does that calm occur? It occurs when one knows the gratification of sensual pleasures as gratification, the danger as danger, the escape as escape, and when one knows the lowliness, the defilement, the purification of sensual pleasures, and the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma). In that knowing, whatever investigation and examination (wisdom) there is, is called Insight (vipassanā). These two qualities, calm and insight, reach the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā). When these two qualities are developed, the two qualities of craving and ignorance are abandoned. When these two qualities are abandoned, the four types of clinging cease.

With the cessation of clinging, existence (bhava) ceases. With the cessation of existence, birth (jāti) ceases. With the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus, there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. In this way, the two previously mentioned truths of Suffering and Origin, the Truth of the Path which is Calm and Insight, and Nibbāna which is the cessation of existence (the Truth of Cessation), constitute the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Arouse yourselves, go forth from the defilements."
37:
Just as a tree, though cut down, grows again if its root is firm and undisturbed, even so, as long as the latent tendency of craving (taṇhānusaya) is not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again.

This is the latent tendency of craving. What is that craving? It is the craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). The cause of this state is ignorance (avijjā). For craving for existence arises because of ignorance. These two defilements are craving and ignorance. They are the four types of clinging (upādāna). The aggregates accompanied by clinging that arise because of those four types of clinging are suffering (dukkha). The four types of clinging are the origin (samudaya). The five aggregates are suffering. The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding and abandoning of those five aggregates—for the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of the origin.

That by which one completely and well uproots the latent tendency of craving is tranquility (samatha). That by which one prevents ignorance, the cause of the latent tendency of craving, is insight (vipassanā). These two states, tranquility and insight, reach the fulfillment of mental development (bhāvanā). Therein, the fruit of tranquility is the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) through the fading away of lust (rāga). The fruit of insight is the liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti) through the fading away of ignorance. Thus, the two preceding truths are suffering and the origin; tranquility and insight are the path (magga); and the two liberations are cessation (nirodha). These are the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Just as [if the root]..."

"Not to do any evil, to cultivate the wholesome, to purify one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas."

What is called "all evil" (sabbapāpa) refers to the three types of misconduct: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. These are the ten unwholesome paths of action (akusala kammapatha): killing living beings (pāṇātipāta), taking what is not given (adinnādāna), sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra), false speech (musāvāda), malicious speech (pisuṇā vācā), harsh speech (pharusā vācā), idle chatter (samphappalāpa), covetousness (abhijjhā), ill will (byāpāda), and wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). These unwholesome paths of action are of two kinds: volitional action (cetanā-kamma) and mental-factor action (cetasika-kamma). Among them, killing living beings, malicious speech, and harsh speech originate from hatred (dosa). Taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech originate from greed (lobha). Idle chatter originates from delusion (moha). These seven causes are volitional action. Covetousness is the unwholesome root of greed. Ill will is the unwholesome root of hatred.
38:
Wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) exists; this is the wrong path. These three causes are mental-factor action (cetasika-kamma). Therefore, it is said: "volitional action and mental-factor action."

When the unwholesome roots reach the stage of exertion (payoga), they go into the four wrong courses (agati): through desire (chanda), hatred (dosa), fear (bhaya), and delusion (moha). Therein, going into a wrong course through desire originates from greed. Going into a wrong course through hatred originates from hatred. Going into a wrong course through fear and delusion originates from delusion. Therein, greed is abandoned by [meditation on] the foul (asubha). Hatred is abandoned by loving-kindness (mettā). Delusion is abandoned by wisdom (paññā). Likewise, greed is abandoned by equanimity (upekkhā). Hatred is abandoned by loving-kindness and compassion (karuṇā). Delusion reaches abandonment and cessation through appreciative joy (muditā). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Not to do any evil."

What is called "all evil" (sabbapāpa) are the eight wrong factors (micchatta): wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. These eight states are called "all evil." The non-doing, non-performance, and non-transgression of these eight wrong factors is called "not to do any evil."

When the eight wrong factors are abandoned, the eight right factors (sammatta) are fulfilled. The performance, doing, and fulfillment of these eight right factors is called "to cultivate the wholesome" (kusalassa upasampadā). "To purify one's own mind" shows the practice of developing the past path. When the mind is purified, the five aggregates become purified. Thus, the Blessed One said: "Monks, the holy life is lived under the Tathāgata for the sake of the purification of the mind." Purification is of two kinds: the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and the uprooting of the latent tendencies (anusaya). There are also two stages of purification: the stage of seeing (dassana-bhūmi) and the stage of development (bhāvanā-bhūmi). Therein, the five aggregates which one purifies through penetration are the truth of suffering. The hindrances and latent tendencies from which one purifies are the truth of the origin. The journey of seeing and development by which one purifies is the truth of the path. The Nibbāna which is purified is the truth of cessation. These are the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Not to do any evil."

Dhamma indeed protects the one who practices the Dhamma,
Just as a large umbrella protects in the rainy season.
This is the benefit of the Dhamma well-practiced:
The practitioner of the Dhamma does not go to a state of misery (duggati).
39:
Dhamma is of two kinds: restraint of the senses (indriya-saṃvara) and the Path (magga). What is called a woeful destination (duggati) is also of two kinds. In comparison with devas and humans, the four woeful planes are called duggati. In comparison with Nibbāna, however, all rebirths in a new existence are called duggati. Among these two, the practice of keeping the virtue of restraint unbroken and unblemished is a Dhamma well-practiced that protects one from the woeful planes. Thus, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there are two destinations for a virtuous person: the heavenly world and the human world."

In this way, at the village of Nāḷandā, the headman Asibandhakaputta approached the Blessed One and addressed him thus: "Venerable Sir, there are Brahmins of the West who carry water-pitchers, wear garlands of moss, descend into water, and tend the sacred fire. They supposedly cause one who has died and passed away to go to heaven, lead them well to heaven, and establish them in heaven. Venerable Sir, is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, able to do such a thing so that all the world, after the breakup of the body, after death, might arise in a happy destination, a heavenly world?"

"Headman, if that is so, I will question you in return on this matter. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, headman? Suppose there is a man here who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, engages in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill-will, and holds wrong view. Then a great crowd of people, having gathered and assembled, were to pray, praise, and circumambulate him with joined palms, saying: 'May this man, after the breakup of the body, after death, arise in a happy destination, a heavenly world!' What do you think, headman? Would that man, because of the prayers, praise, and circumambulation with joined palms of that great crowd, arise in a happy destination, a heavenly world, after the breakup of the body, after death?" To which he replied, "No, Venerable Sir."

"Headman, suppose a man were to throw a large stone slab into a deep lake. Then a great crowd of people, having gathered and assembled, were to pray, praise, and circumambulate it with joined palms, saying: 'O great stone slab, rise up! O great stone slab, float up! O great stone slab, float ashore!' What do you think, headman? Would that great stone slab, because of the prayers, praise, and circumambulation with joined palms of that great crowd, rise up, or float up, or float ashore?" To which he replied, "No, Venerable Sir (it would not)..."
40:
"No, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Just so, headman, a man who kills living beings... (pe)... and holds wrong view; even if a great crowd of people, having gathered and assembled, were to pray, praise, and circumambulate him with joined palms, saying: 'May this man, after the breakup of the body, after death, arise in a happy destination, a heavenly world!', yet that man, after the breakup of the body, after death, would only arise in a state of loss, a woeful destination, perdition, hell.

What do you think, headman? Suppose there is a man here who abstains from killing living beings, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from speaking falsehood, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, abstains from idle chatter, is not covetous, does not have a mind corrupted by destructive anger, and holds right view. Then a great crowd of people, having gathered and assembled, were to pray, praise, and circumambulate him with joined palms, saying: 'May this man, after the breakup of the body, after death, arise in a state of loss, a woeful destination, perdition, hell!' What do you think, headman? Would that man, because of the prayers, praise, and circumambulation with joined palms of that great crowd, arise in a state of loss, a woeful destination, perdition, hell, after the breakup of the body, after death?" To which he replied, "No, Venerable Sir."

"Headman, suppose a man were to take a pot of ghee or a pot of oil, descend into a deep lake, and break it. The gravel or shards therein would sink downwards. But the ghee or oil therein would float upwards. Then a great crowd of people, having gathered and assembled, were to pray, praise, and circumambulate it with joined palms, saying: 'O ghee and oil, sink! O ghee and oil, sink well! O ghee and oil, go downwards!' What do you think, headman? Would that ghee and oil, because of the prayers, praise, and circumambulation with joined palms of that great crowd, sink, or sink well, or go downwards?" To which he replied, "No, Venerable Sir."

"Just so, headman, a man who abstains from killing living beings... (pe)... and holds right view. Even if a great crowd of people, having gathered and assembled, were to pray: 'May this man...'
41:
"After the breakup of the body, after death, may he reach the plane of misery, the unhappy destination, the perdition, and hell"—even if such is said, that person, after the breakup of the body, after death, would only reach a happy destination, the heavenly world. Thus, the Dhamma well-practiced protects from the woeful planes. Among those practices, there is the sharpness and excellence of the Path that seeks Nibbāna; such Dhamma well-practiced protects from all types of rebirth. The Blessed One said thus:

"Therefore, with a well-guarded mind, with right intention as his domain, with right view placed in the forefront, knowing arising and passing away, the monk who overcomes sloth and torpor should abandon all unhappy destinations."

In that context, the causes of unhappy destinations are craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā); these are the four types of clinging (upādāna). The aggregates accompanied by clinging that arise because of these four types of clinging are called the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The four types of clinging are called the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). The five aggregates are suffering; the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding and abandoning of those five aggregates—for the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of the origin. Among craving and ignorance, the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of craving is the five physical faculties. The proximate cause of ignorance is the mind faculty (manindriya). One who guards the five physical faculties develops concentration (samādhi) and subdues craving. One who guards the mind faculty develops insight (vipassanā) and subdues ignorance. By subduing craving, two types of clinging are abandoned: clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna) and clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna). By subduing ignorance, two types of clinging are abandoned: clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna) and clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna). When the four types of clinging are abandoned, the two states of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) reach the fulfillment of development. This is called the holy life (brahmacariya).

In that context, the fruits of the holy life are the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala): the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the highest fruit, the fruit of arahantship. These are the four fruits of the holy life. Thus, there are the two preceding truths of suffering and origin; the path consisting of serenity, insight, and the holy life; and the fruits of the holy life and the unconditioned element, cessation (nirodha), which is the object of that path and fruit. These are the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "The Dhamma indeed protects."

In that context, that which protects through penetration is the Truth of Suffering. That from which it protects is the Truth of the Origin. That by which it protects is the Truth of the Path. That which it protects is the Truth of Cessation. These are the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "In a single proximate cause."

## The Mode of Conveying a Reversal is concluded.
42:
## 8. Analysis of the Mode of Conveying a Classification

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying a Classification? 'The classification of states (dhamma), proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna), and planes (bhūmi)' is the Mode of Conveying a Classification. Suttas are of two kinds: those dealing with subconscious inclinations (vāsanābhāgiya) and those dealing with penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). Practices (paṭipadā) are also of two kinds: those dealing with merit (puññabhāgiya) and those dealing with the fruit (phalabhāgiya). Virtues (sīla) are also of two kinds: virtue as restraint (saṃvara-sīla) and virtue as abandoning (pahāna-sīla). Among these, the Blessed One teaches a sutta dealing with subconscious inclinations by way of the practice dealing with merit. Established in virtue as restraint, one becomes a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārī) through that holy life. The Blessed One teaches a sutta dealing with penetration by way of the practice dealing with the fruit. Established in virtue as abandoning, one becomes a practitioner of the holy life through that holy life.

Among those two, what is a sutta dealing with subconscious inclinations? A sutta that shows talk on giving (dāna-kathā), talk on virtue (sīla-kathā), talk on heaven (sagga-kathā), the danger of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnava), and the benefit of renunciation (nekkhamma) is called a sutta dealing with subconscious inclinations.

Among those two, what is a sutta dealing with penetration? The manifestation of the Four Truths is called a sutta dealing with penetration. In a sutta dealing with subconscious inclinations, there is no specific understanding (pajānanā), no Path, and no Fruit. In a sutta dealing with penetration, however, there is specific understanding, the Path, and the Fruit. *Imāni cattāri suttāni.* These four suttas should be combined by way of the Mode of Conveying Logic (yutti-hāra) according to the extent of the plane of knowledge, having selected them by way of the teaching, fruit, virtue, holy life, and the Mode of Conveying Investigation (vicaya-hāra) in every respect.

Among those states, what are the shared (sādhāraṇa) states? There are two kinds: shared by name (nāma-sādhāraṇa) and shared by basis (vatthu-sādhāraṇa). Furthermore, other states of a similar nature should also be known as shared. For beings fixed in wrongness (micchatta-niyata) and beings who are not fixed (aniyata), the defilements to be abandoned by vision (dassana-pahātabba) are shared. For worldlings (puthujjana) and stream-enterers (sotāpanna), sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill will (byāpāda) are shared. For worldlings and non-returners (anāgāmī), the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana) are shared. Whatever mundane attainment (lokiya-samāpatti) a noble disciple enters into, all those are shared with those who are not free from lust (avītarāga). Shared states do not exceed their respective domains in relation to one another in this way. One who is endowed with these states does not transcend that nature of states. These are shared states.

Among those states, what are the unshared (asādhāraṇa) states? They should be sought based on the given teaching as: those in training (sekha), those beyond training (asekha), those capable of liberation (bhabba), and those incapable (abhabba). For the eighth person (one on the path to stream-entry) and the stream-enterer, although sensual lust and ill will are shared, their nature (dhammatā) is unshared (distinct). For the eighth person and the non-returner...
43:
The fetters belonging to the higher part (uddhambhāgiya saṃyojana) have a common nature and an uncommon nature (according to the individual). The name of all trainees (sekha) has a common nature and an uncommon nature. The name of all those who have entered the path (paṭipannaka) has a common nature and an uncommon nature. The trainee's virtue (sekhasīla) of all trainees has a common nature and an uncommon nature. Thus, one who contemplates the specific nature should seek [the uncommon nature] based on the inferior, the medium, and the superior.

The plane of vision (dassanabhūmi—Stream-entry) is the proximate cause for entering the fixed course of rightness (niyāma). The plane of development (bhāvanābhūmi—higher paths) is the proximate cause for attaining the higher fruits. The painful practice with sluggish intuition is the proximate cause for serenity (samatha). The pleasant practice with swift intuition is the proximate cause for insight (vipassanā). The ground for making merit consisting in giving (dānamaya puññakiriyavatthu) is the common proximate cause for the voice of another (parato ghosa). The ground for making merit consisting in virtue (sīlamaya puññakiriyavatthu) is the common proximate cause for wisdom consisting in reflection (cintāmayā paññā). The ground for making merit consisting in development (bhāvanāmaya puññakiriyavatthu) is the common proximate cause for wisdom consisting in development (bhāvanāmayā paññā).

The ground for making merit consisting in giving is the common proximate cause for the voice of another and wisdom consisting in learning (sutamayā paññā). The ground for making merit consisting in virtue is the common proximate cause for wisdom consisting in reflection and wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). The ground for making merit consisting in development is the common proximate cause for wisdom consisting in development and right view (sammādiṭṭhi).

Living in a suitable locality is the common proximate cause for seclusion and concentration (samādhi). Resorting to superior persons is the common proximate cause for the three unwavering faiths and serenity. Right self-direction is the common proximate cause for shame (hiri) and insight. Abandoning the unwholesome is the common proximate cause for the investigation of the wholesome and the faculty of concentration. The well-expounded nature of the Dhamma is the common proximate cause for planting the roots of the wholesome and the attainment of fruition. The good conduct of the Saṅgha is the common proximate cause for the excellence of the Saṅgha. The perfection of the Teacher is the common proximate cause for the faith of those without faith and the increase of faith for those who have faith. The unobstructed nature of the Pātimokkha is the common proximate cause for the restraint of ill-behaved persons and the comfortable living of well-behaved persons. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: 'The Dhamma and the proximate cause'.

## The Analysis of the Mode of Formulation (Vibhatti Hāra) is finished.
44:
## 9. Analysis of the Mode of Reversal (Parivattana-hāra-vibhaṅga)

Therein, what is the Mode of Reversal? It is 'wholesome and unwholesome states'. For a person with Right View (sammādiṭṭhi), wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is worn away (exhausted). And whatever numerous evil unwholesome states would arise with wrong view as condition, those are also worn away for him. And with Right View as condition, numerous wholesome states arise for him, and they reach fulfillment through development (bhāvanā).

For a person with Right Intention (sammāsaṅkappa), wrong intention (micchāsaṅkappa) is worn away. And whatever numerous evil unwholesome states would arise with wrong intention as condition, those are also worn away for him. And with Right Intention as condition, numerous wholesome states arise for him, and they reach fulfillment through development.

In this same way, for a person with Right Speech (sammāvācā), Right Action (sammākammanta), Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva), Right Effort (sammāvāyāma), Right Mindfulness (sammāsati), Right Concentration (sammāsamādhi), Right Liberation (sammāvimutta), and Right Knowledge and Vision of Liberation (sammāvimuttiñāṇadassana), the wrong knowledge and vision of liberation is worn away. And whatever numerous evil unwholesome states would arise with wrong knowledge and vision of liberation as condition, those are also worn away for him. And with Right Knowledge and Vision of Liberation as condition, numerous wholesome states arise for him, and they reach fulfillment through development.

Alternatively, for one who abstains from taking life, taking life is abandoned. For one who abstains from taking what is not given, stealing is abandoned. For one who leads a holy life, unchastity is abandoned. For one who speaks the truth, false speech is abandoned. For one who abstains from malicious speech, malicious speech is abandoned. For one who speaks gently, harsh speech is abandoned. For one who speaks at the right time, frivolous chatter is abandoned. For one who is not covetous, covetousness (abhijjhā) is abandoned. For one who is without ill-will, ill-will (byāpāda) is abandoned. For one with Right View, wrong view is abandoned.

Those who criticize the Noble Eightfold Path, to them come blameworthy accusations along with their reasons even in the present. Those venerable ones criticize the state of Right View. Because of that criticism, only those who have wrong view are worthy of their worship and praise. In this way, those venerable ones criticize Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration, Right Liberation, and Right Knowledge and Vision of Liberation. Because of that criticism, only those who have wrong knowledge and vision of liberation are worthy of their worship and praise.
45:
Certain people say: "Sensual pleasures should be enjoyed, should be consumed, should be indulged in, should be practiced, should be developed, should be cultivated." For them, abstaining from sensual pleasures is not the Dhamma (unrighteous).

Alternatively, some say: "The practice of self-mortification is the Dhamma." For them, the Dhamma that leads out [of suffering] is not the Dhamma (unrighteous). Indeed, some say: "The Dhamma is suffering." For them, the faultless and happy nature of the Dhamma is not the Dhamma (unrighteous). Furthermore, for a monk who dwells contemplating the foulness in all conditioned things (saṅkhāras), the perverted perception of beauty (subhasaññā) is abandoned. For a monk who dwells contemplating suffering, the perverted perception of happiness is abandoned. For a monk who dwells contemplating impermanence, the perverted perception of permanence is abandoned. For a monk who dwells contemplating non-self, the perverted perception of self is abandoned.

Moreover, whatever Dhamma one delights in with the mind or adheres to with a view, whatever is the opposite of that Dhamma, that opposite Dhamma becomes undesirable to him. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "Wholesome and unwholesome states (dhammas)."

## The Parivattana Hāra, which is the cleansing of rotation, has been extracted from the Pāḷi and compared.

## 10. Vevacana-hāra-vibhaṅga (Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms)

Among those eighteen modes (hāras), what is the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacana-hāra)? "Knowing many synonymous terms" is called the Mode of Conveying Synonyms. It is as when the Blessed One points out a single Dhamma by means of various different synonyms. As the Blessed One said:

"Longing (āsā), yearning (pihā), and great delight (abhinandanā),
Craving that moves and craving that stays fixed in many elements (dhātus),
Craving rooted in ignorance (moha) and craving that is manifoldly desired,
All these cravings have been eradicated by me, along with their roots."

Longing for a future benefit is called 'āsā'. This longing occurs in the manner: "The benefit will surely come to me." Longing for a present benefit is called 'pihā'. This longing occurs when one sees a superior object and thinks: "If only it were like this." Waiting for the fulfillment of a benefit is called 'abhinandanā'. One greatly delights in a dear relative, or greatly delights in a dear Dhamma, or greatly delights without aversion.
46: Anekadhātu (many elements) refers to: the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the flavor element, the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible element, the body-consciousness element; the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element. Sarā (inclining) means: some are inclined toward forms, some toward sounds, some toward odors, some toward flavors, some toward tangibles, and some toward mental objects. Among these six sense objects, the six types of grief based on the household life, the six types of joy based on the household life, the six types of grief based on renunciation, and the six types of joy based on renunciation—these twenty-four categories belong to the side of craving (taṇhā); these are synonyms for craving. The six types of equanimity based on the household life belong to the side of views (diṭṭhi). That same craving, in the form of yearning, is called delight in the Dhamma (dhammanandī), love for the Dhamma (dhammapema), and obsession with the Dhamma (dhammajjhosāna); these are synonyms for craving. Citta, mano, and viññāṇa are synonyms for the mind. Manindriya, manodhātu, manāyatana, and vijānanā (cognizing) are synonyms for the mind. Paññindriya (faculty of wisdom), paññābala (power of wisdom), adhipaññāsikkhā (training in higher wisdom), paññā (wisdom), paññākkhandha (aggregate of wisdom), dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga (enlightenment factor of investigation of states), ñāṇa (knowledge), sammādiṭṭhi (right view), tīraṇā (judgment), vipassanā (insight), knowledge of the Dhamma, knowledge of the meaning (attha), knowledge of the sequence (anvaya), knowledge of destruction (khaya), knowledge of non-arising (anuppāda), aññātaññassāmītindriya, aññindriya, aññātāvindriya, cakkhu (eye), vijjā (true knowledge), buddhi (intellect), bhūri (vastness), medhā (sagacity), āloka (light), or any other terms of this nature, are synonyms for wisdom (paññā). The five supramundane faculties are all wisdom. Furthermore, it is called faith (saddhā) in the sense of predominance, energy (vīriya) in the sense of exertion, mindfulness (sati) in the sense of non-forgetfulness, concentration (samādhi) in the sense of non-distraction, and wisdom (paññā) in the sense of full understanding. As stated in the recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati): For this reason, the Blessed One is called Arahaṃ, Sammāsambuddho, Vijjācaraṇasampanno, Sugato, Lokavidū, Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi, Satthā Devamanussānaṃ, Buddho, and Bhagavā. He has reached the fulfillment of the ten powers, attained fearlessness, acquired the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), abandoned the four yokes (yoga), transcended the wrong courses (agati), pulled out the arrow of defilements, is free from the wound of defilements, has trampled the thorns of defilements, has extinguished the obsession of defilements, has transcended bonds, has untied the knots (gantha), has transcended desires, has destroyed the darkness of ignorance, is endowed with the five eyes, has well transcended the worldly conditions (lokadhamma), is free from attraction and repulsion toward desirable and undesirable things, has reached Nibbāna which is beyond calculation, has transcended bonds, has laid down the battle [against Māra], is most excellent, is the bearer of the torch of wisdom, the maker of light, the maker of radiance, the dispeller of darkness, the abandoner of the enemy of defilements, possessed of immeasurable virtues, possessed of incomparable virtues, possessed of incalculable virtues, the maker of luster, the maker of brilliance...
47:
The Lord who illuminates with the light of the Dhamma and the Blessed One—these names are synonyms for Buddhānussati (recollection of the Buddha).

Just as it is stated in the Dhammānussati: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, worthy of being applied, to be personally realized by the wise.' This Dhamma crushes pride, removes the thirst of craving, uproots attachment, cuts off the round of rebirth, is void of defilements, is extremely rare to attain, is the destruction of craving, the fading of lust, the cessation of suffering, and the peaceful Nibbāna.

'The unconditioned (asaṅkhata), the endless (anata), the taintless (anāsava), and the truth (sacca), the further shore, the subtle, the very hard to see,
The undecaying, the stable, the undisintegrating, the invisible, the free from proliferation, the peaceful.

'The deathless, the sublime, the auspicious, the secure, the destruction of craving, the wonderful, the marvelous,
The free from calamity, the nature free from calamity—this Nibbāna is taught by the Sugata.

'The unborn, the unbecome, the free from distress, the unmade, the sorrowless, and also the free from grief,
The free from affliction, the nature free from affliction—this Nibbāna is taught by the Sugata.

'The profound, the hard to see, the superior, the unsurpassed,
The unequalled, the matchless, the foremost, and the best, it is called.

'The shelter, the protection, the harmless, the free from blemish, the faultless, and the stainless, it is called,
The island, the bliss, the immeasurable, the support, the possessionless, and the free from proliferation, it is said.'

These are the synonyms for Dhammānussati.
48:
Just as it is stated in the Saṅghānussati: The community of the Blessed One's disciples practices well, practices uprightly, practices for the sake of the right path, practices properly. These four pairs of men, the eight individuals—this community of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. They are perfect in virtue, perfect in concentration, perfect in wisdom, perfect in liberation, and perfect in the knowledge and vision of liberation. They are the essence of beings, the cream of beings, the ones who lift beings up (from saṃsāra), they have the unshakable quality of a pillar for beings, they are worthy of worship like fragrant flowers for beings, and they are worthy of worship by both devas and humans. These are the synonyms for Saṅghānussati.

Just as it is stated in the Sīlānussati: There are those virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unspotted, unmottled, noble, pleasing to the noble ones, leading to freedom, praised by the wise, untouched (by craving and views), and conducive to concentration. Virtue is an ornament because it beautifies the noble limbs. Virtue is a treasure because it overcomes all misfortune and ruin. Virtue is the art of archery because it enables one to pierce the Four Noble Truths without missing. Virtue is a shore because it is not to be transgressed. Virtue is wealth that cuts off poverty because it can sever suffering. Virtue is a mirror because it is the means for reflecting on the Dhamma. Virtue is a palace because it is the vantage point for observing the world with the eye of higher knowledge. Virtue revolves through all the planes of merit and has Nibbāna as its culmination. These are the synonyms for Sīlānussati.

Just as it is stated in the Cāgānussati: At such time as the noble disciple dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, responsive to requests, delighting in giving and sharing. These are the synonyms for Cāgānussati. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said, "Synonyms are many."

## The Mode of Synonyms is concluded.

## 11. Analysis of the Mode of Designation

Therein, what is the Mode of Designation (Paññatti-hāra)? "The Blessed One teaches one Dhamma through various designations"—this is the Mode of Designation. The teaching by way of natural discourse is the Designation of Deposition (Nikkhepa-paññatti). And what is the teaching by way of natural discourse? It is the Four Noble Truths. Just as the Blessed One said, "This is suffering," this designation is the Designation of Deposition for the five aggregates, the six elements, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the ten faculties.
49:
Monks, if there is lust, delight, and craving for the nutriment of edible food, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations. Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of future renewed existence. Where there is the production of future renewed existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Monks, where there is future birth, aging, and death, I say that is accompanied by sorrow, accompanied by anguish, and accompanied by despair.

If there is [lust, delight, and craving] for the nutriment of contact... [pe]... for the nutriment of mental volition. Monks, if there is lust, delight, and craving for the nutriment of consciousness, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations. Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of future renewed existence. Where there is the production of future renewed existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Monks, where there is future birth, aging, and death, I say that is accompanied by sorrow, accompanied by anguish, and accompanied by despair. This is the designation of the origin (pabhava-paññatti) of suffering and its origin.

Monks, if there is no lust, no delight, and no craving for the nutriment of edible food, consciousness is not established there and does not grow. Where consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of volitional formations. Where there is no growth of volitional formations, there is no production of future renewed existence. Where there is no production of future renewed existence, there is no future birth, aging, and death. Monks, where there is no future birth, aging, and death, I say that is without sorrow, without anguish, and without despair.

If there is no [lust, delight, and craving] for the nutriment of contact... [pe]... for the nutriment of mental volition. Monks, if there is no lust, no delight, and no craving for the nutriment of consciousness, consciousness is not established there and does not grow. Where consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of volitional formations. Where there is no growth of volitional formations, there is no production of future renewed existence. Where there is no production of future renewed existence, there is no future birth, aging, and death. Monks, where there is no future birth, aging, and death, I say that is without sorrow, without anguish, and without despair.
50:
This teaching is the designation of the full understanding (pariññā-paññatti) of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca); it is the designation of the abandoning (pahāna-paññatti) of the truth of origin (samudaya-sacca); it is the designation of the development (bhāvanā-paññatti) of the truth of the path (magga-sacca) leading to Nibbāna; it is the designation of the realization (sacchikiriya-paññatti) of the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca).

Monks, develop concentration (samādhi). Monks, a monk who is concentrated, diligent, discerning, and mindful, knows things as they really are. And what does he know as they really are? He knows as it really is that "the eye is impermanent." He knows as it really is that "forms are impermanent." He knows as it really is that "eye-consciousness is impermanent." He knows as it really is that "eye-contact is impermanent." Whatever feeling arises—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—conditioned by eye-contact, he knows as it really is that "that feeling is also impermanent."

He knows in the same way regarding the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body. He knows as it really is that "the mind is impermanent." He knows as it really is that "mental phenomena are impermanent." He knows as it really is that "mind-consciousness is impermanent." He knows as it really is that "mind-contact is impermanent." Whatever feeling arises—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—conditioned by mind-contact, he knows as it really is that "that feeling is also impermanent."

This teaching is the designation of the development (bhāvanā-paññatti) of the truth of the path (magga-sacca) leading to Nibbāna; it is the designation of the full understanding (pariññā-paññatti) of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca); it is the designation of the abandoning (pahāna-paññatti) of the truth of origin (samudaya-sacca); it is the designation of the realization (sacchikiriya-paññatti) of the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca).

Rādha, scatter form (rūpa), disperse it, destroy it, make it a plaything; practice for the destruction of craving (taṇhā) through wisdom. With the destruction of craving comes the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering comes Nibbāna. [He knows in the same way regarding] feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), volitional formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa)—scatter them, disperse them, destroy them, make them a plaything; practice for the destruction of craving through wisdom. With the destruction of craving comes the destruction of suffering; with the destruction of suffering comes Nibbāna.

This teaching is the designation of the cessation (nirodha-paññatti) of Nibbāna, which is called cessation; it is the designation of the disenchantment (nibbidā-paññatti) with gratification (assāda); it is the designation of the full understanding (pariññā-paññatti) of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca); it is the designation of the abandoning (pahāna-paññatti) of the truth of origin (samudaya-sacca); it is the designation of the development (bhāvanā-paññatti) of the truth of the path (magga-sacca); it is the designation of the realization (sacchikiriya-paññatti) of the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca).

That noble disciple knows as it really is: "This is the mass of suffering"; he knows as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; he knows as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he knows as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
51:
This is the designation of the penetration (paṭivedha-paññatti) of the truths; the designation of the establishment (nikkhepa-paññatti) in the ground of vision (dassana-bhūmi); the designation of the development (bhāvanā-paññatti) of the path; and the designation of the realization (sacchikiriya-paññatti) of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). That noble disciple knows as it really is: "These are the taints (āsava)"; he knows as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; he knows as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints"; he knows as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints"; he knows as it really is: "These taints cease without remainder."

This is the designation of the arising (uppāda-paññatti) of the knowledge of destruction [of defilements]; the designation of the occasion (okāsa-paññatti) for the knowledge of non-arising [of defilements]; the designation of the development (bhāvanā-paññatti) of the path; the designation of the full understanding (pariññā-paññatti) of suffering; the designation of the abandoning (pahāna-paññatti) of the origin; the designation of the undertaking (ārambha-paññatti) of the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya); the designation of the crushing (āsāṭana-paññatti) of the defilements; the designation of the establishment (nikkhepa-paññatti) in the ground of development (bhāvanā-bhūmi); and the designation of the total suppression (abhinighāta-paññatti) of evil, unwholesome states.

"This is suffering"—monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me the eye, there arose knowledge, there arose wisdom, there arose true knowledge, there arose light. "This is the origin of suffering"—monks, [similarly]... "This is the cessation of suffering"—monks, [similarly]... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me the eye, there arose knowledge, there arose wisdom, there arose true knowledge, there arose light.

This is the designation of the teaching (desanā-paññatti) of the truths; the designation of the establishment (nikkhepa-paññatti) in wisdom based on hearing (suta-maya-paññā); the designation of the realization (sacchikiriya-paññatti) of the faculty of "I shall know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya); and the designation of the setting in motion (pavattana-paññatti) of the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka).

"This truth of suffering should be fully understood"—monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me the eye, there arose knowledge, there arose wisdom, there arose true knowledge, there arose light. "This origin of suffering should be abandoned"—monks, [similarly]... "This cessation of suffering should be realized"—monks, [similarly]... "This practice leading to the cessation of suffering should be developed"—monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me the eye, there arose knowledge, there arose wisdom, there arose true knowledge, there arose light.

This is the designation of the development (bhāvanā-paññatti) of the path; the designation of the establishment (nikkhepa-paññatti) in wisdom based on reflection (cintā-maya-paññā); and the designation of the realization (sacchikiriya-paññatti) of the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya).
52:
Monks, 'This Noble Truth of Suffering has been fully understood'—thus, in things unheard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose in me. Monks, 'This Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering has been abandoned'—thus [in things unheard before, vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light arose in me]. Monks, 'This Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering has been realized'—thus [in things unheard before, vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light arose in me]. Monks, 'This Noble Truth of the Path leading to Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering, has been developed'—thus, in things unheard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose in me. This teaching is the designation of development (bhāvanā-paññatti) for the Noble Truth of the Path. It is the designation of deposition (nikkhepa-paññatti) for the wisdom consisting in development by establishing it in the continuity of those to be led. It is the designation of realization (sacchikiriyā-paññatti) for the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya). It is the designation of setting in motion (pavattanā-paññatti) for the wheel of instruction which is the Dhamma.

The Blessed One, having known the measurable (tula)—the cycle of formations which is the cause of the birth-existence—and the immeasurable (atula)—Nibbāna—abandoned the formations that produce existence. Delighting in his own internal nature and being concentrated, he broke the round of defilements within himself like a coat of mail.

'Tula' means the element of formations (saṅkhāra-dhātu). 'Atula' means the element of Nibbāna (nibbāna-dhātu). This designation, 'Tulam-atulañca sambhavaṃ', is the designation of higher knowledge (abhiññā-paññatti) for all phenomena. It is the designation of deposition (nikkhepa-paññatti) for the discrimination of Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) in the continuity of those to be led. 'Bhava-saṅkhāram-avassaji muni' is the designation of relinquishment (pariccāga-paññatti) for the Noble Truth of the Origin. It is the designation of full understanding (pariññā-paññatti) for the Noble Truth of Suffering. 'Ajjhattarato samāhito' is the designation of development (bhāvanā-paññatti) for mindfulness directed to the body. It is the designation of stability (ṭhiti-paññatti) for one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). 'Abhindi kavacam-ivatta-sambhavaṃ' is the designation of non-rebirth (abhinibbida-paññatti) for the mind. It is the designation of grasping (upādāna-paññatti) for omniscience (sabbaññutā). It is the designation of breaking (padālana-paññatti) for the egg-shells of ignorance. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Tulam-atulañca sambhavaṃ'.

He who has seen suffering and the cause from which that suffering arises—how could that being incline towards sensual pleasures? Knowing that sensual pleasures are a bond that clings in the world, a mindful person should train in the trainings for the sake of removing those sensual pleasures.

'Yo dukkhaṃ' is the synonym designation (vevacana-paññatti) of the Noble Truth of Suffering and the designation of full understanding (pariññā-paññatti). 'Yato-nidānaṃ' is the designation of origin (pabhava-paññatti) of the Noble Truth of the Origin and the designation of abandoning (pahāna-paññatti). 'Addakkhi' is the synonym designation (vevacana-paññatti) of the eye of knowledge and the designation of penetration (paṭivedha-paññatti). 'Kāmesu so jantu kathaṃ nameyya' is the synonym designation (vevacana-paññatti) of craving for sensual pleasures and the designation of adherence (abhinivesa-paññatti). 'Kāmā hi loke saṅgoti ñatvā' is the designation of seeing (dassana-paññatti) sensual pleasures as an enemy. Sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals, like a piece of meat, like fire, like a precipice, and like snakes. Being mindful, it is the designation of reduction (apacaya-paññatti) for the sake of abandoning those sensual pleasures by destroying them, and mindfulness directed to the body...
53:
The teaching "They are mindful" is a designation of reduction (apacayapaññatti) for the sake of abandoning. It is a designation of placement (nikkhepapaññatti) of mindfulness directed to the body in one's own continuity. It is a designation of development (bhāvanāpaññatti) of the path. The teaching "One should train for removal" is a designation of penetration (paṭivedhapaññatti) regarding the removal of lust, hatred, and delusion. The word "Being" (jantū) is a designation of synonym (vevacanapaññatti) for a yogi. For when a yogi knows, "I am attached to sensual pleasures," he generates wholesome states so that sensual pleasures do not arise; he strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. This is a designation of effort (vāyāmapaññatti) for the attainment of what has not yet been attained. It is a designation of placement (nikkhepapaññatti) regarding non-contentment with mere limited [wholesome states] in one's own continuity. In that striving, the effort for the persistence of arisen wholesome states is a designation of heedfulness (appamādapaññatti) in development. It is a designation of placement (nikkhepapaññatti) of the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) in one's own continuity. It is a designation of guarding (ārakkhapaññatti) of wholesome states. It is a designation of stability (ṭhitipaññatti) in the training of higher mind (adhicittasikkhā). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "He who has seen suffering and the source from which it arises."

"The world is bound by delusion, appearing as if beautiful.
The fool is bound by acquisitions (upadhi), surrounded by darkness.
It appears as if without glory, but to one who sees (with wisdom), there is no impediment (kiñcana) whatsoever."

"The world is bound by delusion" is a teaching that is a designation of the perversions (vipallāsa). "Appearing as if beautiful" is a designation of the world's perverted nature. "The fool is bound by acquisitions" is a designation of origin (pabhavapaññatti) of those with evil desires, and a designation of function (kiccapaññatti) of the obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna). It is a designation of strength (balavapaññatti) of the defilements. It is a designation of growth (virūhanapaññatti) of the formations (saṅkhāra). "Surrounded by darkness" is a designation of the darkness of ignorance (avijjā) and a designation of synonym. "It appears as if without glory" is a designation of seeing (dassanapaññatti) of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) and a designation of placement (nikkhepapaññatti) of the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu). "To one who sees, there is nothing" is a designation of penetration (paṭivedhapaññatti) regarding the impediments of lust, hatred, and delusion of beings. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "The world is bound by delusion."

"There is, monks, the unborn, the unbecome, the unmade, the unconditioned (Nibbāna). Monks, if there were not this unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, then the escape from the born, become, made, and conditioned (saṅkhata) would not be known here. But because, monks, there is the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, therefore the escape from the born, become, made, and conditioned is known."

"Monks, if there were not this [Nibbāna]" is a teaching that is a designation of Nibbāna and a designation of synonym. "The escape from the born, become, made, and conditioned would not be known here" is a teaching that is a designation of synonym for the conditioned (saṅkhata).
54:
There is also a designation of induction (upanayanapaññatti). "But because, monks, there is the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned" is a designation of synonym (vevacanapaññatti) for Nibbāna and a designation of illumination (jotanapaññatti). "Therefore the escape from the born, become, made, and conditioned is known" is a designation of synonym for Nibbāna, a designation of leading out (niyyānikapaññatti) for the path, and a designation of escape (nissaraṇapaññatti) from Saṃsāra. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, if there were not this..." Thus, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "The Blessed One teaches a single Dhamma by means of various designations."

## The Mode of Conveying Designations is finished.

## 12. Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Entry (Otaraṇahāravibhanga)

Among those (sixteen modes), what is the Mode of Conveying Entry (Otaraṇahāra)? "That which is dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda)" is the Mode of Conveying Entry.

"Released above, below, and everywhere,
Not perceiving 'I am this';
Thus released, he has crossed the flood,
Never crossed before, for the sake of no further becoming."

"Above" refers to the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial realm (arūpadhātu). "Below" refers to the sensual realm (kāmadhātu). "Released everywhere" refers to the liberation of one beyond training (asekhavimutti) in the three realms. These five faculties of one beyond training are themselves the entry (otaraṇā) by means of these faculties.

These five faculties of one beyond training are themselves knowledge (vijjā). With the arising of knowledge, ignorance (avijjā) ceases. With the cessation of ignorance, formations (saṅkhāra) cease. With the cessation of formations, consciousness (viññāṇa) ceases. With the cessation of consciousness, mind-and-body (nāmarūpa) cease. With the cessation of mind-and-body, the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) cease. With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact (phassa) ceases. With the cessation of contact, feeling (vedanā) ceases. With the cessation of feeling, craving (taṇhā) ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging (upādāna) ceases. With the cessation of clinging, becoming (bhava) ceases. With the cessation of becoming, birth (jāti) ceases. With the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This is the entry (otaraṇā) by means of dependent origination.
55: Those same five faculties of one beyond training (asekha) are included in the three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom. This is the entry (otaraṇa) by way of the aggregates. Those same five faculties of one beyond training are included in formations. Those formations which are untainted and not part of the life-continuum are included in the Dhamma element. This is the entry by way of the elements. That Dhamma element is included in the Dhamma base, that base which is untainted and not part of the life-continuum. This is the entry by way of the bases. 'Not repeatedly viewing as "I am this"' is the total eradication of self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). That eradication is the liberation of one in training (sekha-vimutti). Those faculties are the same five faculties of one in training. This is the entry by way of the faculties. Those same five faculties of one in training are called knowledge (vijjā). With the arising of knowledge, ignorance (avijjā) ceases; with the cessation of ignorance, formations (saṅkhāra) cease. In this way, the entire dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) occurs. This is the entry by way of dependent origination. That same knowledge is the aggregate of wisdom. This is the entry by way of the aggregates. That same knowledge is included in formations. Those formations which are untainted and not part of the life-continuum are included in the Dhamma element. This is the entry by way of the elements. That Dhamma element is included in the Dhamma base, that base which is untainted and not part of the life-continuum. This is the entry by way of the bases. One who is liberated through the liberation of one in training and the liberation of one beyond training has crossed over the flood (ogha) of saṃsāra, which had never been crossed before, for the sake of non-becoming. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Above, below...'. 'For one who is dependent, there is agitation. For one who is independent, there is no agitation. When there is no agitation, there is tranquillity (passaddhi). When there is tranquillity, there is no inclination. When there is no inclination, there is no coming and going. When there is no coming and going, there is no passing away and reappearing. When there is no passing away and reappearing, there is no "here", no "beyond", nor "in between the two". This itself is the end of suffering.' Regarding 'nissitassa calitaṃ' (for one who is dependent, there is agitation): dependence (nissaya) is of two kinds: dependence on craving (taṇhā-nissaya) and dependence on view (diṭṭhi-nissaya). Therein, the volition (cetanā) of one who is lustful is the dependence on craving. The volition of one who is deluded is the dependence on view. Volition, however, is formations (saṅkhāra). Formations...
56: ...because of [formations] as a condition, consciousness arises; because of consciousness as a condition, name-and-form arises. In this way, the entire dependent origination should be known. This is the entry (otaraṇa) by way of dependent origination. Among those two types of persons, the feeling that arises for one who is intensely lustful is pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). The feeling that arises for one who is greatly deluded is neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā). These two feelings are called the aggregate of feeling. This is the entry by way of the aggregates. Among those feelings, pleasant feeling becomes two faculties: the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) and the faculty of joy (somanassindriya). Neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling is the faculty of equanimity (upekkhindriya). This is the entry by way of the faculties. Those same faculties are included in the aggregate of formations. Those formations which are the objects of taints and are the causes of becoming are counted in the Dhamma element. This is the entry by way of the elements. That Dhamma element is included in the Dhamma base. That base which is the object of taints and is the cause of becoming exists. This is the entry by way of the bases. 'For one who is independent, there is no agitation' means being independent of craving through the power of calm (samatha) or being independent of view through the power of insight (vipassanā). That which is insight is called knowledge (vijjā). With the arising of knowledge, ignorance ceases; with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases. In this way, the entire dependent origination should be known. This is the entry by way of dependent origination. That same insight is called the aggregate of wisdom. This is the entry by way of the aggregates. That same insight becomes two faculties: the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). This is the entry by way of the faculties. That same insight is included in formations. Those formations which are not the objects of taints and are not the causes of becoming are counted in the Dhamma element. This is the entry by way of the elements. That Dhamma element is included in the Dhamma base. That base which is not the object of taints and is not the cause of becoming exists. This is the entry by way of the bases. Regarding 'When there is tranquillity (passaddhi)': there are two kinds of tranquillity, bodily and mental. That which is bodily ease is called bodily tranquillity (kāya-passaddhi). That which is mental ease is called mental tranquillity (cetasika-passaddhi). One with a tranquil body experiences happiness; the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated; one who is concentrated knows according to reality; one who knows according to reality becomes disenchanted;
57:
One who knows according to reality becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there arises the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He understands: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.' Due to the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, that person no longer inclines towards forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects. By the destruction, fading away, cessation, giving up, and relinquishment of that form by which one describing the Tathāgata—whether standing or walking—might describe him, the Tathāgata is liberated from being reckoned as form. He does not come to [the view] 'exists', nor 'does not exist', nor 'both exists and does not exist', nor 'neither exists nor does not exist'. Rather, due to the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, and reaches only the designation 'extinguished' (nibbuto).

By whatever feeling... by whatever perception, by whatever formations, by whatever consciousness one describing the Tathāgata—whether standing or walking—might describe him, by the destruction, fading away, cessation, giving up, and relinquishment of that consciousness, the Tathāgata is liberated from being reckoned as consciousness. He does not come to [the view] 'exists', nor 'does not exist', nor 'both exists and does not exist', nor 'neither exists nor does not exist'. Rather, due to the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is deep, immeasurable, and unfathomable, and reaches only the designation 'extinguished' (nibbuto). 'Āgati' means coming to this life from another life. 'Gati' means the future life (the next existence). Such coming and going do not exist [for him]. 'Nevidha' (not here) refers to the six internal sense bases. 'Na huraṃ' (not beyond) refers to the six external sense bases. 'Na ubhayamantaraṃ' (not in between both) means not seeing a self in the phenomena that arise together with contact. 'This is the end of suffering' refers to dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). That dependent origination is of two kinds: mundane and supramundane. Among them, mundane dependent origination starts from formations conditioned by ignorance and goes up to aging and death. Supramundane dependent origination starts from the arising of non-remorse (avippaṭisāra) in a virtuous person and goes up to the knowledge: 'There is no more for this state of being.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'For one who is dependent, there is trembling; for one who is independent, there is no trembling... this absence of trembling is itself the end of suffering.'

Whatever sorrows or lamentations,
Whatever sorrows or lamentations,
And various forms of suffering in the world,
These arise dependent on the beloved;
When the beloved is absent, these do not arise.
58:
Because of that absence of the beloved, those for whom there is nothing beloved anywhere in the world are free from sorrow and are happy. Therefore, one who desires the state of Nibbāna, which is free from sorrow and free from the dust of defilements, should not make anything in the world beloved.
