'Whatever sorrows, lamentations, and many forms of suffering arise in the world; these sorrows etc. arise dependent on the beloved'—this teaching is painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). 'When the beloved is absent, these sorrows etc. do not arise'—this teaching is pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). Feeling is called the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). This inclusion is called entry by way of the aggregates (khandhehi otaraṇā).

With feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging and death arise. Thus, the arising of all these conditions should be understood. This inclusion is called entry by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādehi otaraṇā).

Among those feelings, pleasant feeling consists of two faculties: the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy. Painful feeling consists of two faculties: the faculty of pain and the faculty of grief. This inclusion is called entry by way of the faculties (indriyehi otaraṇā).

Those very faculties are included in formations. Those formations that are subject to taints and are factors of existence are reckoned in the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu). This inclusion is called entry by way of the elements (dhātūhi otaraṇā).

That element of mental objects is included in the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) which is subject to taints and is a factor of existence. This inclusion is called entry by way of the bases (āyatanehi otaraṇā).

Because of that absence of the beloved, those for whom there is nothing beloved anywhere in the world are free from sorrow and are happy. Therefore, one who desires the state of Nibbāna, which is free from sorrow and free from the dust of defilements, should not make anything in the world beloved.

This is the abandoning of craving. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; thus, the cessation of all these conditions should be understood. This inclusion is called entry by way of dependent origination.

That very abandoning of craving is called tranquility (samatha). That tranquility consists of two faculties: the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of concentration. This inclusion is called entry by way of the faculties.

That very tranquility is called the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). This inclusion is called entry by way of the aggregates.

That very tranquility is included in formations. Those formations that are taintless and are not factors of existence are reckoned in the element of mental objects. This inclusion is called entry by way of the elements.
59:
That element of phenomena (dhamma-dhātu) is included in the base of phenomena (dhammāyatana), which is a base that is taintless (anāsava) and is not a constituent of becoming (bhavaṅga). This inclusion is called 'inclusion by way of bases' (āyatanā otaraṇā). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Whatever sorrows..."

If that sensual pleasure is fulfilled for that being who desires it,
that mortal certainly becomes joyful in mind, having obtained what he wished for.
If those desired sensual pleasures for that being who is filled with desire and longing
should diminish and perish, he suffers like one pierced by an arrow.
He who avoids sensual pleasures as one avoids the head of a snake with his foot,
he, being mindful, overcomes this craving (visattikā) in the world.

In those verses, that state of being joyful in mind is called affection (anunaya). By the words "he suffers like one pierced by an arrow," this suffering is called aversion (paṭigha). Both affection and aversion belong to the side of craving (taṇhā), and for craving, the ten material bases are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). This is inclusion by way of bases.

Those ten material bases themselves are the material body (rūpakāya) associated with the mental (nāma); both together are called name-and-form (nāmarūpa). With name-and-form as condition, the six bases (saḷāyatana) arise; with the six bases as condition, contact (phassa) arises; with contact as condition, feeling (vedanā) arises; with feeling as condition, craving (taṇhā) arises; thus all should be understood. This is inclusion by way of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).

That same name-and-form is the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha); this is inclusion by way of aggregates. That same name-and-form is the eighteen elements (dhātu); this is inclusion by way of elements. In that name-and-form, whatever is the material body (rūpakāya), these are the five material faculties (rūpīni indriyāni). Whatever is the mental body (nāmakāya), these are the five immaterial faculties (arūpīni indriyāni). These are the ten faculties. This is inclusion by way of faculties.

In those verses, where it is said: "He who avoids sensual pleasures as one avoids the head of a snake with his foot, he, being mindful, overcomes this craving in the world"—this is the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (saupādisesa nibbānadhātu). This is inclusion by way of elements.

That same Nibbāna element with residue remaining is knowledge (vijjā). With the arising of knowledge, ignorance (avijjā) ceases; with the cessation of ignorance, formations (saṅkhāra) cease; and so on for all. This is inclusion by way of dependent origination.
60:
That very knowledge (vijjā) is called the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). This way of entry is the entry by way of aggregates (khandha). That very knowledge constitutes two faculties: the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya). This way of entry is the entry by way of faculties (indriya). That very knowledge is included within formations (saṅkhāra); those formations which are taintless (anāsava) and are not life-continuum (bhavanga) are included in the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu). This way of entry is the entry by way of elements (dhātu). That element of mental objects is included in the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana), which is a base that is taintless and not life-continuum. This way of entry is the entry by way of bases (āyatana). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "To one desiring the object of desire."

To this extent, dependent origination, faculties, aggregates, elements, and bases are converged and entered. In this way, dependent origination, faculties, aggregates, elements, and bases should be entered. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "And that which is dependent origination."

## The Mode of Conveyance of Landing (Niyutto Otaraṇo Hāro).

## 13. Analysis of the Mode of Conveyance of Clearing (Sodhana-hāra-vibhaṅga)

Among those modes of conveyance, what is the Mode of Conveyance of Clearing? It is the verse beginning with "When the question is answered." Just as the Venerable Ajita asked a question to the Blessed One in the Pārāyana:

"By what is the world enveloped? Why does it not shine?
What do you say is its smear? What is its great fear?"

"The world is enveloped by ignorance (avijjā), [O Ajita, said the Blessed One],
It does not shine because of doubt (vivicchā) and heedlessness (pamāda);
I say craving (jappā) is its smear; suffering (dukkha) is its great fear."

In the question "By what is the world enveloped?", the Blessed One clears the term (pada) with "The world is enveloped by ignorance," but not yet the initiation (ārambha). In the question "Why does it not shine?", the Blessed One clears the term with "It does not shine because of doubt and heedlessness," but not yet the initiation. In the question "What do you say is its smear?", the Blessed One clears the term with "I say craving is its smear," but not yet the initiation. In the question "What is its great fear?", in the statement "Suffering is its great fear," the initiation is purified. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "The world is enveloped by ignorance."
61:
The Venerable Ajita asked: "O Blessed One, the streams [of craving and so forth] flow everywhere. What is the restraint for these streams? Tell me the restraint of the streams. By what are the streams shut off?"

The Blessed One replied: "Ajita, whatever streams there are in the world, mindfulness is their restraint. I tell you the restraint of the streams; they are shut off by wisdom."

In the question, "The streams flow everywhere; what is the restraint for these streams?", the Blessed One cleanses the term (pada) with the answer, "Whatever streams there are in the world, mindfulness is their restraint," but not yet the beginning (ārambha). In the question, "Tell me the restraint of the streams; by what are the streams shut off?", the beginning is purified with the answer, "I tell you the restraint of the streams; they are shut off by wisdom." Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Whatever streams there are in the world," and so forth.

The Venerable Ajita asked: "O Blessed One, wisdom, mindfulness, and name-and-form—tell me, when asked, where does this cease?"

In that question, the Blessed One replied: "Ajita, I shall tell you the problem you have asked. Where name-and-form cease without remainder: by the cessation of consciousness, this [name-and-form] ceases here."

The beginning is purified. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "That problem which you asked," and so forth. A question where the beginning is thus purified is considered answered. If the beginning is not purified, the question is not yet answered. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said, "In the answered question."

## The Mode of Cleaning (Sodhana Hāra) is combined.

## 14. Analysis of the Mode of Formulation (Adhiṭṭhāna Hāra)

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Formulation? It is said: "Those states which are indicated by way of unity and also by way of diversity." Those states which are indicated there should be maintained as they are indicated.
62:
"Dukkha" (Suffering) is unity. What is dukkha? Birth (jāti) is suffering, aging (jarā) is suffering, sickness (byādhi) is suffering, death (maraṇa) is suffering, association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. Form (rūpa) is suffering, feeling (vedanā) is suffering, perception (saññā) is suffering, mental formations (saṅkhāra) are suffering, consciousness (viññāṇa) is suffering. This is diversity.

"Dukkha-samudaya" (Origin of Suffering) is unity. What is the origin of suffering? It is that craving (taṇhā) which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; namely, craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). This is diversity.

"Dukkha-nirodha" (Cessation of Suffering) is unity. What is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, its giving up, relinquishment, release, and non-attachment. This is diversity.

"Dukkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadā" (The Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering) is unity. What is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; namely, Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. This is diversity.

"Magga" (Path) is unity. What is the path? The path leading to hell, the path leading to the animal realm, the path leading to the realm of ghosts, the path leading to the realm of asuras, the path leading to the heavenly world, the path leading to the human world, and the path leading to Nibbāna. This is diversity.

"Nirodha" (Cessation) is unity. What is cessation? Cessation through reflection, cessation not through reflection, cessation of affection, cessation of aversion, cessation of conceit, cessation of disparaging, cessation of domineering, cessation of envy, cessation of stinginess, and the cessation of all defilements. This is diversity.

"Rūpa" (Form) is unity. What is form? The form which is the collection of the four great elements and the designation of derived form based on the four great elements. What are the four great elements? The earth element (pathavī), the water element (āpo), the fire element (tejo), and the air element (vāyo).

One grasps the elements in two ways: in brief and in detail. How does one grasp the elements in detail? By twenty aspects (one grasps the earth element). In this body, there are: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, gorge, dung, and the brain in the head.
63:
One grasps the earth element in detail; one grasps the water element in detail by way of twelve aspects; one grasps the fire element in detail by way of four aspects; one grasps the air element in detail by way of six aspects.

What are the twenty aspects by which one grasps the earth element in detail? In this body, there are: head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, gorge, dung, and the brain in the head. By these twenty aspects, one grasps the earth element in detail.

What are the twelve aspects by which one grasps the water element in detail? In this body, there are: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine. By these twelve aspects, one grasps the water element in detail.

What are the four aspects by which one grasps the fire element in detail? That by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested. By these four aspects, one grasps the fire element in detail.

What are the six aspects by which one grasps the air element in detail? Up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds coursing through the limbs, out-breath, and in-breath. By these six aspects, one grasps the air element in detail.

Thus, while characterizing, weighing, investigating, penetrating, and reviewing the elements in detail by way of these forty-two aspects according to their nature, one does not see any body or part of the body that is fit to be grasped. Just as a person investigating a cesspool would not see anything fit to be grasped; just as a person investigating a rubbish heap would not see anything fit to be grasped; just as a person investigating a privy would not see anything fit to be grasped; just as a person investigating a cemetery would not see anything fit to be grasped. In the same way, by way of these forty-two aspects, thus in detail the elements...
64:
...while characterizing, weighing, thoroughly investigating, penetrating, and reviewing [the elements] according to their nature, one no longer sees any body or part of the body that is fit to be grasped.

Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Whatever earth element there is, whether internal or external, it is just the earth element. That should be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Having seen it thus as it actually is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the earth element." Whatever water element there is, whether internal or external... (and so on) ...Whatever fire element there is, whether internal or external... (and so on) ...Whatever air element there is, whether internal or external, it is just the air element. That should be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Having seen it thus as it actually is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the air element. This is the distinction [of the elements].

"Ignorance" (avijjā) is a single state [in general]. Therein, what is ignorance? It is non-knowledge of suffering, non-knowledge of the origin of suffering, non-knowledge of the cessation of suffering, non-knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, non-knowledge of the past, non-knowledge of the future, non-knowledge of both the past and the future, and non-knowledge of states dependently arisen through specific conditionality. Such non-knowledge, non-seeing, non-realization, non-awakening, non-enlightenment, non-penetration, non-discernment, non-comprehension, non-scrutiny, non-investigation, non-perception, lack of sagacity, foolishness, lack of clear comprehension, delusion, intense delusion, utter delusion, ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the barrier of ignorance, delusion, the root of unwholesomeness. This is the distinction [of ignorance].

"Knowledge" (vijjā) is a single state [in general]. Therein, what is knowledge? It is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the past, knowledge of the future, knowledge of both the past and the future, and knowledge of states dependently arisen through specific conditionality. Such wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of states, discernment, comprehension, scrutiny, sagacity, proficiency, subtlety, clarity of exposition, reflection, examination, breadth of wisdom, quickness of wisdom, guiding wisdom, insight, clear comprehension, the goad of wisdom, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom...
65:
The light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the illumination of wisdom, the treasure of wisdom, non-delusion, the investigation of the [Four Noble] Truths, right view, the enlightenment factor of investigation of states, a factor of the path, that which is included in the Noble Path. This is diversity (vemattatā).

"Attainment" (samāpatti) is unity (ekattatā). Therein, what is attainment? Perception attainment, non-perception attainment, the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the attainment of the disappearance of perception, and the attainment of cessation. This is diversity.

"Meditator" (jhāyī) is unity. Therein, who is a meditator? There is the meditator who is a trainee (sekha), the meditator who is beyond training (asekha), the meditator who is neither trainee nor beyond training, the meditator like a thoroughbred, the meditator like a difficult-to-train horse, the meditator dominated by views, the meditator dominated by craving, and the meditator dominated by wisdom. This is diversity.

"Concentration" (samādhi) is unity. Therein, what is concentration? Concentration with defilements, concentration without defilements, concentration with enmity, concentration without enmity, concentration with ill-will, concentration without ill-will, concentration with rapture, concentration without rapture, concentration with carnal motives, concentration without carnal motives, concentration with effort (sasaṅkhāra), concentration without effort (asaṅkhāra), concentration developed on one side, concentration developed on both sides, concentration with development developed from both sides, concentration with initial and sustained thought, concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only, concentration without initial and sustained thought, concentration partaking of decline, concentration partaking of stability, concentration partaking of distinction, concentration partaking of penetration, mundane concentration, supramundane concentration, wrong concentration, and right concentration. This is diversity.

"Practice" (paṭipadā) is unity. Therein, what is practice? The practice that is intense (like a cow), the practice of self-torment, the middle practice, the intolerant practice, the tolerant practice, the calm practice, the taming practice, the painful practice with slow direct-knowledge, the painful practice with quick direct-knowledge, the pleasant practice with slow direct-knowledge, and the pleasant practice with quick direct-knowledge. This is diversity.

"Body" (kāya) is unity. Therein, what is the body? The mental body (nāma-kāya) and the form body (rūpa-kāya). Therein, what is the form body? Hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, gorge, dung, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat...
66:
...fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, urine, and brain—this is the form body. The mental body consists of feeling, perception, volition, consciousness, contact, and attention—this is the mental body. This is diversity (vemattatā).

In this way, whatever state is similar in nature to another state, that state becomes one with that state through unity (ekattatā). By whatever characteristic it is different, by that it reaches diversity (vemattatā). Thus, when a question is asked in a Sutta, a prose exposition (veyyākaraṇa), or a verse, it should be investigated: "Is the question asked in terms of unity or in terms of diversity?" If asked in terms of unity, it should be answered in terms of unity. If asked in terms of diversity, it should be answered in terms of diversity. If asked in terms of persons (sattādhiṭṭhāna), it should be answered in terms of persons. If asked in terms of phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), it should be answered in terms of phenomena. In whatever way it is asked, in that way it should be answered. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "States in terms of unity."

## The Mode of Conveying a Terms of Reference (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra) is finished.

## 15. Parikkhāra-hāra-vibhaṅga (Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Equipment)

Among those modes, what is the Mode of Conveying Equipment (Parikkhāra-hāra)? It is the mode: "Those states which generate a state."

Whatever state generates another state, that is the equipment (parikkhāra) of that [resultant] state. What is the characteristic of equipment? Equipment has the characteristic of generating (janaka). Two states generate [results]: root cause (hetu) and condition (paccaya). Among these, what is the characteristic of root cause, and what is the characteristic of condition? Root cause has the characteristic of being specific (asādhāraṇa), and condition has the characteristic of being general (sādhāraṇa). For example, how? Just as for the arising of a sprout, the seed is the specific cause (hetu), while the earth and water are general causes (paccaya). For the sprout, earth and water are the conditions, and the nature of the seed is the root cause. Or, just as when fresh milk is put in a pot and becomes curd, there is no simultaneous existence of the fresh milk and the curd. In the same way, there is no simultaneous existence of the root cause and the condition.

This Saṃsāra arises with root causes and conditions. As it was said: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises," and so on for the entire Dependent Origination. Thus, the root cause of ignorance is ignorance itself, and the condition is unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). Preceding ignorance is the root cause for subsequent ignorance. Among those preceding and subsequent ignorances...
67:
Ignorance that arises previously is called the latent tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya); ignorance that arises subsequently is called the obsession of ignorance (avijjāpariyuṭṭhāna). The previous latent tendency of ignorance is the cause for the growth of the subsequent obsession of ignorance, acting as an immediate cause (samanantara-hetu) like a seed and its sprout. Just as when a fruit is produced, the seed is the cause of that fruit by way of being a successive cause (parampara-hetu). There are two kinds of causes: the immediate cause and the successive cause; likewise, in the case of ignorance, there are also two kinds of causes: the immediate cause and the successive cause.

Alternatively, the lamp-dish, the wick, and the oil are the supporting conditions (paccaya) for the lamp, but they are not the intrinsic cause (hetu). This is because it is impossible to light the lamp-dish, the wick, and the oil as a lamp without fire. Only the fire, which shares the same nature as the light, is the intrinsic cause (hetu). Thus, the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is the cause (hetu), while the external nature (parabhāva) is the condition (paccaya). That which is internal (ajjhattika) is the cause; that which is external (bāhira) is the condition. The producer (janaka) is the cause; the supporter (pariggāhaka) is the condition. The specific (asādhāraṇa) is the cause; the general (sādhāraṇa) is the condition.

The meaning of non-interruption is the meaning of continuity (santati). The meaning of production (nibbatti) through a cause is the meaning of fruit (phala). The meaning of linking (paṭisandhi) is the meaning of renewed existence (punabbhava). The meaning of obstruction (palibodha) is the meaning of obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna). The meaning of non-eradication (asamugghāta) is the meaning of latent tendency (anusaya). The meaning of non-penetration (asampaṭivedha) is the meaning of ignorance (avijjā). The meaning of being unrecognized (apariññāta) is the meaning of the seed (bīja) of consciousness. Where there is non-interruption, there is continuity; where there is continuity, there is production; where there is production, there is fruit; where there is fruit, there is linking; where there is linking, there is renewed existence; where there is renewed existence, there is obstruction; where there is obstruction, there is obsession; where there is obsession, there is non-eradication; where there is non-eradication, there is latent tendency; where there is latent tendency, there is non-penetration; where there is non-penetration, there is ignorance; where there is ignorance, the consciousness accompanied by taints (āsava) is unrecognized; where the consciousness accompanied by taints is unrecognized, there is the meaning of the seed.

The aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) is the condition for the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha); the aggregate of concentration is the condition for the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha); the aggregate of wisdom is the condition for the aggregate of liberation (vimuttikkhandha); the aggregate of liberation is the condition for the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha). Knowing the landing place (titthaññutā) is the condition for knowing the drink (pītaññutā); knowing the drink is the condition for knowing the reach (pattaññutā); knowing the reach is the condition for knowing oneself (attaññutā).

Alternatively, eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye-sensitivity and visible forms. In that process, the eye is the cause by way of being predominant (adhipati-paccaya); visible forms are the cause by way of being the object (ārammaṇa-paccaya). Light is the cause by way of being the support (sannissaya); attention (manasikāra) is the intrinsic cause (sabhāva-hetu).
68:
Volitional formations (saṅkhāra) are the condition for consciousness (viññāṇa), and their own intrinsic nature is the cause (hetu). Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. The six sense bases are the condition for contact (phassa), and their intrinsic nature is the cause. Contact is the condition for feeling (vedanā), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Feeling is the condition for craving (taṇhā), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Craving is the condition for clinging (upādāna), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Clinging is the condition for existence (bhava), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Existence is the condition for birth (jāti), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Birth is the condition for aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Aging and death are the condition for sorrow (soka), and their intrinsic nature is the cause. Sorrow is the condition for lamentation (parideva), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Lamentation is the condition for pain (dukkha), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Pain is the condition for grief (domanassa), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Grief is the condition for despair (upāyāsa), and its intrinsic nature is the cause. Thus, all such various and indefinite decisive support conditions (upanissaya) are called requisites (parikkhāra) because they successively produce their respective effects. Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "Those states which generate a certain state [through successive causal efficacy]."

## The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra) is concluded.
## 16. Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Induction (Samāropana-hāra)
Among those various modes of conveying, what is induction (samāropana)? It is the induction stated as: "Which states have which roots, and which are declared by the Sage to have the same meaning."

In a single proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), as many other proximate causes as are included must all be inducted. It is like in the Mode of Conveying the Rotation (Āvatta-hāra), where many proximate causes are included. In this Mode of Conveying Induction, there are four types of induction: proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), synonyms (vevacana), development (bhāvanā), and abandoning (pahāna).

Among these four, what is induction by way of proximate cause?

"Not doing any evil,
Fulfillment of the wholesome,
Purifying one's own mind—
This is the teaching of the Buddhas."

What is the proximate cause of that teaching? It is the three types of right conduct: bodily right conduct, verbal right conduct, and mental right conduct. These three types of right conduct are the proximate causes of the Dispensation. Among these three, bodily right conduct and verbal right conduct are called the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). In mental right conduct, non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) and non-ill will (avyāpāda) are called the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). Right view (sammādiṭṭhi) is called the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). This is the proximate cause. Among those states...
69:
The aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration are called tranquillity (samatha); the aggregate of wisdom is called insight (vipassanā). This is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). Among these, the fruit of tranquillity is the liberation of mind (ceto-vimutti) through the fading away of lust, and the fruit of insight is the liberation by wisdom (paññā-vimutti) through the fading away of ignorance. This also is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

The forest (vana) is the proximate cause of the undergrowth (vanatha). What is the forest? What is the undergrowth? The forest refers to the five cords of sensual pleasure, and craving is called the undergrowth. This is the proximate cause. The forest is the grasping of signs (nimittaggāha) such as "woman" or "man." The undergrowth is the grasping of details (anubyañjanaggāha) of various limbs and parts, such as "Ah, the eye! Ah, the ear! Ah, the nose! Ah, the tongue! Ah, the body!" This is the proximate cause. The forest refers to the six internal and external bases that are not fully understood; the fetter that arises depending on both is called the undergrowth. This is the proximate cause. The forest is the latent tendency (anusaya), and the undergrowth is the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna). This is the proximate cause. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Having cut down the forest and the undergrowth." This is the presentation by proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna-samāropanā).

Among those, what is the presentation by synonyms (vevacana-samāropanā)? The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the fruit of one in training (sekkhaphala); the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the fruit of one beyond training (asekkhaphala). This is a synonym. The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala); the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the highest fruit, the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). This is a synonym. The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is the transcending of the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu); the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the transcending of the three elements of existence (tedhātu). This is a synonym. The faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the training in higher wisdom, the aggregate of wisdom, the enlightenment factor of investigation of states, the enlightenment factor of equanimity, knowledge, right view, investigation, examination, moral shame, insight, and knowledge of dhammas—all these are synonyms [of wisdom]. This is the presentation by synonyms.

Among those, what is the presentation by development (bhāvanā-samāropanā)? It is as the Blessed One said: "Therefore, monk, dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and grief in the world." Being ardent (ātāpī) is the faculty of energy. Clearly comprehending (sampajāno) is the faculty of wisdom. Being mindful (satimā) is the faculty of mindfulness. Removing covetousness and grief in the world is the faculty of concentration. For one who dwells thus contemplating the body in the body, the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) reach fulfillment of development. For what reason? Because the four faculties have the same characteristic. When the four foundations of mindfulness are developed, the four right strivings (sammappadhāna) reach fulfillment of development. When the four right strivings are developed, the four bases of power (iddhipāda) reach fulfillment of development. When the four bases of power are developed, the five faculties (indriya) reach fulfillment of development. Thus...
70:
...all [the factors of enlightenment reach the fulfillment of development]. For what reason? Because all the factors belonging to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhammā) have a single characteristic, namely the characteristic of leading out (niyyānika); because they have a single characteristic, they reach the fulfillment of development. This is the presentation by development (bhāvanā-samāropanā).

Among those, what is the presentation by abandoning (pahāna-samāropanā)? One who dwells contemplating the body in the body abandons the perversion (vipallāsa) of "beauty in the foul" (asubhe subhaṃ). For such a person, nutriment (physical nutriment) comes to be fully understood (pariññā). Through the clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna), one becomes one without clinging. One becomes detached from the yoke of sensual pleasure (kāmayoga). One is released from the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha). One becomes free from the taint of sensual pleasure (kāmāsava). One has crossed over the flood of sensual pleasure (kāmogha). One becomes free from the dart of lust (rāgasalla). The station of consciousness consisting of form (rūpūpikā viññāṇaṭṭhiti) comes to be fully understood. One's lust for the form element is abandoned. And one does not go to a wrong course through favoritism (chandāgati).

One who dwells contemplating feelings in feelings abandons the perversion of "pleasure in suffering." Contact as nutriment comes to be fully understood. Through the clinging to existence (bhavupādāna), one becomes one without clinging. One becomes detached from the yoke of existence (bhavayoga). One is released from the bodily tie of ill-will (byāpāda-kāyagantha). One becomes free from the taint of existence (bhavāsava). One has crossed over the flood of existence (bhavogha). One becomes free from the dart of hatred (dosasalla). The station of consciousness consisting of feeling comes to be fully understood. One's lust for the feeling element is abandoned. And one does not go to a wrong course through hatred (dosāgati).

One who dwells contemplating the mind in the mind abandons the perversion of "permanence in the impermanent." Consciousness as nutriment comes to be fully understood. Through the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), one becomes one without clinging. One becomes detached from the yoke of views (diṭṭhiyoga). One is released from the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsa-kāyagantha). One becomes free from the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava). One has crossed over the flood of views (diṭṭhogha). One becomes free from the dart of conceit (mānasalla). The station of consciousness consisting of perception comes to be fully understood. One's lust for the perception element is abandoned. And one does not go to a wrong course through fear (bhayāgati).

One who dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena abandons the perversion of "self in what is non-self." Mental volition as nutriment comes to be fully understood. Through the clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna), one becomes one without clinging. One becomes detached from the yoke of ignorance (avijjāyoga). One is released from the bodily tie of insistence that "This is the truth" (idamsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha). One becomes free from the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). One has crossed over the flood of ignorance (avijjogha). One becomes free from the dart of delusion (mohasalla)...
71:
For that person, the station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) established in formations (saṅkhāra) comes to be fully understood (pariññā); lust (rāga) for the element of formations (saṅkhāradhātu) is abandoned; and he does not go to a wrong course (agati) through delusion (moha). This is called attribution by way of abandoning (samāropanā).

Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said:
"Whatever states have whatever roots, and whatever are declared by the Sage to have the same meaning, those should be attributed; this is the Mode of Attribution (samāropana-hāra)."

## The Mode of Attribution (Samāropana-hāra) is concluded.

## The Analysis of the Modes (Hāra-vibhaṅga) is finished.

## 1. The Combination of the Mode of Teaching (Desanā-hāra-sampāta)

It has been said: "Having first looked at the sixteen modes with the eye of vision, and having summarized them with the 'Hook' (aṅkusa), one should explain the meaning of the Sutta by the three guidelines (naya)."

Where should the explanation (niddesa) of that verse be seen? It should be seen in the Combination of the Modes (hāra-sampāta). Among those combinations, what is the Combination of the Mode of Teaching (desanā-hāra-sampāta)?

"With an unguarded mind, and smitten by wrong view,
Overcome by sloth and torpor, one goes under the power of Māra."

What is taught by the phrase "with an unguarded mind"? It teaches that heedlessness (pamāda) is the path to death. "Smitten by wrong view" means when one sees "the permanent in the impermanent," that is called being smitten by wrong view. That is a perversion (vipallāsa). What is the characteristic of that perversion? It has the characteristic of misapprehending. What does that perversion distort? It distorts three states: perception (saññā), mind (citta), and view (diṭṭhi). Where does that perversion distort? It distorts in the four bases of selfhood (attabhāva-vatthu): one regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. In this same way, one regards feeling... perception... formations... consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
72:
Among those objects of perversion, form (rūpa) is the object of the first perversion, which considers 'the beautiful in the unbeautiful.' Feeling (vedanā) is the object of the second perversion, which considers 'the pleasurable in the painful.' Perception (saññā) and volitional formations (saṅkhāra) are the objects of the third perversion, which considers 'self in the non-self.' Consciousness (viññāṇa) is the object of the fourth perversion, which considers 'the permanent in the impermanent.' Two states are the defilements of the mind: craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā). A mind shrouded by craving is perverted by two perversions: 'the beautiful in the unbeautiful' and 'the pleasurable in the painful.' A mind shrouded by wrong view (diṭṭhi) is perverted by two perversions: 'the permanent in the impermanent' and 'self in the non-self.'

Among those perversions, that which is the perversion of view regards past form as self, regards past feeling... past perception, past volitional formations... past consciousness as self. Among those perversions, that which is the perversion of craving greatly delights in future form, greatly delights in future feeling... future perception, future volitional formations, and future consciousness. Two states are the corruptions (upakkilesa) of the mind: craving and ignorance. A mind that is purified from these states becomes pure. For those beings who are hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, who run and wander on—once to hell, once to the animal realm, once to the realm of hungry ghosts, once to the host of asuras, once to the heavens, and once to the human world—the first beginning cannot be known.

Regarding "thinamiddhābhibhūtena": 'Thina' (sloth) is the unhealthiness and unworkability of the mind; 'middha' (torpor) is the sluggishness of the physical body (kāya). "Vasaṃ mārassa gacchati" means falling under the power of the Māra of defilements (kilesamāra) and the Māra of death (sattamāra). One who thus falls under the power of Māra is shrouded by defilements and is headed towards saṃsāra. The Blessed One has taught these two truths: suffering (dukkha) and the origin (samudaya). The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for the full understanding and for the abandonment of these truths—for the full understanding of suffering and for the abandonment of the origin. That by which one fully understands and that by which one abandons is the path (magga). The abandonment of craving and ignorance is cessation (nirodha). These are the Four Noble Truths. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "With an unguarded mind." Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: "By way of gratification and danger."

## The Conjunction of the Mode of Conveyance of the Teaching is concluded.
73:
## 2. Vicayahārasampāta

Among those (modes), what is the combination of the investigation mode (vicayahārasampāta)? In that investigation mode, craving (taṇhā) is of two kinds: wholesome and unwholesome. Unwholesome craving leads to the round of rebirth (saṃsāra); wholesome craving is the craving for abandoning, which leads to the reduction of defilements. Conceit (māna) is also of two kinds: wholesome and unwholesome. That conceit by depending on which one abandons (further) conceit is called wholesome conceit. That conceit which produces suffering is called unwholesome conceit. Among those (two types of craving), there is the distress (domanassa) based on renunciation: 'When shall I realize and dwell in the attainment of that peaceful state (the fruit of the path) which the Noble Ones realize and dwell in?' Thus, longing (pihā) arises in him; because of that longing, distress arises. This craving of longing is wholesome and, due to the fading away of lust, is called liberation of mind (cetovimutti). Wholesome craving that has that (Arahantship) as its object, due to the fading away of ignorance, is called liberation by wisdom (paññāvimutti).

What is the investigation of that (liberation)? It is the eight path factors: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. Where should that (concentration) be observed? It should be observed in the fourth jhāna because of its excellence. Indeed, in the fourth jhāna, one develops a mind endowed with eight factors: purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability. In that (fourth jhāna), he attains eight qualities: the six supernormal powers (abhiññā) and two special distinctions. Because that mind is purified, it is bright. Because it is bright, it is unblemished. Because it is unblemished, it is free from defilements. Because it is free from defilements, it is malleable. Because it is malleable, it is wieldy. Because it is wieldy, it is well-established. Because it is well-established, it has attained imperturbability. Among those (eight factors), both blemishes (aṅgaṇa) and defilements (upakkilesa) belong to the side of craving. Wavering and the lack of steadiness of the mind belong to the side of views (diṭṭhi).

The four faculties—the faculty of pain, the faculty of grief, the faculty of pleasure, and the faculty of joy—cease in the fourth jhāna; for that person, the faculty of equanimity remains. That person attends to the higher attainment as peaceful. As he attends to the higher attainment as peaceful, the gross perception in the fourth jhāna remains, and the perception of resistance (paṭighasaññā) also remains. By the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'Space is infinite,' he realizes and dwells in the attainment of the sphere of infinite space. The designation of the perception of form, which leads to supernormal power, surmounts the perception of diversity, and for him, the perception of resistance comes to an end. Thus, for that person who is well-concentrated, the light of that concentration disappears, and the seeing of forms also disappears. That concentration is endowed with six factors...
74:
That concentration should be reviewed. 'In the whole world, my mind is free from covetousness; towards all beings, my mind is free from ill-will; my energy is aroused and exerted; my body is tranquil and not distressed; my mind is concentrated and not distracted; my mindfulness is established and not forgotten.' Among those states, the mind free from covetousness in the whole world, the mind free from ill-will towards all beings, the energy aroused and exerted, and the mind concentrated and not distracted—this is called calm (samatha). The body that is tranquil and not distressed—this is the requisite for concentration. The mindfulness that is established and not forgotten—this is called insight (vipassanā).

That concentration should be known in five ways. The knowledge and vision arises within himself: 'This concentration is pleasant in the present.' The knowledge and vision arises within himself: 'This concentration has a happy result in the future.' The knowledge and vision arises within himself: 'This concentration is noble and unworldly.' The knowledge and vision arises within himself: 'This concentration is practiced by superior men.' The knowledge and vision arises within himself: 'This concentration is peaceful, sublime, attained through tranquility, reached a state of unification, and is not attained by forced suppression.' Furthermore, the knowledge and vision arises within himself: 'I enter this attainment mindfully, and I emerge from it mindfully.' Among those five, the concentration that is pleasant in the present and the concentration that has a happy result in the future—this is called calm (samatha). The concentration that is noble and unworldly, the concentration practiced by superior men, the concentration that is peaceful, sublime, and does not require forced suppression, and the knowledge that 'I enter mindfully and emerge mindfully'—this is called insight (vipassanā).

That concentration should be known in five ways: pervasion of rapture (pīti), pervasion of happiness (sukha), pervasion of mind (ceto), pervasion of light (āloka), and the sign of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-nimitta). Among those five, the pervasion of rapture, the pervasion of happiness, and the pervasion of mind—this is called calm (samatha). The pervasion of light and the sign of reviewing—this is called insight (vipassanā).
75:
The ten kasina bases are the earth kasina, the water kasina, the fire kasina, the air kasina, the blue kasina, the yellow kasina, the red kasina, the white kasina, the space kasina, and the consciousness kasina. Among these ten, the eight kasinas including the earth kasina, the water kasina, and so forth, up to the white kasina, are called serenity (samatha). The space kasina and the consciousness kasina, these two are called insight (vipassanā). In this way, the entire Noble Path is taught according to various aspects; it should be integrated with serenity and insight according to those respective aspects. These serenity and insight are included within the three characteristics: impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anattā). When that person develops serenity and insight, he develops the three doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha). When he develops the three doors to liberation, he develops the three aggregates (khandha). When he develops the three aggregates, he develops the Noble Eightfold Path.

A person of lustful temperament (rāgacarita) exits [from saṃsāra] through the signless door to liberation (animitta-vimokkhamukha). While training in the higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), abandoning greed which is an unwholesome root, not approaching the contact that leads to pleasant feeling, fully understanding pleasant feeling, washing away the impurity of lust, shaking off the dust of lust, vomiting the poison of lust, extinguishing the fire of lust, pulling out the dart of lust, and untangling the tangle of lust, [he exits]. A person of hateful temperament (dosacarita) exits through the undirected door to liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkhamukha). While training in the higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), abandoning hatred which is an unwholesome root, not approaching the contact that leads to painful feeling, fully understanding painful feeling, washing away the impurity of hatred, shaking off the dust of hatred, vomiting the poison of hatred, extinguishing the fire of hatred, pulling out the dart of hatred, and untangling the tangle of hatred, [he exits]. A person of deluded temperament (mohacarita) exits through the emptiness door to liberation (suññata-vimokkhamukha). While training in the higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā), abandoning delusion which is an unwholesome root, not approaching the contact that leads to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, fully understanding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, washing away the impurity of delusion, shaking off the dust of delusion, vomiting the poison of delusion, extinguishing the fire of delusion, pulling out the dart of delusion, and untangling the tangle of delusion, [he exits].

Among those doors to liberation, the emptiness door to liberation is called the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha), the signless door to liberation is called the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), and the undirected door to liberation is called the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). When that person develops the three doors to liberation, he develops the three aggregates; when he develops the three aggregates, he develops the Noble Eightfold Path. In that path, Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood are called the aggregate of virtue, and that which...
76:
...Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma), Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati), and Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi) are called the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) and Right Intention (sammā-saṅkappa) are called the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha).

Among those aggregates, the aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration are serenity (samatha), and the aggregate of wisdom is insight (vipassanā). For one who develops serenity and insight, two things—body and mind—reach development. The practice leading to the cessation of existence, Nibbāna, consists of two factors: virtue and concentration. That monk becomes one with a developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, and developed wisdom. When the body is developed, two factors reach development: Right Action and Right Effort. When virtue is developed, two factors reach development: Right Speech and Right Livelihood. When the mind is developed, two factors reach development: Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration. When wisdom is developed, two factors reach development: Right View and Right Intention.

Among those factors, Right Action and Right Effort may be physical or they may be mental. Of these two, the part pertaining to the body reaches development when the body is developed. The part pertaining to the mind reaches development when the mind is developed. When that person develops serenity and insight, he reaches five kinds of attainment (adhigama): quick attainment, attainment through liberation [from defilements], great attainment, abundant attainment, and complete attainment. Among those five, quick attainment, great attainment, and abundant attainment occur through serenity. Attainment through liberation and complete attainment occur through insight.

The Teacher, the Blessed One, who possesses the ten powers and teaches these truths, does not mislead his disciples with his advice. The Blessed One advises in three ways: "Do this; do it by this means; doing this will be for your welfare and happiness." When thus advised and instructed, it is impossible that one who acts and practices according to that advice would not reach that stage [of liberation]. However, it is also impossible that one who is thus advised and instructed but does not fulfill the aggregate of virtue would reach that stage. There is only the possibility that one who is thus advised and instructed and fulfills the aggregate of virtue will reach that stage. There is no ground for anyone to reasonably charge the Fully Enlightened One, saying, "You have not yet fully realized these truths." For one who has exhausted all taints (āsava), there is no ground [to charge], "These taints are not yet exhausted"...
77:
It is impossible that this could happen. It is impossible that the Dhamma taught for someone's benefit would not lead that practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering. It is impossible that your disciple, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing properly, and living according to the Dhamma, would not realize a higher and more noble distinction than before.

It is impossible that one who indulges in qualities that are obstacles (to the paths and fruits) would not face obstacles. It is impossible that qualities which do not lead out of Saṃsāra would lead a practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering. It is possible that qualities which lead out of Saṃsāra would lead a practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering. It is impossible that your disciple, with residue remaining, would not reach the Nibbāna element without residue remaining.

It is impossible that a person possessed of right view (a Sotāpanna) would deprive his mother of life, or severely kill or harm her with hands or feet. It is possible that an ordinary person (a puthujjana) would deprive his mother of life, or severely kill or harm her with hands or feet. Likewise with his father, an Arahant, or a monk (it is impossible for a Sotāpanna, but possible for an ordinary person). It is impossible that a person possessed of right view would cause a schism in the Saṅgha or create a rift within the Saṅgha. It is possible that an ordinary person would cause a schism in the Saṅgha or create a rift within the Saṅgha. It is impossible that a person possessed of right view, with a malicious mind, would draw the blood of a Tathāgata, or with a malicious mind, would destroy a Stupa of a Tathāgata who has attained Parinibbāna. It is possible that an ordinary person, with a malicious mind, would draw the blood of a Tathāgata, or with a malicious mind, would destroy a Stupa of a Tathāgata who has attained Parinibbāna. It is impossible that a person possessed of right view would designate another teacher, even for the sake of his life. It is possible that an ordinary person would designate another teacher. It is impossible that a person possessed of right view would seek another recipient of offerings outside of this Dispensation. It is possible that an ordinary person would seek another recipient of offerings outside of this Dispensation. It is impossible that a person possessed of right view would believe in purification through superstitious omens. It is possible that an ordinary person would believe in purification through superstitious omens.

It is impossible that a woman would be a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti). It is possible that a man would be a Wheel-turning Monarch. It is impossible that a woman would be Sakka, the king of devas. It is possible that a man would be Sakka, the king of devas. It is impossible that a woman would be the wicked Mara. It is possible that a man would be the wicked Mara...
78:
...It is possible that a man would be the wicked Mara. It is impossible that a woman would be a Mahābrahmā; it is possible that a man would be a Mahābrahmā. It is impossible that a woman would be a Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; it is possible that a man would be a Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

It is impossible that two Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, would arise simultaneously in a single world system or teach the Dhamma together. It is possible that only a single Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, will arise in a single world system or teach the Dhamma.

It is impossible that the three types of misconduct (of body, speech, and mind) would result in desirable, pleasant, agreeable, and delightful consequences. It is possible that the three types of misconduct would result in undesirable, unpleasant, disagreeable, and painful consequences. It is impossible that the three types of good conduct would result in undesirable, unpleasant, disagreeable, and painful consequences. It is possible that the three types of good conduct would result in desirable, pleasant, agreeable, and delightful consequences.

It is impossible that a certain ascetic or brahmin who is a deceiver, a flatterer, or a fortune-teller, and who, being led by such deceit, flattery, and fortune-telling, without abandoning the five hindrances which defile the mind and weaken wisdom, and while living with unestablished mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness, without developing the seven factors of enlightenment, would realize the unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment. It is possible that a certain ascetic or brahmin who is free from all faults, and who, having abandoned the five hindrances which defile the mind and weaken wisdom, and while living with established mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, would realize the unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment. Whatever knowledge exists here regarding what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, in an unlimited way, this is called the Knowledge of the Possible and the Impossible (Ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa), the first Power of a Tathāgata.

Thus, all things that have reached the state of being possible or impossible are subject to exhaustion, subject to decay, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Some beings go to heaven, some go to the states of deprivation (hell), and some reach Nibbāna. Thus the Blessed One spoke.
79:
All beings will die, for life ends in death.
They will go according to their kamma, reaching the results of their meritorious and evil deeds.
Those of evil deeds go to hell, and those of meritorious deeds go to a happy destination.
And others, having developed the path, being free from taints (āsava), attain final Nibbāna (so the Blessed One said).

"All beings" refers to the Noble Ones (Ariyas), the non-noble ones (Anariyas), those included in the identity (sakkāya), and those who have transcended the identity. "Will die" means they will die through two types of death: slow death (dandha-maraṇa) and non-slow death (adandha-maraṇa). For those included in the identity, there is non-slow death; for those who have transcended the identity, there is slow death. "Life ends in death" means that due to the exhaustion of life and the cessation of the faculties (indriya), the end of life is indeed death. "They will go according to their kamma" refers to the fact of being the owner of one's own kamma (kammassakatā). "Reaching the results of their meritorious and evil deeds" refers to the seeing of the results of kamma and the non-separation from the results of kamma.

"Those of evil deeds go to hell" refers to unmeritorious volitional formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra). "Those of meritorious deeds go to a happy destination" means that those with meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) will go to a happy destination (sugati). "And others, having developed the path, being free from taints, attain final Nibbāna" refers to the transcending of all formations (saṅkhāra). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "All... [pe]... are free from taints."

The text "All beings will die, for life ends in death. They will go according to their kamma, reaching the results of their meritorious and evil deeds. Those of evil deeds go to hell" represents the harsh practice (āgāḷhā paṭipadā) and the burning practice (nijjhāmā paṭipadā). "And others, having developed the path, being free from taints, attain final Nibbāna" is the Middle Way (majjhimā paṭipadā). "All beings will die, for life ends in death; they will go according to their kamma, reaching the results of their meritorious and evil deeds; those of evil deeds go to hell" is defilement (saṃkilesa). In this way, it brings about the round of rebirth (saṃsāra). These three—"All beings will die... [pe]... those of evil deeds go to hell"—are the three rounds: the round of suffering (dukkha-vaṭṭa), the round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa), and the round of defilements (kilesa-vaṭṭa). "And others, having developed the path, being free from taints, attain final Nibbāna" is the cessation of the three rounds (vivaṭṭana). "All beings will die... [pe]... those of evil deeds go to hell" is the danger (ādīnava); "those of meritorious deeds go to a happy destination" is the gratification (assāda); and "others, having developed the path, being free from taints, attain final Nibbāna" is the escape (nissaraṇa). "All beings will die... [pe]... those of evil deeds go to hell" is cause and effect; the five aggregates are the effect, and craving (taṇhā) is the cause. "And others, having developed the path, being free from taints, attain final Nibbāna" is the path and the fruit (phala). "All beings will die, for life ends in death. They will go according to their kamma, reaching the results of their meritorious and evil deeds; those of evil deeds go to hell" is defilement. That defilement is of three kinds: defilement of craving (taṇhā-saṃkilesa), defilement of view (diṭṭhi-saṃkilesa), and defilement of misconduct (duccarita-saṃkilesa).
80:
Among those three (defilements), the defilement of craving (taṇhā-saṃkilesa) is shown by way of the three cravings: sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). Alternatively, it is shown by whatever object one is attached to; it is shown by that very object. Its expansion consists of the thirty-six wanderings of the net of craving. Among those (defilements), the defilement of views (diṭṭhi-saṃkilesa) is shown by way of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) and eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi). Alternatively, it is shown by whatever object one adheres to through the power of views, thinking, "This alone is the truth, all else is empty"; it is shown by that very object. Its expansion consists of the sixty-two types of views. Among those (defilements), the defilement of misconduct (duccarita-saṃkilesa) is shown by way of volitional action (cetanā-kamma) and mental action (cetasika-kamma). It is shown by way of the three types of misconduct: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. Its expansion consists of the ten unwholesome courses of action. The teaching that "others, having developed the path, attain Nibbāna, being free from taints" is called purification (vodāna).

That purification is of three kinds. The defilement of craving is purified by serenity (samatha); that serenity is the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). The defilement of views is purified by insight (vipassanā); that insight is the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). The defilement of misconduct is purified by good conduct (sucarita); that good conduct is the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).

"All beings will die, for life ends in death; they will go according to their kamma, experiencing the results of merit and evil; those of evil actions go to hell"—this teaching is the practice of demerit (apuññappaṭipadā). "Those of meritorious actions go to a happy destination"—this teaching is the practice of merit (puññappaṭipadā). "Others, having developed the path, attain Nibbāna, being free from taints"—this teaching is the practice of transcending both merit and evil (puññapāpasamatikkamappaṭipadā). Among those practices, these two practices—the practice of merit and the practice of demerit—constitute a single practice that leads to all [realms of] existence. One (the practice of demerit) leads to the planes of misery; one (the practice of merit) leads to the heavens. The practice that transcends both merit and evil is the practice that leads to that [Nibbāna].

There are three groups (rāsi): the group fixed in wrongness (micchattaniyata-rāsi), the group fixed in rightness (sammattaniyata-rāsi), and the unfixed group (aniyata-rāsi). Among those three, the group fixed in wrongness and the group fixed in rightness constitute a single practice leading to those respective [destinations]. Among those three, the unfixed group is the practice leading to all destinations. For what reason? If one obtains the [necessary] conditions, one might be reborn in hell; if one obtains the conditions, one might be reborn in the animal realm; if one obtains the conditions, one might be reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts; if one obtains the conditions, one might be reborn in the realm of asuras; if one obtains the conditions, one might be reborn in the realm of devas; if one obtains the conditions, one might be reborn in the human realm; if one obtains the conditions, one might attain Nibbāna. Therefore, this practice is the practice leading to all destinations. The knowledge here that is based on cause, based on occasion, and is without limitation, is called the knowledge of the practice leading to all destinations (sabbatthagāminī-paṭipadā-ñāṇa), which is the second Power of a Tathāgata (tathāgatabala).
81:
Thus, the practice leading to all destinations is the world of many elements (anekadhātu-loka); the practice leading to specific destinations is the world of diverse elements (nānādhātu-loka). Among those two, what is the world of many elements? They are the eye element, form element, eye-consciousness element; ear element, sound element, ear-consciousness element; nose element, odor element, nose-consciousness element; tongue element, flavor element, tongue-consciousness element; body element, tangible element, body-consciousness element; mind element, mental-object element, mind-consciousness element; earth element, water element, fire element, air element, space element, consciousness element, sense-desire element, ill-will element, cruelty element, renunciation element, non-ill-will element, non-cruelty element, suffering element, grief element, ignorance element, pleasure element, joy element, equanimity element, fine-material element, immaterial element, cessation element, formations element, and Nibbāna element. This is the world of many elements.

Among those two, what is the world of diverse elements? The eye element is one, the form element is another, the eye-consciousness element is another. Thus, all elements are distinct. The Nibbāna element is also distinct. The knowledge here that is based on cause, based on occasion, and is without limitation, is called the knowledge of many elements and diverse elements (anekadhātu-nānādhātu-ñāṇa), which is the third Power of a Tathāgata.

Thus, in the world of many elements and diverse elements, beings are inclined toward whatever element they desire; they resolve upon and adhere to that very element. Some are inclined toward forms, some toward sounds, some toward odors, some toward flavors, some toward tangibles, some toward mental objects, some toward women, some toward men, some toward generosity, some toward the base, some toward the sublime, some toward the state of devas, some toward the state of humans, and some toward Nibbāna. In this diversity of inclinations of beings, the knowledge that knows "this being is teachable, this being is not teachable, this one is headed for heaven, this one is headed for a state of misery" based on cause, based on occasion, and without limitation, is called the knowledge of the diverse inclinations of beings (sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikatā-ñāṇa), which is the fourth Power of a Tathāgata.

Thus, as they are inclined, so do they undertake their respective kammas. They undertake six kinds of kamma: some by the power of greed, some by the power of hatred, some by the power of delusion, some by the power of faith, some by the power of energy, and some by the power of wisdom. When that kamma is analyzed, there are two kinds: that which leads to the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) and that which leads to Nibbāna.

Among those six kinds of kamma, whatever kamma one performs by the power of greed, hatred, and delusion, this kamma is dark and has dark results. Among those six kinds of kamma, whatever kamma one performs by the power of faith, this kamma is...
82:
White kamma has white results. Among those six types of kamma, the kamma performed through the power of greed, the power of hatred, the power of delusion, and the power of faith is both black and white, with black and white results. Among those kammas, the kamma performed through the power of energy and the power of wisdom—this supramundane wholesome kamma—is neither black nor white, with neither black nor white results; being the most excellent of kammas and the supreme kamma, it leads to the destruction of kammas.

There are four ways of undertaking kamma: there is the undertaking of kamma that is pleasant in the present but has painful results in the future; there is the undertaking of kamma that is painful in the present but has pleasant results in the future; there is the undertaking of kamma that is painful in the present and has painful results in the future; and there is the undertaking of kamma that is pleasant in the present and has pleasant results in the future. There exists the undertaking of kamma of such a nature. Knowing that the unwholesome kamma accumulated by this person stands before him to yield results, and that he is not capable of reaching the Noble Path known as abhinibbidhā, the Blessed One does not advise that person. He does not advise those such as Devadatta, Kokālika, and Sunakkhatta the Licchavi prince. Or else, there are other beings of a perverted nature who possess unwholesome kamma that is fixed in yielding bad results immediately after death. Knowing that the unwholesome kamma accumulated by these fixed (niyata) individuals has not yet reached completion, before it yields fruit, before it obstructs the Path, and before they pass beyond the state of being trainable, the Blessed One advises those whose kamma is incomplete. This is like the advice given to Puṇṇa who followed the bovine practice and the naked ascetic (Acela) who followed the canine practice.

Knowing that if this person's accumulated unwholesome kamma reaches completion, it will obstruct the Path, but before it reaches completion, before it yields fruit, before it obstructs the Path, and before he passes beyond the state of being trainable, the Blessed One advises that person whose anantariya-kamma is not yet complete. This is like the advice given to the Venerable Angulimāla Thera.

There is the state of being dull, medium, or superior for all kammas. Among these three, the dull are the imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra); the medium are the remaining wholesome formations; and the superior are the unwholesome formations. The knowledge that understands the results of this kamma through their causes, through their occasions, and without limitation—such as 'this is the result of kamma to be experienced in this very life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya)', 'this is the result of kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya)', 'this is the result of kamma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparāpariyavedanīya)', 'this is the result to be experienced in hell', 'this is the result to be experienced in the animal realm', 'this is the result to be experienced in the realm of hungry ghosts', 'this is the result to be experienced in the realm of asuras', 'this is the result to be experienced in the deva world', and 'this is the result to be experienced in the human world'—this knowledge of the diversity of results of kammas undertaken in the past, future, and present, understood through their causes, occasions, and without limitation, is called the fifth Tathāgata Power.

Thus, the knowledge that understands the defilement (saṃkilesa), the purification (vodāna), and the emergence (vuṭṭhāna) of kammas, jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments undertaken in such a manner—knowing 'it will be defiled in this way', 'it will be purified in this way', 'it will emerge in this way'—is the Buddha's Unobstructed Knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa).
83:
Among those (jhānas, etc.), how many are the jhānas? There are four jhānas. How many are the liberations (vimokkha)? They are eleven, eight, seven, three, and two. How many are the concentrations (samādhi)? There are three concentrations: concentration with initial and sustained thought, concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only, and concentration with neither initial nor sustained thought. How many are the attainments (samāpatti)? There are five attainments: the attainment of perception, the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the attainment of vanished perception (vibhūtasaññā), and the attainment of cessation (nirodha).

Among those (defilement, etc.), what is defilement (saṃkilesa)? Sensual desire and ill will are the defilements of the first jhāna. Also, the two initial jhānas obtained without revulsion, or any concentration that partakes of decline—this is called defilement. Among those, what is purification (vodāna)? Purity from the hindrances is the purification of the first jhāna. Also, the two subsequent jhānas obtained without revulsion, or any concentration that partakes of distinction—this is called purification. Among those, what is emergence (vuṭṭhāna)? Skillfulness in emerging from an attainment is called emergence. The knowledge of the Blessed One regarding these (defilement, purification, and emergence of jhānas, etc.) which occurs through causes, through occasions, and without limitation, is called the knowledge of defilement, purification, and emergence of all jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; this is the sixth Tathāgata Power.

Thus, the three factors that are the retinue of that concentration are the faculties (indriya), the powers (bala), and energy (vīriya). These same faculties become powers through the strength of energy. They are faculties in the sense of predominance and powers in the sense of being unshakable. Thus, there are the states of being dull, medium, and sharp among them: 'this person has dull faculties', 'this person has medium faculties', 'this person has sharp faculties'. Among them, the Blessed One advises the person of sharp faculties with a brief instruction. He advises the person of medium faculties with an instruction that is both brief and detailed. He advises the person of dull faculties with a detailed instruction. Among them, the Blessed One points out a gentle Dhamma teaching to the person of sharp faculties. He points out a Dhamma teaching that is both gentle and sharp to the person of medium faculties. He points out a sharp Dhamma teaching to the person of dull faculties. Among them, the Blessed One points out serenity (samatha) to the person of sharp faculties. He points out both serenity and insight (vipassanā) to the person of medium faculties. He points out insight to the person of dull faculties. Among them, the Blessed One points out the escape (from saṃsāra) to the person of sharp faculties. He points out the danger and the escape to the person of medium faculties. He points out the gratification, the danger, and the escape to the person of dull faculties. Among them, the Blessed One prescribes the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) to the person of sharp faculties. He prescribes the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) to the person of medium faculties. He prescribes the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) to the person of dull faculties.
84:
Thus, there is the knowledge of the Blessed One regarding the dullness, medium state, or extreme sharpness of the faculties of beings, which occurs by way of cause, by way of occasion, and without limitation. This knowledge is such that: "This person, at this time, through this instruction, in this plane, and in this development (bhāvanā), acts; this person is of such a nature; this is this individual's underlying tendency (āsaya); this is the latent disposition (anusaya)." This knowledge is called the Knowledge of the Higher and Lower Faculties of other beings and other individuals (Indriyaparopariyattañāṇa), which is the seventh Power of a Tathāgata (Tathāgatabala).

Among those knowledges of the Buddha, He recollects the manifold past dwellings (pubbenivāsa). That is to say: one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, many hundreds of thousands of births, many aeons of contraction (saṃvaṭṭakappa), many aeons of expansion (vivaṭṭakappa), many aeons of contraction and expansion. "In such a place, I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit of lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn in such a place; there too, I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit of lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn here." Thus, with their aspects and particulars, He recollects the manifold past dwellings.

In that recollection, among beings who have reached the deva realm, the human realm, or the states of deprivation (apāya), He knows: "For this individual, greed and so on are abundant, while non-greed and so on are weak; for this individual, non-greed and so on are abundant, while greed and so on are weak," thus knowing the abundant and the weak qualities.
