He knows: "This individual, in such a ten-millionth aeon, a hundred thousand aeons, a thousand aeons, a hundred aeons, an aeon, an interim aeon, a half-aeon, a year, a half-year, a month, a fortnight, a day, or a moment (muhutta), has accumulated these faculties through such negligence or through such faith, or has not accumulated these faculties." The Blessed One, recollecting various existences, knows them without remainder. Among those knowledges, with the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), which is purified and surpasses the human vision, He sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and sublime, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and He understands how beings pass on according to their kamma: "Alas, these beings were endowed with misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; they were revilers of the Noble Ones..."
85:
"...they held wrong views and undertook actions based on wrong views; with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell.

But these beings, sirs, were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; they were not revilers of the Noble Ones; they held right views and undertook actions based on right view; with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, even in a heavenly world." Among those beings who have reached the heavenly world, the human world, or the states of deprivation, He knows: "By this individual, such a kamma was accumulated in such a ten-millionth aeon, or a hundred thousand aeons, or a thousand aeons, or a hundred aeons, or an aeon, or an interim aeon, or a half-aeon, or a year, or a half-year, or a month, or a fortnight, or a day, or a moment, through such negligence or through such faith." These two knowledges of the Blessed One—the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Dwellings and the Divine Eye—are the eighth and ninth Powers of a Tathāgata.

Thus, among those knowledges, that which reached Omniscience (Sabbaññuta) is known; all dhammas are understood; the stainless and pure Knowledge of Omniscience arose, and Māra was defeated at the foot of the Bodhi tree. This knowledge of the total destruction of all taints (āsava) is the tenth Power of the Blessed One. Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are endowed with the Ten Powers.

## The Collection of the Mode of Investigation (Vicayahāra-sampāta) is finished.

## 3. Yuktihāra-sampāta (The Collection of the Mode of Construing)

In that collection, what is the Mode of Construing (Yuktihāra-sampāta)?

"Therefore, for one with a guarded mind,
Whose range is right intention,
Who places right view in the forefront, 
Knowing arising and passing away,
The bhikkhu who overcomes sloth and torpor
Should abandon all bad destinations."

"For one with a guarded mind, there will be the range of right intention"—this is fitting. "For one whose range is right intention, there will be right view"—this is fitting. "One who dwells placing right view in the forefront will penetrate arising and passing away"—this is fitting. "One who penetrates arising and passing away will abandon all bad destinations"—this is fitting. "One who abandons all bad destinations will transcend all fears of bad destinations and ruin"—this is fitting.

## The Collection of the Mode of Construing (Yuktihāra-sampāta) is finished.
86:
## 4. Padaṭṭhāna-hāra-sampāta
Among those modes, what is the combined application of the mode of proximate cause (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra-sampāta)?

It is the verse beginning with: "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro." The phrase "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa" is the proximate cause of the three types of good conduct. The phrase "Sammāsaṅkappagocaro" is the proximate cause of tranquility (samatha). The phrase "Sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāro" is the proximate cause of insight (vipassanā). The phrase "Ñatvāna udayabbayaṃ" is the proximate cause of the plane of vision (dassanabhūmi). The phrase "Thinamiddhābhibhū bhikkhū" is the proximate cause of energy (vīriya). The phrase "Sabbā duggatiyo jahe" is the proximate cause of development (bhāvanā).

## The combined application of the mode of proximate cause is concluded.

## 5. Lakkhaṇa-hāra-sampāta
Among those modes, what is the combined application of the mode of characteristic (Lakkhaṇa-hāra-sampāta)?

It is the verse beginning with: "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro." This teaching, "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro," is the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya). When the faculty of mindfulness is taken, the five faculties are also taken (due to having similar characteristics). By taking Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) through the phrase "Sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāro," the Noble Eightfold Path is also taken. Why is that? Because from Right View, Right Intention arises; from Right Intention, Right Speech arises; from Right Speech, Right Action arises; from Right Action, Right Livelihood arises; from Right Livelihood, Right Effort arises; from Right Effort, Right Mindfulness arises; from Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration arises; from Right Concentration, Right Liberation arises; from Right Liberation, Right Knowledge and Vision of Liberation arises.

## The combined application of the mode of characteristic is concluded.

## 6. Catubyūha-hāra-sampāta
Among those modes, what is the combined application of the mode of the fourfold array (Catubyūha-hāra-sampāta)?

It is the verse beginning with: "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro." In the phrase "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa," there is this linguistic analysis (nirutti): it is called 'guarded' because it is well-protected. What is the Buddha's intention in this verse? The Buddha's intention here is that those who wish to be liberated from woeful states (duggati) will practice the Dhamma. This is because Kokālika,
87:
having harbored malice in his mind toward the Elders Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna, was reborn in the Mahāpaduma hell. The Blessed One is also endowed with a mind that has mindfulness as its guard; as stated in the Sutta: "The mind should be guarded with mindfulness."

## The combined application of the mode of the fourfold array has been extracted from the Pāḷi and applied.

## 7. Āvaṭṭa-hāra-sampāta

Among those (six modes), what is the combined application of the mode of revolving (Āvaṭṭa-hāra-sampāta)?

It is the verse beginning with: "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro." Here, (having a guarded mind) is called tranquility (samatha). "Sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāro" is called insight (vipassanā). "Ñatvāna udayabbayaṃ" is the full understanding of suffering (dukkha-pariññā). "Thinamiddhābhibhū bhikkhū" is the abandoning of the origin (samudaya-pahāna). "Sabbā duggatiyo jahe" is cessation (nirodha). These are the Four Noble Truths.

## The combined application of the mode of revolving has been extracted from the Pāḷi and applied.

## 8. Vibhatti-hāra-sampāta

Among those (six modes), what is the combined application of the mode of classification (Vibhatti-hāra-sampāta)?

It is the verse beginning with: "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro." The wholesome side (kusalapakkha) should be shown only by the wholesome side. The unwholesome side (akusalapakkha) should be shown only by the unwholesome side.

## The combined application of the mode of classification has been extracted from the Pāḷi and applied.

## 9. Parivattana-hāra-sampāta

Among those (six modes), what is the combined application of the mode of transformation (Parivattana-hāra-sampāta)?

It is the verse beginning with: "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro." When tranquility and insight are developed, cessation is the fruit (phala), suffering is fully understood, the origin is abandoned, and the path is developed through its opposite.

## The combined application of the mode of transformation has been extracted from the Pāḷi and applied.
88:
## 10. Vevacana-hāra-sampāta

Among those six modes, what is the combined application of the mode of synonyms (Vevacana-hāra-sampāta)?

It is this verse: "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro." In the passage "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa," the terms citta, mano, viññāṇa, manindriya, manāyatana, the state of cognizing an object, and the nature of one who cognizes an object are synonyms (vevacana) for the mind. In the passage "Sammāsaṅkappagocaro," the terms thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa), thought of non-ill will (abyāpāda-saṅkappa), and thought of non-harming (avihiṃsā-saṅkappa) are synonyms for Right Intention. In the passage "Sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāro," what is called Right View has these synonyms: the weapon of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the goad of wisdom, and the palace of wisdom.

## The combined application of the mode of synonyms has been extracted from the Pāḷi and applied.

## 11. Paññatti-hāra-sampāta

Among those six modes, what is the combined application of the mode of designation (Paññatti-hāra-sampāta)?

It is this verse: "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro." This designation "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa" is the designation of proximate cause for mindfulness. This designation "Sammāsaṅkappagocaro" is the designation of development for tranquility. This designation "Sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāro, ñatvāna udayabbayaṃ" is the designation of placement (nikkhepa-paññatti) in the plane of vision. "Thinamiddhābhibhū bhikkhū" is the designation of the abandoning of the origin without remainder. "Sabbā duggatiyo jahe" is the designation of development for the path.

## The combined application of the mode of designation has been extracted from the Pāḷi and applied.

## 12. ဩတရဏဟာရသမ္ပာတော (Otaraṇa-hāra-sampāta)

Among those six modes, what is the combined application of the mode of entry (Otaraṇa-hāra-sampāta)?

It is this verse: "Tasmā rakkhitacittassa, sammāsaṅkappagocaro." Therefore, one should have a guarded mind and have Right Intention as one's domain. When Right View is taken through the phrase "Sammādiṭṭhipurekkhāro," the five faculties are also taken; this is the entry (otaraṇa) by way of the faculties.

Those very faculties are called knowledge (vijjā); with the arising of knowledge, there is the cessation of ignorance; with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness; thus all is known. This is the entry by way of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).

Those five faculties are also subsumed under the three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), and the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). This is the entry by way of the aggregates (khandha).
89:
These five faculties alone are included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Those mental formations which are not objects of the taints (anāsava) and are not the cause of existence (no ca bhavaṅgā), those mental formations are categorized under the element of phenomena (dhamma-dhātu); this is the descent by way of elements (dhātu).

That element of phenomena is included in the sphere of phenomena (dhammāyatana). That sphere which is not an object of the taints and is not the cause of existence; this is the descent by way of spheres (āyatana).

## The combination of the descent mode (otaraṇa-hāra-sampāta) is concluded.

## 13. The Combination of the Cleansing Mode (Sodhana-hāra-sampāta)

In that regard, what is the combination of the cleansing mode?

"Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, right thought is the range" is the verse. In a problem, if the beginning (or the extracted meaning) is pure, then that problem is answered. However, if the beginning is not yet pure, then that problem is not yet answered.

## The combination of the cleansing mode is concluded.

## 14. The Combination of the Manifestation Mode (Adhiṭṭhāna-hāra-sampāta)

In that regard, what is the combination of the manifestation mode?

"Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, right thought is the range" is the verse. "For one with a guarded mind" is unity (ekattatā). Mind (citta), mentation (mano), and consciousness (viññāṇa) are diversity (vemattatā). "Right thought is the range" is unity. Thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa), thought of non-ill-will (abyāpāda-saṅkappa), and thought of non-harming (avihiṃsā-saṅkappa) are diversity. "Giving precedence to right view" is unity. Right view means: knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the path, knowledge of the cause, knowledge of the phenomena arisen from a cause, knowledge of the condition, and knowledge of the phenomena arisen from a condition; the seeing and knowing according to reality in various instances, the realization, the penetration, and the arrival at the truths; this is diversity. "Knowing the rise and fall" is unity. By way of rise (udaya): with ignorance as condition, formations come to be; with formations as condition, consciousness comes to be; thus is the origin (samudaya) of all things. By way of fall (vaya): with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; thus is the cessation (nirodha) of all things; this is diversity. "The bhikkhu who overcomes sloth and torpor" is unity. Sloth (thina) is the sickness of the mind, the unworkability; torpor (middha) is the sluggishness of the (mental) body; this is diversity. "He should abandon all woeful states" is unity. Whether in regard to devas and humans...
90:
...compared to devas and humans, the lower realms are called woeful states (duggati); or compared to Nibbāna, all rebirths (upapatti) are called woeful states; this is diversity (vemattatā).

## The combination of the manifestation mode is concluded.

## 15. The Combination of the Requisite Mode (Parikkhāra-hāra-sampāta)

In that regard, what is the combination of the requisite mode?

"Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, right thought is the range" is the verse. This is the requisite (parikkhāra) for serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).

## The combination of the requisite mode is concluded.

## 16. The Combination of the Patterning Mode (Samāropana-hāra-sampāta)

In that regard, what is the combination of the patterning mode?

"Therefore, for one with a guarded mind, having right thought as his range,
Giving precedence to right view, knowing the rise and fall,
The bhikkhu who overcomes sloth and torpor should abandon all woeful states" is the verse.

"For one with a guarded mind" is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the three types of good conduct. When the mind is guarded, the bodily action, verbal action, and mental action are guarded. "Giving precedence to right view" means: when right view is developed, the Noble Eightfold Path is developed. Why is that? From right view, right thought arises; from right thought, right speech arises; from right speech, right action arises; from right action, right livelihood arises; from right livelihood, right effort arises; from right effort, right mindfulness arises; from right mindfulness, right concentration arises; from right concentration, right liberation arises; from right liberation, the knowledge and vision of right liberation arises. This person is one without remainder (anupādisesa), and it is the Nibbāna-element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

## The combination of the patterning mode is concluded.
91:
Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said this:
"Having first considered the sixteen modes of conveyance (hāra) through the eyes of the directions (disā), and having condensed them with the hook (aṅkusa), one should explain the Sutta through the three ways (naya)."

## The Combination of Modes of Conveyance is concluded.

## The Arising of the Ways (Nayasamuṭṭhāna)

Among those sixteen modes of conveyance, what is the Arising of the Ways? The first beginning is not apparent due to ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhavataṇhā). Between these two, ignorance is a hindrance (nīvaraṇa) and craving is a fetter (saṃyojana). Beings who are obstructed by ignorance, being associated with ignorance, wander on the side of ignorance; they are called those of visionary temperament (diṭṭhicarita). Beings who are bound by craving, being associated with craving, wander on the side of craving; they are called those of craving temperament (taṇhācarita). Those of visionary temperament, having gone forth outside this Dispensation, live devoted to the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga). Those of craving temperament, having gone forth outside this Dispensation, live devoted to the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasures (kāmasukhallikānuyoga).

In living thus, for what reason do those of visionary temperament, having gone forth outside this Dispensation, practice self-mortification, while those of craving temperament, having gone forth outside this Dispensation, practice indulgence in sensual pleasures? Outside this Dispensation, there is no determination of the truths. How then could there be the proclamation of the Four Noble Truths, or skill in calm and insight (samatha-vipassanā), or the attainment of the bliss of pacification? Not knowing the bliss of pacification, and having perverted minds, they say: "There is no happiness through happiness; happiness is to be attained only through suffering." Those who indulge in sensual pleasures increase the world; those who increase the world produce much merit—having such perceptions and such views, and seeking happiness through suffering, they live perceiving merit in sensual pleasures and practicing both self-mortification and indulgence in sensual pleasures. Knowing thus, they only increase the disease (roga) of the defilements of the individual existence, they only increase the abscess (gaṇḍa), they only increase the dart (salla). Being greatly afflicted by the disease, oppressed by the abscess, and pierced by the dart, they emerge and sink in hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the host of asuras. Experiencing high and low births, they do not find the medicine of calm and insight that can treat that disease, abscess, and dart.

Among those things, self-mortification and indulgence in sensual pleasures are called defilement (saṅkilesa); calm and insight are called purification (vodāna). Self-mortification and indulgence in sensual pleasures are called the disease (roga); calm and insight are called the medicine that destroys and pacifies the disease. Self-mortification and indulgence in sensual pleasures are called the abscess (gaṇḍa); calm and insight are...
92:
...like the medicine that destroys the abscess. Self-mortification and indulgence in sensual pleasures are called the dart (salla); calm and insight are called the medicine that extracts the dart.

Among those things, defilement (saṅkilesa) is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); the craving that clings to that suffering is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca); the cessation of craving is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca); calm and insight are the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca), which is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. These are the Four Noble Truths. Suffering is to be fully understood; the origin of suffering is to be abandoned; the path is to be developed; cessation is to be realized.

Among those persons, those of visionary temperament regard form as self. They regard feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness as self. Those of craving temperament regard self as possessing form. Or they regard form as being in self, or self as being in form. They regard self as possessing feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness. Or they regard consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness. This is called the identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) with twenty bases.

The opposite of that wrong view is the supramundane Right View (lokuttara-sammādiṭṭhi), and following that Right View are Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration. This is the Noble Eightfold Path. These are the three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha), and the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). The aggregate of virtue and the aggregate of concentration are called calm (samatha); the aggregate of wisdom is called insight (vipassanā). Among those things, the identity (sakkāya) is called suffering; the origin of identity is called the origin of suffering; the cessation of identity is called the cessation of suffering; the Noble Eightfold Path is called the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. These are the Four Noble Truths. Suffering is to be fully understood; the origin of suffering is to be abandoned; the path is to be developed; cessation is to be realized.

Among those persons, those who regard form as self, and regard feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness as self, are called "annihilationists" (ucchedavādī). Those who regard self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form, and those who regard self as possessing feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness, are called "eternalists" (sassatavādī). Among those doctrines, annihilationism and eternalism are the two extremes. This is the continuation of the cycle of birth (pavatti). The opposite of that continuation of the cycle is the Middle Way, which is the Noble Eightfold Path. This is the cessation of the cycle of birth (nivaṭṭi). Between those two, the continuation (pavatti) is called suffering; the craving that clings to that continuation is called the origin of suffering; the cessation of craving is called the cessation of suffering; the Noble Eightfold Path is...
93:
The Truth of the Path, which is the practice leading to Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering—these are the four truths. The Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) should be fully understood; the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) should be abandoned; the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) should be developed; and the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) should be realized.

In that regard, within the views of annihilationism and eternalism, there is the self-view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) which consists of twenty points in brief, and sixty-two types of views in detail. The opposites of these views are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), the eight deliverances (vimokkha), and the ten kasina bases (kasiṇāyatana). The sixty-two types of views are the net of delusion (moha-jāla) that proceeds without beginning or end. The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the wisdom like a diamond weapon (ñāṇa-vajira) that destroys the net of delusion. Therein, delusion (moha) is called ignorance (avijjā), and the net (jāla) is called craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). Therefore, it is said, "The first beginning of ignorance and craving for existence is not known."

In this matter, when a person of view-tempered character (diṭṭhi-carita) goes forth in this Dispensation, they practice the conduct of effacement (sallekha) and have great respect for effacement. When a person of craving-tempered character (taṇhā-carita) goes forth in this Dispensation, they practice the training rules (sikkhāpada) continuously without break and have great respect for the training. When a person of view-tempered character enters the path of rightness (sammatta-niyāma), they become a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī). When a person of craving-tempered character enters the path of rightness, they become a faith-follower (saddhānusārī). A person of view-tempered character is liberated through the pleasant practice (sukha-paṭipadā) with either slow direct knowledge (dandhābhiññā) or quick direct knowledge (khippābhiññā). A person of craving-tempered character is liberated through the painful practice (dukkha-paṭipadā) with either slow direct knowledge or quick direct knowledge.

In that regard, what is the reason why a person of craving-tempered character is liberated through the painful practice with slow or quick direct knowledge? It is because for that craving-tempered person, sensual pleasures (kāma) have not yet been abandoned. When that person is being separated from sensual pleasures, they are liberated with difficulty and understand the Dhamma slowly. However, this person of view-tempered character has no desire for sensual pleasures from the very beginning. When that person is separated from sensual pleasures, they are liberated quickly and understand the Dhamma quickly.

Painful practice is also of two kinds: slow direct knowledge and quick direct knowledge. Pleasant practice is also of two kinds: slow direct knowledge and quick direct knowledge. Beings are also of two kinds: those with dull faculties (mudindriya) and those with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya). Those with dull faculties are liberated slowly and understand the Dhamma slowly. Those with sharp faculties are liberated quickly and understand the Dhamma quickly. These are the four modes of practice. Whoever has been liberated, is being liberated, or will be liberated, they all do so only through these four modes of practice. Thus, the Noble Ones (ariyas) prescribe the fourfold path to cut off the turning of craving for existence, which is resorted to by the ignorant, desired by the foolish, and which dwells in those infatuated by lust. This is called the ground of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. Therefore, it is said, "[One should extinguish] both craving and ignorance through serenity (samatha)."
94:
In the Expositions (Veyyākaraṇa), those things which are wholesome and unwholesome should be appropriately examined in two ways: according to the round of the world (loka-vaṭṭa) and according to the ending of the round of the world (loka-vivaṭṭa). The round (vaṭṭa) is Saṃsāra. The ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) is Nibbāna. Kamma and defilements (kilesa) are the causes of Saṃsāra. Among those kamma and defilements, kamma should be pointed out as volition (cetanā) and mental factors (cetasika). How should that kamma be understood? It should be understood by the moment of accumulation (upacaya). All defilements should also be pointed out by way of the four perversions (vipallāsa). Where should those perversions be understood? They should be understood in the collection of defilements consisting of ten bases.

What are the ten bases? They are the four nutriments (āhāra), the four perversions (vipallāsa), the four graspings (upādāna), the four yokes (yoga), the four ties (gantha), the four taints (āsava), the four floods (ogha), the four barbs (salla), the four stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the four wrong courses (agatigamana).

In the first nutriment, the first perversion occurs; in the second nutriment, the second perversion occurs; in the third nutriment, the third perversion occurs; and in the fourth nutriment, the fourth perversion occurs. In the first perversion, the first grasping occurs; in the second perversion, the second grasping occurs; in the third perversion, the third grasping occurs; and in the fourth perversion, the fourth grasping occurs. In the first grasping, the first yoke occurs; in the second grasping, the second yoke occurs; in the third grasping, the third yoke occurs; and in the fourth grasping, the fourth yoke occurs. In the first yoke, the first tie occurs; in the second yoke, the second tie occurs; in the third yoke, the third tie occurs; and in the fourth yoke, the fourth tie occurs. In the first tie, the first taint occurs; in the second tie, the second taint occurs; in the third tie, the third taint occurs; and in the fourth tie, the fourth taint occurs. In the first taint, the first flood occurs; in the second taint, the second flood occurs; in the third taint, the third flood occurs; and in the fourth taint, the fourth flood occurs. In the first flood, the first barb occurs; in the second flood, the second barb occurs; in the third flood, the third barb occurs; and in the fourth flood, the fourth barb occurs. In the first barb, the first station of consciousness occurs; in the second barb, the second station of consciousness occurs; in the third barb, the third station of consciousness occurs; and in the fourth barb, the fourth station of consciousness occurs. In the first station of consciousness, the first wrong course occurs; in the second station of consciousness, the second wrong course occurs; in the third station of consciousness, the third wrong course occurs; and in the fourth station of consciousness, the fourth wrong course occurs.
95:
Among those four nutriments, physical nutriment and contact as nutriment are the defilements of a person led by craving (taṇhācarita). Mental volition as nutriment and consciousness as nutriment are the defilements of a person led by views (diṭṭhicarita).

Among those four perversions (vipallāsa), the perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the foul (asubha) and the perversion of perceiving the pleasant in the painful (dukkha) are the defilements of a person led by craving. The perversion of perceiving the permanent in the impermanent (anicca) and the perversion of perceiving the self in the non-self (anatta) are the defilements of a person led by views.

Among those four kinds of grasping (upādāna), grasping at sense pleasures and grasping at existence are the defilements of a person led by craving. Grasping at views and grasping at the doctrine of self are the defilements of a person led by views.

Among those four yokes (yoga), the yoke of sense pleasure and the yoke of existence are the defilements of a person led by craving. The yoke of views and the yoke of ignorance are the defilements of a person led by views.

Among those four bodily ties (kāyagantha), the bodily tie of covetousness and the bodily tie of ill will are the defilements of a person led by craving. The bodily tie of misapprehension and the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence that 'this is the truth' are the defilements of a person led by views.

Among those four taints (āsava), the taint of sense pleasure and the taint of existence are the defilements of a person led by craving. The taint of views and the taint of ignorance are the defilements of a person led by views.

Among those four floods (ogha), the flood of sense pleasure and the flood of existence are the defilements of a person led by craving. The flood of views and the flood of ignorance are the defilements of a person led by views.

Among those four darts (salla), the dart of lust (rāga) and the dart of hatred (dosa) are the defilements of a person led by craving. The dart of conceit (māna) and the dart of delusion (moha) are the defilements of a person led by views.

Among those stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti), the station of consciousness associated with form (rūpa) and the station of consciousness associated with feeling (vedanā) are the defilements of a person led by craving. The station of consciousness associated with perception (saññā) and the station of consciousness associated with mental formations (saṅkhāra) are the defilements of a person led by views.

Among those four wrong courses (agatigamana), the wrong course through favoritism and the wrong course through hatred are the defilements of a person led by craving. The wrong course through fear and the wrong course through delusion are the defilements of a person led by views.

Among those objects of defilement, in physical nutriment, the perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the foul should be noted. In contact as nutriment, the perversion of perceiving the pleasant in the painful should be noted. In consciousness as nutriment...
96:
...In consciousness as nutriment, there is the perversion of perceiving the permanent in the impermanent; in mental volition as nutriment, there is the perversion of perceiving the self in the non-self. One established in the first perversion grasps firmly at sense pleasures; this is called grasping at sense pleasures (kāmupādāna). One established in the second perversion grasps firmly at future existence; this is called grasping at existence (bhavupādāna). One established in the third perversion grasps firmly at the view that delights in the round of rebirths; this is called grasping at views (diṭṭhupādāna). One established in the fourth perversion conceives and grasps firmly at a self; this is called grasping at the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna).

Through grasping at sense pleasures, one is yoked to the objects of sense pleasure; this is called the yoke of sense pleasure (kāmayoga). Through grasping at existence, one is yoked to existences; this is called the yoke of existence (bhavayoga). Through grasping at views, one is yoked to evil views; this is called the yoke of views (diṭṭhiyoga). Through grasping at the doctrine of self, one is yoked to ignorance; this is called the yoke of ignorance (avijjāyoga).

One established in the first yoke ties the mental body (nāmakāya) with covetousness; this covetousness, being the cause of the tie, is called the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhākāyagantha). One established in the second yoke ties the mental body with ill will; this ill will is called the bodily tie of ill will (byāpādakāyagantha). One established in the third yoke ties the mental body with misapprehension; this misapprehension is called the bodily tie of misapprehension (parāmāsakāyagantha). One established in the fourth yoke ties the mental body with the dogmatic insistence that 'this is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesa); this dogmatic insistence is called the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence that 'this is the truth' (idaṃsaccābhinivesakāyagantha).

For such a person, these bound defilements flow out as taints (āsava). Why is it said that they 'flow out' (āsavanti)? Because they arise from underlying tendencies (anusaya) or from outbursts (pariyuṭṭhāna). Among those ties, the taint of sense pleasure arises through the bodily tie of covetousness, the taint of existence through the bodily tie of ill will, the taint of views through the bodily tie of misapprehension, and the taint of ignorance through the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence that 'this is the truth'.

When these four taints reach abundance in that person, they become floods (ogha). Thus, the abundance of taints is the abundance of floods. Among those taints, the flood of sense pleasure arises from the taint of sense pleasure, the flood of existence from the taint of existence, the flood of views from the taint of views, and the flood of ignorance from the taint of ignorance.

For that person, these four floods, occurring together with underlying tendencies, enter the disposition and remain striking the heart; because they enter and strike the heart, they are called darts (salla). Among those floods, the dart of lust arises from the flood of sense pleasure, the dart of hatred from the flood of existence, the dart of conceit from the flood of views, and the dart of delusion from the flood of ignorance.
97:
For that person, consciousness, which is seized from all sides by these four arrows (salla), stands in the four states: form, feeling, perception, and mental formations. Therein, due to the arrow of lust, with consciousness sprinkled with delight and craving, there is a station of consciousness approaching form. Due to the arrow of hatred, with consciousness sprinkled with delight and craving, there is a station of consciousness approaching feeling. Due to the arrow of conceit, with consciousness sprinkled with delight and craving, there is a station of consciousness approaching perception. Due to the arrow of delusion, with consciousness sprinkled with delight and craving, there is a station of consciousness approaching mental formations.

For that person, consciousness, which is supported and strengthened by these four stations of consciousness, goes to the wrong courses (agati) that should not be gone to, through the four states: desire (due to love), hatred (due to anger), fear (due to fright), and delusion (due to bewilderment). Among those wrong courses, one goes to the wrong course of desire because of lust; one goes to the wrong course of hatred because of hatred; one goes to the wrong course of fear because of fear; one goes to the wrong course of delusion because of delusion. Thus, both that kamma and these defilements are the causes of saṃsāra. In this way, all defilements should be pointed out by the four perversions (vippallāsa).

Among those states, these four directions (disā) should be known. The first direction consists of: the nutriment of physical food, the perversion of "beauty in the foul," clinging to sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasure, the bodily knot of covetousness, the taint of sensual pleasure, the flood of sensual pleasure, the arrow of lust, the station of consciousness approaching form, and going to the wrong course of desire.

The second direction consists of: the nutriment of contact, the perversion of "pleasure in suffering," clinging to existence, the yoke of existence, the bodily knot of ill-will, the taint of existence, the flood of existence, the arrow of hatred, the station of consciousness approaching feeling, and going to the wrong course of hatred.

The third direction consists of: the nutriment of consciousness, the perversion of "permanence in the impermanent," clinging to views, the yoke of views, the bodily knot of misapprehension, the taint of views, the flood of views, the arrow of conceit, the station of consciousness approaching perception, and going to the wrong course of fear.

The fourth direction consists of: the nutriment of mental volition, the perversion of "self in the non-self," clinging to the doctrine of self, the yoke of ignorance, the bodily knot of insistence that "this is the truth," the taint of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the arrow of delusion, the station of consciousness approaching mental formations, and going to the wrong course of delusion.

Among those nutriments and so forth, whichever is the nutriment of physical food, whichever is the perversion of "beauty in the foul," whichever is clinging to sensual pleasures, whichever is the yoke of sensual pleasure, whichever is the bodily knot of covetousness...
98:
...the taint of sensual pleasure, the flood of sensual pleasure, the arrow of lust, the station of consciousness approaching form, and going to the wrong course of desire—these ten discourses (suttas) are one in meaning, differing only in phrasing. These are the corruptions (upakkilesa) of a person of lustful temperament.

Among those states, the nutriment of contact, the perversion of perceiving pleasure in suffering, clinging to existence, the yoke of existence, the bodily knot of ill-will, the taint of existence, the flood of existence, the arrow of hatred, the station of consciousness approaching feeling, and going to the wrong course of hatred—these ten discourses are one in meaning, differing only in phrasing. These are the corruptions of a person of hateful temperament.

Among those states, the nutriment of consciousness, the perversion of perceiving permanence in the impermanent, clinging to views, the yoke of views, the bodily knot of misapprehension, the taint of views, the flood of views, the arrow of conceit, the station of consciousness approaching perception, and going to the wrong course of fear—these ten discourses are one in meaning, differing only in phrasing. These are the corruptions of a dull person of dogmatic temperament.

Among those states, the nutriment of mental volition, the perversion of perceiving self in the non-self, clinging to the doctrine of self, the yoke of ignorance, the bodily knot of insistence that "this is the truth," the taint of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the arrow of delusion, the station of consciousness approaching mental formations, and going to the wrong course of delusion—these ten discourses are one in meaning, differing only in phrasing. These are the corruptions of a sharp person of dogmatic temperament.

Among those states, the nutriment of physical food and the nutriment of contact reach full understanding (pariññā) through the desireless (appaṇihita) door of liberation. The nutriment of consciousness reaches full understanding through the void (suññata) door of liberation, and the nutriment of mental volition through the signless (animitta) door of liberation. Among those states, the perversion of perceiving beauty in the foul and the perversion of perceiving pleasure in suffering reach abandonment or cessation through the desireless door of liberation. The perversion of perceiving permanence in the impermanent reaches abandonment through the void door of liberation, and the perversion of perceiving self in the non-self through the signless door of liberation. Among those states, clinging to sensual pleasures and clinging to existence reach abandonment through the desireless door of liberation. Clinging to views reaches abandonment through the void door of liberation, and clinging to the doctrine of self through the signless door of liberation. Among those states, the yoke of sensual pleasure and the yoke of existence reach abandonment through the desireless door of liberation. The yoke of views reaches abandonment through the void door of liberation, and the yoke of ignorance through the signless door of liberation. Among those states, the bodily knot of covetousness and the bodily knot of ill-will...
99:
...are abandoned through the desireless door of liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkhamukha). The bodily tie of misapprehension (parāmāsa-kāyagantha) is abandoned through the void door of liberation (suññata-vimokkhamukha). The bodily tie of insistence that 'this is the truth' (idamsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha) is abandoned through the signless door of liberation (animitta-vimokkhamukha).

Among those states, the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and the taint of existence (bhavāsava) are abandoned through the desireless door of liberation. The taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) is abandoned through the void door of liberation. The taint of ignorance (avijjāsava) is abandoned through the signless door of liberation. Among those states, the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha) and the flood of existence (bhavogha) are abandoned through the desireless door of liberation. The flood of views (diṭṭhogha) is abandoned through the void door of liberation. The flood of ignorance (avijjogha) is abandoned through the signless door of liberation. Among those states, the dart of lust (rāgasalla) and the dart of hatred (dosasalla) are abandoned through the desireless door of liberation. The dart of conceit (mānasalla) is abandoned through the void door of liberation. The dart of delusion (mohasalla) is abandoned through the signless door of liberation. Among those states, the station of consciousness associated with form (rūpūpagā viññāṇaṭṭhiti) and the station of consciousness associated with feeling (vedanūpagā viññāṇaṭṭhiti) reach full understanding (pariññā) through the desireless door of liberation. The station of consciousness associated with perception (saññūpagā) reaches full understanding through the void door of liberation. The station of consciousness associated with volitional formations (saṅkhārūpagā) reaches full understanding through the signless door of liberation.

Among those states, going on a wrong path through desire (chandā agatigamana) and going on a wrong path through hatred (dosā agatigamana) are abandoned through the desireless door of liberation. Going on a wrong path through fear (bhayā agatigamana) is abandoned through the void door of liberation. Going on a wrong path through delusion (mohā agatigamana) is abandoned through the signless door of liberation. Thus, all states that follow the round of the world (lokavaṭṭā) emerge from that world through the three doors of liberation.

In that deliverance, these following states are the means of deliverance: the four practices, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four jhānas, the four abidings, the four right efforts, the four marvelous and wonderful qualities, the four foundations, the four developments of concentration, the four things conducive to happiness, and the four immeasurables.

The first practice is the first foundation of mindfulness. The second practice is the second foundation of mindfulness. The third practice is the third foundation of mindfulness. The fourth practice is the fourth foundation of mindfulness. The first foundation of mindfulness is the first jhāna. The second foundation of mindfulness is the second jhāna. The third foundation of mindfulness is the third jhāna. The fourth foundation of mindfulness is the fourth jhāna. The first jhāna is the first abiding. The second jhāna is the second abiding. The third jhāna is the third abiding. The fourth jhāna is the fourth abiding. The first abiding is the first right effort. The second abiding is the second right effort. The third abiding is the third right effort. The fourth abiding is the fourth right effort. The first right effort is the first marvelous and wonderful quality. The second right effort is the second marvelous and wonderful quality. The third right effort is the third marvelous and wonderful quality. The fourth right effort is the fourth marvelous and wonderful quality. The first marvelous and wonderful quality is...
100:
...the first foundation of truth. The second marvelous and wonderful quality is the second foundation of truth. The third marvelous and wonderful quality is the third foundation of truth. The fourth marvelous and wonderful quality is the fourth foundation of truth. The first foundation of truth is the first development of concentration. The second foundation of truth is the second development of concentration. The third foundation of truth is the third development of concentration. The fourth foundation of truth is the fourth development of concentration. The first development of concentration is the first state conducive to happiness. The second development of concentration is the second state conducive to happiness. The third development of concentration is the third state conducive to happiness. The fourth development of concentration is the fourth state conducive to happiness. The first state conducive to happiness is the first immeasurable. The second state conducive to happiness is the second immeasurable. The third state conducive to happiness is the third immeasurable. The fourth state conducive to happiness is the fourth immeasurable.

When the first practice is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness. When the second practice is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the second foundation of mindfulness. When the third practice is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the third foundation of mindfulness. When the fourth practice is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the fourth foundation of mindfulness. When the first foundation of mindfulness is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the first jhāna. When the second foundation of mindfulness is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the second jhāna. When the third foundation of mindfulness is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the third jhāna. When the fourth foundation of mindfulness is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the fourth jhāna.

When the first jhāna is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the first abiding. When the second jhāna is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the second abiding. When the third jhāna is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the third abiding. When the fourth jhāna is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the fourth abiding. When the first abiding is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states. When the second abiding is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states. When the third abiding is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the arising of unarisen wholesome states. When the fourth abiding is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the maintenance, non-disappearance, and further development of arisen wholesome states. When the first right effort is developed and cultivated...
101:
[When the first right effort is developed and cultivated,] it fulfills the abandoning of conceit. When the second right effort is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the uprooting of attachments. When the third right effort is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the abandoning of ignorance. When the fourth right effort is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the calming of existence.

When the abandoning of conceit is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the foundation of truth. When the uprooting of attachments is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the foundation of generosity. When the abandoning of ignorance is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the foundation of wisdom. When the calming of existence is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the foundation of calm.

When the foundation of truth is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the concentration due to desire. When the foundation of generosity is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the concentration due to energy. When the foundation of wisdom is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the concentration due to mind. When the foundation of calm is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the concentration due to investigation.

When the concentration due to desire is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the restraint of the senses. When the concentration due to energy is developed and cultivated, it fulfills austerity. When the concentration due to mind is developed and cultivated, it fulfills intellect (buddhi), which is the development of the factors of enlightenment. When the concentration due to investigation is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the relinquishment of all acquisitions.

When the restraint of the senses is developed and cultivated, it fulfills loving-kindness. When austerity is developed and cultivated, it fulfills compassion. When intellect is developed and cultivated, it fulfills appreciative joy. When the relinquishment of all acquisitions is developed and cultivated, it fulfills equanimity.

Among those, there are these four directions. The first practice, the first foundation of mindfulness, the first absorption, the first abiding, the first right effort, the first wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of truth, the concentration due to desire, the restraint of the senses, and loving-kindness: these are the first direction.

The second practice, the second foundation of mindfulness, the second abiding, the second right effort, the second wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of existence (bhavādhiṭṭhāna), the concentration due to energy, austerity, and compassion: these are the second direction.

The third practice, the third foundation of mindfulness, the third absorption, the third abiding, the third right effort, the third wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of wisdom, the concentration due to mind, intellect, and appreciative joy: these are the third direction.

The fourth practice, the fourth foundation of mindfulness, the fourth absorption, the fourth abiding, the fourth right effort, the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of calm, the concentration due to investigation, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, and equanimity: these are the fourth direction.
102:
Among those, the first practice, the first foundation of mindfulness, the first absorption, the first abiding, the first right effort, the first wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of truth, the concentration due to desire, the restraint of the senses, and loving-kindness: these ten discourses have one meaning, differing only in phrasing. This is the medicine for a person of lustful temperament.

The second practice, the second foundation of mindfulness, the second absorption, the second abiding, the second right effort, the second wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of generosity, the concentration due to energy, austerity, and compassion: these ten discourses have one meaning, differing only in phrasing. This is the medicine for a person of hateful temperament.

The third practice, the third foundation of mindfulness, the third absorption, the third abiding, the third right effort, the third wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of wisdom, the concentration due to mind, intellect (buddhi), and appreciative joy: these ten discourses have one meaning, differing only in phrasing. This is the medicine for a person of speculative temperament who is dull.

The fourth practice, the fourth foundation of mindfulness, the fourth absorption, the fourth abiding, the fourth right effort, the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of calm, the concentration due to investigation, the relinquishment of all acquisitions (Nibbāna), and equanimity: these ten discourses have one meaning, differing only in phrasing. This is the medicine for a person of speculative temperament who is sharp.

Among those, the painful practice with slow direct knowledge and the painful practice with swift direct knowledge are the desireless door to liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkhamukha). The pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge is the void door to liberation (suññata-vimokkhamukha). The pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge is the signless door to liberation (animitta-vimokkhamukha).

Among those, the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body in the body and the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of feelings in feelings are the desireless door to liberation. The foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the mind in the mind is the void door to liberation. The foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of phenomena in phenomena is the signless door to liberation.

Among those, the first absorption and the second absorption are the desireless door to liberation. The third absorption is the void door to liberation. The fourth absorption is the signless door to liberation.

Among those, the first abiding and the second abiding are the desireless door to liberation. The third abiding is the void door to liberation. The fourth abiding is the signless door to liberation.
103:
Among those (Right Efforts), the first Right Effort and the second Right Effort are the desireless (appaṇihita) door of liberation; the third Right Effort is the void (suññata) door of liberation; the fourth Right Effort is the signless (animitta) door of liberation.

Among those (marvelous and wonderful qualities), the abandoning of pride and the uprooting of attachment (ālaya/āsaya) are the desireless door of liberation; the abandoning of ignorance is the void door of liberation; the stilling of existence is the signless door of liberation.

Among those (resolves), the resolve on truth and the resolve on generosity are the desireless door of liberation; the resolve on wisdom is the void door of liberation; the resolve on stillness is the signless door of liberation.

Among those (developments of concentration), concentration of desire and concentration of energy are the desireless door of liberation; concentration of mind is the void door of liberation; concentration of investigation is the signless door of liberation.

Among those (qualities partaking of happiness), restraint of the sense faculties and austerity (practice) are the desireless door of liberation; intelligence (wisdom) is the void door of liberation; the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi) is the signless door of liberation.

Among those (illimitables), loving-kindness and compassion are the desireless door of liberation; appreciative joy is the void door of liberation; equanimity is the signless door of liberation.

That is the display (vikkīḷita) of those (Buddhas, etc.). The opposites of the four nutriments are the four practices... The opposites of the four perversions (vipallāsa) are the four foundations of mindfulness. The opposites of the four clingings (upādāna) are the four jhanas. The opposites of the four yokes (yoga) are the four abidings (vihara). The opposites of the four ties (gantha) are the four right efforts. The opposites of the four taints (āsava) are the four marvelous and wonderful qualities. The opposites of the four floods (ogha) are the four resolves. The opposites of the four darts (salla) are the four developments of concentration. The opposites of the four stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti) are the four qualities partaking of happiness. The opposites of the four wrong paths (agativagamana) are the four illimitables.

The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples who have destroyed greed, hatred, and delusion are like lions (sīha). Their display (vikkīḷita) consists of development (bhāvanā), realization (sacchikiriyā), and the removal of defilements (byantīkiriyā). Mastery over the sense faculties and the non-arising (abandoning) of perversions are also called display. The sense faculties are the domain (gocara) of the true Dhamma; the perversions are the domain of the defilements. This is called the ground (bhūmi) of the 'Lion's Display' method and the 'Surveying the Directions' method. Therefore, it is said: "He leads away from defilements caused by perversions." In the discourses (veyyākaraṇa), there are also mentions of "wholesome and unwholesome."
104:
Among those persons, there are these two: those who emerge through painful practice with slow direct knowledge and those with quick direct knowledge. There are these two: those who emerge through pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge and those with quick direct knowledge. For these four persons, the factors of defilement (saṃkilesa) are: the four nutriments, the four perversions (vipallāsa), the four clingings (upādāna), the four yokes (yoga), the four ties (gantha), the four taints (āsava), the four floods (ogha), the four darts (salla), the four stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti), and the four wrong paths (agati).

For these four persons, the factors of purification (vodāna) are: the four practices (paṭipadā), the four foundations of mindfulness, the four jhanas, the four abidings (vihara), the four right efforts, the four marvelous and wonderful qualities, the four resolves, the four developments of concentration, the four qualities partaking of happiness (sukhabhāgiya), and the four illimitables.

Among those persons, there are these two: those who emerge through painful practice with slow direct knowledge and those with quick direct knowledge. There are these two: those who emerge through pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge and those with quick direct knowledge. Among these, the person who emerges through pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge is called 'one of quick understanding' (ugghaṭitaññū). The person who emerges through common practice is called 'one who understands through elaboration' (vipañcitaññū). The person who emerges through painful practice with slow direct knowledge is called 'one who needs guidance' (neyya).

Among these three types of persons, the Blessed One points out calm (samatha) to the person of quick understanding; he points out insight (vipassanā) to the person who needs guidance; and he points out both calm and insight to the person who understands through elaboration. Among these three persons, the Blessed One points out a gentle Dhamma teaching to the person of quick understanding; a sharp Dhamma teaching to the person who needs guidance; and a teaching that is both gentle and sharp to the person who understands through elaboration. Among these three persons, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma in brief to the person of quick understanding; in brief and in detail to the person who understands through elaboration; and in detail to the person who needs guidance. Among these three persons, the Blessed One points out the escape (nissaraṇa) to the person of quick understanding; the danger (ādīnava) and the escape to the person who understands through elaboration; and the gratification (assāda), the danger, and the escape to the person who needs guidance. Among these three persons, the Blessed One prescribes the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) for the person of quick understanding; the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) for the person who understands through elaboration; and the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) for the person who needs guidance.

Among those persons, there are these two: those who emerge through painful practice with slow direct knowledge and those with quick direct knowledge. There are these two: those who emerge through pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge and those with quick direct knowledge. Thus, the four persons become three: the one of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), and the one who needs guidance (neyya).

For these three persons, the factors of defilement (saṃkilesa) are the three unwholesome roots: the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
105:
There are three types of misconduct: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. There are three types of unwholesome thoughts: thought of sensual desire, thought of ill will, and thought of cruelty. There are three types of unwholesome perceptions: perception of sensual desire, perception of ill will, and perception of cruelty. There are three types of perverted perceptions (vipariīta-saññā): perception of permanence, perception of pleasure, and perception of self. There are three types of feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. There are three types of suffering (dukkhatā): suffering as pain (dukkha-dukkhatā), suffering as formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā), and suffering as change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā). There are three fires: the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion. There are three arrows: the arrow of lust, the arrow of hatred, and the arrow of delusion. There are three tangles (jaṭā): the tangle of lust, the tangle of hatred, and the tangle of delusion. There are three unwholesome accessories (akusalūpaparikkhā): unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and unwholesome mental action. There are three failures (vipatti): failure in virtue (sīla-vipatti), failure in view (diṭṭhi-vipatti), and failure in conduct (ācāra-vipatti). The purification (vodāna) for these three types of persons is as follows: There are three wholesome roots: the wholesome root of non-greed, the wholesome root of non-hatred, and the wholesome root of non-delusion. There are three types of good conduct: bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct. There are three types of wholesome thoughts: thought of renunciation, thought of non-ill will, and thought of non-cruelty. There are three types of concentration: concentration with initial and sustained thought, concentration without initial thought but with sustained thought only, and concentration without initial and sustained thought. There are three types of wholesome perceptions: perception of renunciation, perception of non-ill will, and perception of non-cruelty. There are three types of non-perverted perceptions (avipariīta-saññā): perception of impermanence, perception of suffering, and perception of non-self. There are three wholesome accessories (kusalūpaparikkhā): wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action, and wholesome mental action. There are three purities (soceyya): bodily purity, verbal purity, and mental purity. There are three attainments (sampatti): attainment in virtue, attainment in concentration, and attainment in wisdom. There are three trainings (sikkhā): the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. There are three aggregates (khandha): the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom. There are three doors to liberation (vimokkhamukha): emptiness (suññata), signless (animitta), and undirected (appaṇihita).

Thus, four become three, and three become two: the person of craving-temperament (taṇhā-carita) and the person of view-temperament (diṭṭhi-carita).

The defilements (saṃkilesa) for these two types of persons are as follows: craving, ignorance, shamelessness (ahirika), fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa), lack of mindfulness (assati), lack of clear comprehension (asampajañña), unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra), laziness (kosajja), being difficult to admonish (dovacassatā), ego-conception (ahaṃkāra), possessiveness (mamaṃkāra), lack of faith (assaddhā), negligence (pamāda), not hearing the true Dhamma (asaddhammassavana), lack of restraint (asaṃvara), covetousness (abhijjhā), ill will (byāpāda), hindrances (nīvaraṇa), fetters (saṃyojana), anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), depreciation of others' virtues (makkha), rivalry (palāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchera), deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi), and annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi).
106:
The purification (vodāna) for these two types of persons is as follows: tranquillity (samatha), insight (vipassanā), shame (hiri), fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), mindfulness (sati), clear comprehension (sampajañña), wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), arousal of energy (vīriyārambha), being easy to admonish (sovacassatā), knowledge in the Dhamma, knowledge in consequence (anvaye ñāṇa), knowledge of destruction (khaye ñāṇa), knowledge of non-arising (anuppāde ñāṇa), faith (saddhā), heedfulness (appamāda), hearing the true Dhamma, restraint (saṃvara), non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), non-ill will (abyāpāda), liberation of mind through the fading of lust (rāga-virāgā cetovimutti), liberation by wisdom through the fading of ignorance (avijjā-virāgā paññāvimutti), realization (abhisamaya), fewness of wishes (appicchatā), contentment (santuṭṭhi), non-anger (akkodha), non-enmity (anupanāha), non-depreciation (amakkha), non-rivalry (apalāsa), the abandoning of envy, the abandoning of stinginess, true knowledge (vijjā), liberation (vimutti), liberation with a conditioned object, liberation with an unconditioned object, the Nibbāna element with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu), and the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

This is called the ground (bhūmi) for the Tipukkhala method and the Aṅkusa method. Therefore, it was said: "He who leads away the unwholesome along with its roots," and "Having looked with the eye of the quarters (disā-locana)."

## The origin of the methods is joined.

## Sāsanapaṭṭhāna

Among those [root terms of the methods], where are the eighteen root terms (mūlapada) to be noted? They are to be noted in the Sāsanapaṭṭhāna (The Dispensation's Setting Forth). In that context, what is the Sāsanapaṭṭhāna? It consists of: Suttas dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), Suttas dealing with tendencies (vāsanābhāgiya), Suttas dealing with penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), Suttas dealing with the adept (asekhabhāgiya), Suttas dealing with both defilement and tendencies, Suttas dealing with both defilement and penetration, Suttas dealing with both defilement and the adept, Suttas dealing with defilement, penetration, and the adept, Suttas dealing with defilement, tendencies, and penetration, Suttas dealing with both tendencies and penetration, Suttas dealing with the defilement of craving, Suttas dealing with the defilement of view, Suttas dealing with the defilement of misconduct, Suttas dealing with the purification of craving, Suttas dealing with the purification of view, and Suttas dealing with the purification of misconduct.

In that context, defilement (saṃkilesa) is of three kinds: defilement of craving, defilement of view, and defilement of misconduct. Among these three, the defilement of craving is purified by tranquillity (samatha); that tranquillity is called the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). The defilement of view is purified by insight (vipassanā).
107:
That insight (vipassanā) is called the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha). The defilement of misconduct is purified by good conduct; that good conduct is called the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). If attachment to existences arises in one established in that virtue, then his Samatha and Vipassanā become a merit-making activity consisting in development (bhāvanāmaya puññakiriyavatthu), leading to rebirth in various appropriate existences. When these four suttas, such as the one partaking in defilement, are combined, they become eight; when those eight are combined, they become sixteen.

By these sixteen suttas differentiated by the Sāsanapaṭṭhāna method, the Sutta, which is the ninefold teaching (pariyatti-sāsana), is differentiated. A verse should be inferred by a verse, an exposition (veyyākaraṇa) by an exposition, and a sutta by a sutta.

Among those suttas, which is the sutta partaking in defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya sutta)?

Blinded by sensual lust, covered by the net [of craving], shrouded by the canopy of craving, bound by the bond of heedlessness, beings follow old age and death, like fish in the mouth of a trap, or like a suckling calf following its mother.

## This is a sutta partaking in defilement.

Monks, there are these four wrong courses (agati). Which four? One goes on a wrong course through desire (chandāgati), through hatred (dosāgati), through delusion (mohāgati), and through fear (bhayāgati). Monks, these are the four wrong courses. The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this:

“Whoever transgresses the Dhamma through desire, hatred, fear, or delusion, his fame declines like the moon in the waning fortnight.”

## This is a sutta partaking in defilement.

“Mind is the forerunner of all states, mind is their chief, they are mind-made. If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, suffering follows him even as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox.”

## This is a sutta partaking in defilement.
108:
"When one is a glutton, drowsy, and a sluggard, rolling over as he sleeps like a great hog fed on grain, such a dullard comes to the womb again and again."

## This is a Sutta partaking of defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya).

"Just as rust arising from iron eats away that very iron from which it was born, so too, the deeds of one who transcends the proper practice of reflecting on the four requisites lead him to a woeful state."

## This is a Sutta partaking of defilement.

"Just as a thief caught at the mouth of a tunnel is beaten and bound because of his own deed, so too, this generation of beings, having passed away, is beaten and bound in the next world because of their own deeds."

## This is a Sutta partaking of defilement.

"He who, seeking his own happiness, harms with a weapon other beings who also desire happiness, will not find happiness after death in the next world."

## This is a Sutta partaking of defilement.

"If the lead bull among a herd of cattle crossing a river goes crookedly, all the other cattle also go crookedly because the leader has gone crookedly.

Even so among human beings, he who is considered the chief, if he practices unrighteousness, how much more so will the rest of the people? The whole country dwells in suffering if the king is unrighteous."

## This is a Sutta partaking of defilement.

"These human beings are of a very miserable nature; being bound by the lust for acquisitions (upadhi), they commit evil. They go to the Avīci hell, the abode of many beings, which is bitter and terrifying."

## This is a Sutta partaking of defilement.
109:
“Truly, its fruit destroys the banana tree; its fruit the bamboo, its fruit the reed. Honor destroys the bad man, just as the embryo destroys the mule.”

## This is a sutta partaking in defilement.

“A monk who values anger and disparaging, who respects gains and honors, does not flourish in the True Dhamma, like a rotten seed in a good field.”

## This is a sutta partaking in defilement.

Monks, here I know a certain person with a corrupted mind, having encompassed his mind with my own. (This person behaves in such a way, practices in such a way, and has entered such a path.) If this person were to die at this time, he would be placed in hell as if carried there. Why is that? Because, monks, his mind is corrupted. It is because of the corruption of the mind, monks, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body after death, are reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, perdition, and hell. The Blessed One said this matter. In that regard, this was said:

Having known a certain person here to have a corrupted mind,
The Buddha declared this matter in the presence of the monks.
If this person were to die at this time,
He would be reborn in hell, for his mind is corrupted.
It is because of the corruption of the mind that beings go to a bad destination.
Like one being carried and set down, such a person of little wisdom,
With the breakup of the body, is reborn in hell.

I have heard that this matter was also spoken by the Blessed One.

## This is a sutta partaking in defilement.

“If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you, do not do an evil deed, whether openly or in secret.”
110:
If you should do an evil deed in the future, or are doing one now, there is no escape from suffering for you, even if you flee after having committed it.

## This is a discourse leading to defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta).

Having acquired wealth through unrighteousness and through lying, fools think of both as "mine." How will that turn out? Dangers will arise, and the accumulated wealth will perish. Upon death, they do not go to heaven. Are they not destroyed by this much?

## This is a discourse leading to defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta).

In what way does one dig up oneself? In what way does one decline from friends? In what way does one deviate from the Dhamma? In what way does one not go to heaven? Through greed, one digs up oneself. One who is greedy declines from friends. Through greed, one deviates from the Dhamma. Through greed, one does not go to heaven.

## This is a discourse leading to defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta).

Fools of little wisdom wander about as their own enemies, performing evil deeds that bear bitter fruit. That deed is not well done which, after being done, one regrets, and the result of which one experiences weeping with a tearful face.

## This is a discourse leading to defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta).

The state of a recluse is difficult to practice and difficult to endure for the unwise. Indeed, in that state of a recluse, the fool founders; therein are many obstructions. If a fool should harbor ill-will towards the Tathāgata, who teaches the Dhamma and its meaning, his life is indeed in vain. "Venerable Sir, I, who am not yet free from lust, have harbored ill-will towards the Tathāgatas of immeasurable virtue. This suffering and suffering even more wretched than this is fitting for me," (he says).

## This is a discourse leading to defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta).
111:
How can one who measures a person of immeasurable virtue (thinking, "he has this much virtue or concentration") be considered a wise person? One who measures a person of immeasurable virtue—though he may be thought of as a wise person whose defilements are stilled—I consider him only as one lacking wisdom.

## This is a discourse belonging to the category of defilement.

When a man is born, an axe is born in his mouth. When a fool speaks ill, he cuts himself with that very axe.

Neither a well-sharpened sword nor halāhala poison (can cause one to fall into the lower realms), but ill-spoken words, if wrong, are like that which causes one to fall into the lower realms.

## This is a discourse belonging to the category of defilement.

He who praises one who should be blamed, or blames one who should be praised, accumulates bad luck with his mouth. Because of that bad luck, he finds no happiness.

This loss of wealth in a game of dice is a minor misfortune. This misfortune is far greater: harboring ill-will towards the Sugatas, such as the Buddha, which causes the destruction of all wealth along with oneself.

One who reviles the Noble Ones, having established an evil speech and mind, goes to hell for a period of one hundred thousand Nirabbudas, thirty-six Nirabbudas, and five Abbudas.

## This is a discourse belonging to the category of defilement.

He who is constantly engaged in the quality of greed and threatens others with words—he is without faith, stingy, ignorant of the words of the virtuous, miserly, and constantly engaged in slander.
112:
O you with a foul mouth for a door, destroyer of truth, ignoble one, destroyer of truth, wicked one, doer of evil, vile man, guilty one, low-born son—do not speak much here; you are a denizen of hell.

The wrongdoer reviles the peaceful Noble Ones as if scattering dust to his own disadvantage. Having practiced many misdeeds, he goes to hell for a long time.

## This is a discourse leading to defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya Sutta).

Among those discourses, which is the discourse leading to habituation (Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta)?

Mental phenomena are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are made of the mind. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows him like a shadow that never leaves.

## This is a discourse leading to habituation (Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta).

Mahānāma the Sakyan addressed the Blessed One thus: "Venerable Sir, this city of Kapilavatthu is prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and has narrow streets. Venerable Sir, after I have waited upon the Blessed One or the monks who inspire the mind, and I enter Kapilavatthu in the evening, I encounter frightening elephants, frightening horses, frightening chariots, frightening carts, and frightening men. Venerable Sir, at that time, my mindfulness directed towards the Blessed One is lost; my mindfulness directed towards the Dhamma is lost; my mindfulness directed towards the Saṅgha is lost. Venerable Sir, the thought occurs to me: 'If I were to die at this evening time, what would be my destination? What would be my future state?'"

"Do not fear, Mahānāma! Do not fear, Mahānāma! Your death will not be an evil one; your passing will not be an evil one. Mahānāma, with four things..."
113:
A noble disciple endowed with four things leans towards Nibbāna, slopes towards Nibbāna, and inclines towards Nibbāna. What four? Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is endowed with unshakeable confidence in the Buddha: 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One: an Arahant... the Buddha, the Blessed One.' He is endowed with [unshakeable confidence] in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... He is endowed with virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, and leading to concentration.

Mahānāma, just as a tree that leans towards the east, slopes towards the east, and inclines towards the east, when cut at the root, falls in which direction? "Bhante, it falls in the direction it leans, slopes, and inclines," (replied Mahānāma). Even so, Mahānāma, a noble disciple endowed with these four things leans towards Nibbāna, slopes towards Nibbāna, and inclines towards Nibbāna. Do not fear, Mahānāma! Do not fear, Mahānāma! Your death will not be evil; your passing will not be evil.

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.
