"One who does not harm with a rod beings who desire happiness, while seeking one's own happiness, gains happiness after death."

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

"Among cattle crossing a river, if the lead bull goes straight, all of them go straight when the leader has gone straight.

Even so among human beings, whoever is considered the chief, if he practices the Dhamma, how much more so the rest of the people! The whole country dwells happily if the king is righteous."

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇډika’s Monastery. At that time, many monks were making a robe for the Blessed One, thinking: "When the robe is finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour." At that time, the chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa were residing in Sāketa on some business. The chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa heard: "It is said that many monks are making a robe for the Blessed One. When the robe is finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour."
114:
Then the chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa stationed a man on the road, saying: "My good man, when you see the Blessed One—the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—coming, then inform us." After standing there for two or three days, that man saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he approached the chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa and said: "Sirs, this Blessed One—the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—is coming. Now is the time for whatever you think fit."

Then the chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and followed closely behind him. Then the Blessed One left the road and approached the foot of a certain tree, where he sat down on the prepared seat. The chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the chamberlains Isidatta and Purāṇa said to the Blessed One:

"Bhante, when we hear that the Blessed One will set out on tour from Sāvatthī among the Kosalans, at that time we feel displeasure and distress, thinking: 'The Blessed One will be far from us.' And when we hear that the Blessed One has set out on tour from Sāvatthī among the Kosalans, at that time too we feel displeasure and distress, thinking: 'The Blessed One is far from us.' ...pe...

"Bhante, when we hear that the Blessed One will set out on tour from the Kāsans among the Magadhans, at that time we feel displeasure and distress, thinking: 'The Blessed One will be far from us.' And when we hear that the Blessed One has set out on tour from the Kāsans among the Magadhans, at that time we feel much displeasure and much distress, thinking: 'The Blessed One is far from us.'

"But Bhante, when we hear that the Blessed One will set out on tour from the Magadhans among the Kāsans, at that time we feel joy and happiness, thinking: 'The Blessed One will be near us.' And when we hear that the Blessed One has set out on tour from the Magadhans among the Kāsans, at that time too we feel..."
115:
At that time, (reflecting) 'The Blessed One is near us,' joy and gladness arise in us. ...pe... 

"Bhante, when we hear, 'The Blessed One will set out on a tour to Sāvatthī in the Kosala country,' at that time, joy and gladness arise in us (thinking), 'The Blessed One will be near us.'

"But, Bhante, when we hear, 'The Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery,' at that time, great joy and great gladness arise in us (thinking), 'The Blessed One is near us.'

"Carpenters, because of this, the household life is cramped, a path of dust; the life of renunciation is the open air. It is enough for you, carpenters, to be diligent (appamāda)." "Bhante, is there another crampedness for us that is more cramped and more truly called cramped than this household crampedness?" "Carpenters, what is that other crampedness that is more cramped and more truly called cramped than this household crampedness?"

"Bhante, in this world, when King Pasenadi of Kosala wishes to go to the park, we prepare the riding elephants of King Pasenadi of Kosala and seat the King's dear and beloved wives, one in front and one behind. Bhante, the scent of those sisters is like a perfume box just opened, or like the scent of royal maidens adorned with perfumes. Bhante, the bodily touch of those sisters is like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton, or like the touch of royal maidens raised in comfort. Bhante, at that time, the elephant must be guarded, those sisters must be guarded, and we ourselves must be guarded. Yet, Bhante, we do not recall any evil, unwholesome thought arising towards those sisters. This, Bhante, is for us another crampedness more cramped and more truly called cramped than that household crampedness."
116:
“Carpenters, therefore, the household life is cramped, a path of dust; the life of renunciation is as free as the open air. It is enough for you, carpenters, to be diligent. Carpenters, a noble disciple possessed of four qualities is a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), no longer subject to rebirth in lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their destination.

“What are the four? Here, carpenters, a learned noble disciple is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One: an Arahant... Buddha, the Blessed One.’ In the Dhamma... In the Saṅgha... He dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, with hands purified by giving, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, delighting in sharing gifts, giving without discrimination. Carpenters, a noble disciple possessed of these four qualities is a Stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their destination.

“Carpenters, you are possessed of unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One: an Arahant... Buddha, the Blessed One.’ In the Dhamma... In the Saṅgha... and whatever gift there is in your family, you give it all without discrimination to those of virtuous and good character. Carpenters, what do you think? How many people are there in the Kosala country who are your equals in terms of sharing gifts?”

“Bhante, it is a gain for us, it is well-attained for us, that the Blessed One knows us thus,” they replied.

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

“By offering a single flower, for a thousand crore aeons,
I have been among gods and humans; with the remainder (of merit), I have attained Parinibbāna.”

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

“At the green-shining Assattha tree, well-grown,
Being mindful, I obtained a single perception directed towards the Buddha.

“For thirty aeons from then until today, I have not known a woeful state.
Through the habituation (vāsanā) of that perception, the three knowledges have been realized.”

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.
117:
The Buddha, the Supreme Person, who has compassion for all beings and has utterly destroyed craving, entered the city of Sāvatthī in the Kosala kingdom for alms in the morning.

A man held in his hand a head-garland adorned with various flowers. He saw the Fully Enlightened One, honored by gods and humans, entering via the royal road, preceded by the community of monks.

Seeing the Fully Enlightened One entering by the royal road, honored by gods and humans, he became joyful, and with a devout heart, he approached the Fully Enlightened One.

That man, with a devout heart, offered that fragrant, beautiful, and delightful head-garland to the Fully Enlightened One with his own hands.

Then, from between the lips of the Buddha, rays of light like the color of flames, with a thousand beams like lightning, emerged from his face.

Having circled the head of the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, to the right three times, they disappeared into the top of his head.

Seeing this marvelous and extraordinary event that caused one's hair to stand on end, the Venerable Ānanda, placing his robe over one shoulder, spoke thus:

"O Great Sage, leader of the silent ones, what is the cause of your smile? Please explain. The light of Dhamma shall arise; O Sage, dispel our doubts."

To the Elder Ānanda, who was in doubt and hesitation, the Buddha, whose knowledge always functions regarding all phenomena, spoke thus:

"Ānanda, that man who has gained devotion in me shall not go to a woeful state for eighty-four aeons.

Having enjoyed the splendor of the gods and divine kingship among the gods, he will become a king, a lord of men, in the kingdoms of humans.

In his final birth, having gone forth and realized the nature of Dhamma, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Vaṭaṃsaka, with all lust removed."

When the heart is devout toward the Tathāgata, the Fully Enlightened One, or toward his disciples, no gift is considered small.
118:
"Thus, the Buddhas are inconceivable, and the Dhamma of the Buddhas is inconceivable. For those devout in the inconceivable, the result is also inconceivable (exceedingly great)."

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

"Monks, in this Dispensation, I know a certain person with a devout heart, having encompassed his mind with my own. (This person behaves in such a way, practices such a path, and has embarked on such a way.) If this person were to die at this moment, he would be reborn in heaven, just as one might set down a burden that was carried. Why is that? Monks, it is because his heart is devout. Monks, because of a devout heart, some beings in this world, after the breaking up of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world." The Blessed One said this, and in this regard, it is said:

"The Buddha, having known a certain person in this world to have a devout heart, explained this matter in the presence of the monks.

If this person were to die at this moment, he would be reborn in heaven, for his heart has been made clear.

Because of a devout heart, beings go to a happy destination. Just as one might set down a carried load, so too a wise person with such a devout heart, at the breaking up of the body, is reborn in heaven."

"This meaning was also spoken by the Blessed One; so I have heard."

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

"O Goddess, you stand upon a boat adorned entirely with gold. You descend into the lotus pond and pluck a lotus with your hand.

Why is your complexion, your power, and your radiance like this? Why do all these pleasures that you desire in your mind arise for you?

O Goddess, being questioned by me, please tell me: of what action is this the result?"

That goddess, being questioned by the King of Gods, was delighted and replied thus:
119:
I have heard that the goddess, being questioned by Sakka, replied joyfully: "While traveling, I saw the delightful stupa of the glorious Kassapa Buddha and gained devotion in that stupa. With a devout heart, I worshipped it with lotus flowers; such is the result and fruit of that meritorious deed. Those who perform merit obtain such benefits."

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

Discourse on giving, discourse on virtue, discourse on heaven, discourse on merit, and discourse on the results of merit.

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

"Even in the case of stupas made of earth dedicated to the Buddhas who possess the ten powers, people who perform merit there rejoice in the heavens."

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

"All of you, who have complexions like those of the sons of gods and possess beautiful forms, sprinkle the earth with water and increase the stupa of Kassapa Buddha.

This is the stupa of the Sugata, the Great Sage, the bearer of the Dhamma of the ten powers. These gods and humans, being devout toward it and performing meritorious deeds, are liberated from old age and death."

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

"Indeed, that was a noble deed when I offered four blue lotuses and a garland to the stupa of the Great Sage. From that time until today, for thirty aeons, I have not known a woeful state. I do not go to a state of ruin because I worshipped the stupa of the Teacher."

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

"With a joyful heart, I worshipped the stupa of the Lord of the World, the conqueror of victories, who bears the thirty-two marks. Because of that worship, I have rejoiced for a hundred thousand aeons. Due to that merit I accumulated, I did not reach the four woeful states but obtained the splendor of the gods and kingship. In the Dispensation of the Buddha, who tames the untamed, I have established the noble eye; in that Dispensation, the mind..."
120:
"Whatever merit I have accumulated, by that merit I have achieved heavenly splendor and kingships, without falling into the four woeful states.

Whatever eye of wisdom was established in the Dispensation of the Blessed One, the Tamer of the untamed, all that mind of mine has been attained, with a mind liberated from defilements and the creeper of craving shaken off."

## This is a Sutta partaking of impressions (Vāsanābhāgiya).

"I gave a gift of only a measure of cooked millet rice to a Paccekabuddha who had a liberated mind, who was without blemish, taintless, dwelling in peace, and with a mind free from attachment.

I gained faith in the supreme Dhamma in that Paccekabuddha, and I firmly fixed my mind on that Dhamma. [I prayed:] 'May I have association with such Noble Ones who dwell free from the dust of defilements, and may I never have longing for sensual pleasures in any existence.'

As a result of that deed, I was reborn a thousand times in Uttarakuru, among long-lived beings who have no sense of 'mine', who have an excellent destination, and whose prosperity does not diminish.

As a result of that deed, I was reborn a thousand times in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, as a famous deity endowed with an excellent physical appearance, adorned with various garlands and ointments.

As a result of that very deed, I now have a liberated mind, am without blemish, and am taintless; and I have come to associate with these various Noble Ones who bear their final bodies."
121:
The Tathāgata, the Conqueror who defeated the five Maras, personally said these words: "Whatever a virtuous person wishes for, that wish is fulfilled." In whatever way I have thought with my mind, in those very ways it has been fulfilled for me; this is my final birth.

## This sutta is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

Thirty-one aeons ago, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Conqueror who was free from craving and possessed infinite vision, appeared. The King who was his younger brother was also greatly devoted to the Buddha and the Dhamma.

When the Guide of the World had attained Parinibbāna, he built a vast and great stupa for the Great Sage, the God above gods, the Supreme Man, measuring three gāvutas all around.

At that stupa, a man came to pay homage with a jasmine flower (jātisumana) with a very joyful mind. I picked up a single flower that had fallen due to the wind and gave it to him.

With a very devoted heart, he said to me, "I give this flower only to you." I took that flower and, repeatedly recollecting the Buddha, offered it at that stupa.

From that aeon, this is now the thirtieth aeon. Since then, I have not known a woeful state, nor have I gone to hell; this is the fruit of worshipping the stupa.

## This sutta is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.

The city named Kapila of King Brahmadatta was well-apportioned, had wide main roads, was crowded with people, and was prosperous and flourishing.
122:
I sold balls of cake (kummāsa) there in that supreme city of the Pañcālas (Kapila). Then I saw the famous Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha.

With a joyful mind, having gained faith, I invited the Supreme Man Ariṭṭha (the Paccekabuddha) to a meal that I had in my house.

Afterwards, when the full moon day associated with the Kattika constellation arrived, I took a new pair of robes and offered them to Ariṭṭha.

Knowing my devoted heart, that Sage (the Paccekabuddha), who was compassionate, merciful, and the destroyer of craving, accepted (the offering).

Having performed that good deed praised by the Buddhas, I wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and then passed away from that deva existence.

I was born in the city of Bārāṇasī as the only son of a merchant in a wealthy family, being more beloved than life itself.

Then, having reached the age of wisdom, urged by a son of the devas (a divine messenger), I descended from the palace and approached the Buddha.

That Buddha of the Gotama lineage, out of compassion, taught me the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths: suffering (dukkha-sacca), the cause of suffering (samudaya-sacca), the cessation of suffering (nirodha-sacca), and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering (magga-sacca).

Having heard the words of that Buddha, I lived delighting in the Teaching. Day and night, without laziness, I penetrated and realized Samatha.

All the taints (āsavas) that existed within and without me have been thoroughly cut off; they will not arise again.

I have made an end to suffering. This body is my last. The round of rebirth and death is broken; now there is no more renewed existence.

## This is the Vāsanābhāgiya Sutta.
123:
In that context, which sutta is called the sutta conducive to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya)?

One who is liberated from defilements above, below, and in every direction, and who does not perceive that "this [five aggregates] is I";
Being thus liberated, he has crossed the flood that was never crossed before, for the sake of no more rebirth.

## This is a Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

"Ānanda, for a person of virtue, no volition needs to be made (no effort through intention is required) thinking, 'May freedom from remorse arise in me.' It is the nature (dhammatā), Ānanda, that freedom from remorse arises for a person of virtue. Ānanda, for one who is free from remorse, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May joy arise in me.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that joy arises for one who is free from remorse. Ānanda, for one who is joyful, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May rapture (pīti) arise in me.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that rapture arises for one who is joyful. Ānanda, for one with a rapturous mind, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May my body be tranquil.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that the body becomes tranquil for one with a rapturous mind. Ānanda, for one with a tranquil body, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May I experience happiness.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that one with a tranquil body experiences happiness. Ānanda, for one who is happy, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May concentration (samādhi) arise in me.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that concentration arises for one who is happy. Ānanda, for one who is concentrated, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May I know and see things as they really are.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that one who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are. Ānanda, for one who knows and sees things as they really are, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May disenchantment (nibbidā) arise in me.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that one who knows and sees things as they really are becomes disenchanted. Ānanda, for one who is disenchanted, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May dispassion (virāga) arise in me.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that one who is disenchanted becomes dispassionate. Ānanda, for one who is dispassionate, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May liberation (vimutti) arise in me.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that one who is dispassionate becomes liberated. Ānanda, for one who is liberated, no volition needs to be made thinking, 'May the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana) arise in me.' It is the nature, Ānanda, that the knowledge and vision of liberation arises for one who is liberated."

## This is a Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.
124:
Indeed, when the qualities (dhammas) of enlightenment become manifest to the ardent, meditating Brahmin who has discarded evil, then all his doubts vanish, because he understands the Dhamma along with its cause.

## This sutta is called a sutta conducive to penetration.

Indeed, when the qualities of enlightenment become manifest to the ardent, meditating Brahmin who has discarded evil, then all his doubts vanish, because he has known the destruction of causes (Nibbāna).

## This sutta is called a sutta conducive to penetration.

Tissa, why are you angry? Do not be angry; non-anger is better for you. Indeed, Tissa, the holy life is lived for the purpose of subduing anger, conceit, and disparagement.

## This sutta is called a sutta conducive to penetration.

When shall I see Nanda, who dwells in the forest, wears rag-robes, subsists on unknown alms, and is indifferent to sensual pleasures?

## This sutta is called a sutta conducive to penetration.

"O Gotama, what having killed does one sleep happily? What having killed does one not sorrow? Of what single thing's killing do you approve?"

"Brahmin, having killed anger, which has a poisoned root and a honeyed tip, one sleeps happily; having killed anger, one does not sorrow. The Noble Ones praise the killing of anger, for having killed it, one does not sorrow."

## This sutta is called a sutta conducive to penetration.

What should be killed when it constantly arises? What that has arisen within oneself should be removed? What should the wise person abandon? The realization of what brings happiness?
125:
One should kill anger when it constantly arises; one should remove lust that has arisen. The wise person should abandon ignorance (avijjā); the realization of the Four Noble Truths brings happiness.

## This is a Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

As if pierced by a spear, or as if one's head were on fire, a mindful monk should wander forth to abandon sensual lust.

As if pierced by a spear, or as if one's head were on fire, a mindful monk should wander forth to abandon self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi).

## This is a Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

All accumulated wealth ends in exhaustion; all erected buildings end in collapse. All beings must face death; the lives of all beings are uncertain. Seeing this danger in death, one should perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness.

All accumulated wealth ends in exhaustion; all erected buildings end in collapse. All beings must face death; the lives of all beings are uncertain. Seeing this danger in death, one who seeks peace should abandon the baits of the world, namely sensual pleasures.

## This is a Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

Sages (munis) sleep happily; they do not sorrow in this world. Those whose minds delight in meditation (jhāna), who are wise and well-concentrated, with energy aroused and self-resolute, cross the flood (ogha) that is difficult to cross.

Detached from sensual perception, having transcended all fetters, with craving for existence exhausted, such a person does not sink in the deep ocean of saṃsāra.

## This is a Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

One who has faith in the Dhamma of the Arahants for the attainment of Nibbāna, being heedful and discerning, gains wisdom through the desire to learn.
126:
One who acts appropriately, who is responsible, and who is energetic gains wealth. Through truth, one attains fame. One who gives binds friends through the acts of service. Thus, one endowed with truth and other virtues does not grieve when passing from this world to the next.

## This is the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

For a monk like you, who has abandoned all bonds, who is liberated from defilements, and who is peaceful, it is not good to admonish others (with a corrupt mind).

Association arises through some cause or another. A wise person should not pity such a person with the mind in every way.

If one admonishes another with a clear mind, one is not bound (by sensual fetters etc.) because of that admonition. Whatever compassion and loving-kindness there is, one is bound only by the power of that compassion and love.

## This is the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

Where do lust and hatred originate? From where do boredom, delight, and horripilation arise? From where do mental thoughts arise and release the wholesome mind, like boys surrounding and releasing a crow?

Lust and hatred originate from this (self). Boredom, delight, and horripilation arise from this. Mental thoughts arise from this and release the wholesome mind, like boys releasing a crow.

Born of affection and produced from self, like branches from the trunk of a banyan tree, (defilements) are widely spread and attached to sensual pleasures, like the māluvā creeper spreading in the forest.

Those who know these defilements as originating from this (craving), they dispel them. O Yakkha, they cross this flood, so difficult to cross and never crossed before, for the sake of non-rebirth.

## This is the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.
127:
"Lord, (practicing the life of a monk) is difficult, very difficult," (the young deity) said.

"Kāmada, those in training (sekhas) who are endowed with virtue and composed do even what is difficult. For one who has reached monkhood, contentment brings happiness," (the Blessed One) said.

"Lord, contentment is hard to obtain," (the young deity) said.

"Kāmada, those who delight in the stilling of the mind, whose minds delight in meditation day and night, obtain even the contentment that is hard to obtain," (the Blessed One) said.

"Lord, the mind is hard to compose," (the young deity) said.

"Kāmada, those who delight in the stilling of the faculties compose even the mind that is hard to compose. Those Noble Ones, having cut the net of Death (defilements), go forth," (the Blessed One) said.

"Lord, the path (the Noble Path) is difficult to travel and uneven," (the young deity) said.

"Kāmada, Noble Ones travel even on the path that is difficult and uneven. Those who are not Noble fall headlong on the uneven path. For Noble Ones, the path is even, because Noble Ones practice evenly in the midst of the uneven," (the Blessed One) said.

## This is the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

"This Jeta's Grove is frequented by the community of seers. It is inhabited by the King of Dhamma (the Buddha). It gives me joy.

Action (volition), knowledge, Dhamma (the Path), and virtue—this is the supreme life. By these alone are mortals purified, not by lineage or wealth.

Therefore, a wise man, seeing his own benefit, should investigate the Dhamma in the proper way. Thus investigating, he is purified in that Dhamma."
128:
In wisdom, in virtue, and in the stilling of defilements, even a monk who has reached the further shore (Nibbāna) would find that Sāriputta is supreme.

## This sutta is called the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

One should not follow after the past (five aggregates) with craving and views, nor long for the future. What is past is gone, and the future has not yet come.

But whoever sees with insight the present state just as it is, the wise one should develop that insight, which is unshakeable and immovable (by lust etc.).

Effort should be made today; who knows if death will come tomorrow? There is no bargaining with Death and his great army.

One who dwells thus, ardent, tireless day and night—the peaceful Sage calls such a one 'one who has an auspicious night' (bhaddekaratta).

## This sutta is called the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.

Monks, there are these four things to be realized. Which four? Monks, there are things to be realized by the eye and wisdom; things to be realized by mindfulness and wisdom; things to be realized by the body (mental body) and wisdom; things to be known by wisdom and realized by wisdom.

Monks, what things are to be realized by the eye and wisdom? The divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), which is purified and surpasses the human eye, is to be realized by the eye and wisdom.

Monks, what things are to be realized by mindfulness and wisdom? The recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati) is to be realized by mindfulness and wisdom.

Monks, what things are to be realized by the body (mental body) and wisdom? The various psychic powers (iddhividha) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are to be realized by the body and wisdom.

Monks, what things are to be known by wisdom and realized by wisdom? The knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavas) is to be known by wisdom and realized by wisdom.

## This sutta is called the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta.
129:
Among those suttas, which sutta is an Asekkhabhāgiya sutta (belonging to the category of the Adept)?

“Whose mind is like a rock, standing firm and unshakable,
Detached from objects that provoke lust, and not angered by objects that provoke anger,
For one whose mind is thus developed, from where can suffering come?”

## This is an Asekkhabhāgiya Sutta.

The tenth exposition (Veyyākaraṇa) of Venerable Sāriputta's travels should also be made.

## This is an Asekkhabhāgiya Sutta.

“That Brahmin who has put away evil dhammas, who is free from arrogance, stainless, and self-restrained,
Who has reached the end of the Vedas and lived the holy life, he would rightly speak the word of Brahman,
For whom there are no swellings (of defilements) anywhere in the world.”

## This is an Asekkhabhāgiya Sutta.

“Having put away evil dhammas, those who live always mindful,
With fetters destroyed and awakened (Buddhas), they are truly the Brahmins in the world.”

## This is an Asekkhabhāgiya Sutta.

“Where water, earth, fire, and air find no footing,
There the stars do not shine, the sun is not visible,
The moon does not glow, and darkness is not found there.

When the sage, the Brahmin, knows this for himself through wisdom,
Then he is freed from the material and the immaterial, and from pleasure and pain.”

## This is an Asekkhabhāgiya Sutta.

“When the Brahmin reaches the far shore in his own dhammas (the aggregates) through insight,
Then he transcends this demon and the Asura Pakkula.”

## This is an Asekkhabhāgiya Sutta.
130:
He does not delight in the future life, nor does he grieve for the past life; freed from the five kinds of attachments, with defilements cut off at the root—him I call a Brahmin.

## This is a sutta belonging to the category of the Adept (Asekkhabhāgiya).

In this world, many people bathe by immersing themselves in water. One does not become pure from evil by that water. In whom there is the truth of speech and the truth of abstinence, as well as the remaining factors of the Noble Path—he is pure, and he alone is truly a Brahmin.

## This is a sutta belonging to the category of the Adept (Asekkhabhāgiya).

When the factors of enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) truly become manifest to the ardent, meditating Brahmin, then that Brahmin stands dispelling the army of Māra, just as the sun stands illuminating the sky while destroying the darkness.

## This is a sutta belonging to the category of the Adept (Asekkhabhāgiya).

Behold him who practices with peaceful senses, who has reached the three knowledges (te-vijja), whose dhammas are non-declining, who has transcended all bonds (yogas), and who practices without anxiety, wearing rag-robes.

Many noble deities, having approached the Brahma-mansion with clear minds, pay homage to that noble man who subdues the power of birth (or the strength of the Brahmin caste).

Homage to you, O noble man! Homage to you, O supreme man! We do not know what you are meditating upon.

## This is a sutta belonging to the category of the Adept (Asekkhabhāgiya).

These monks are indeed companions; they have been together for a long time. In the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha, the True Dhamma is harmonious for these monks.
131:
“Being well-trained by Kappina in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones, they bear their final body, having conquered Māra and his army.”

## This is a sutta belonging to the category of the Adept.

“This Nibbāna, which is the release from all suffering, is not to be reached by slackening effort or with little strength.

This monk, as well as this supreme man, bears his final body, having conquered Māra and his army.”

## This is a sutta belonging to the category of the Adept.

“This monk named Mogharāja, of poor appearance and wearing rough robes, is always mindful, with taints destroyed, free from bonds, his task done, and taintless.

Possessing the three knowledges, having reached psychic power, and being skilled in the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-abhiññā), he bears his final body, having conquered Māra and his army.”

## This is a sutta belonging to the category of the Adept.

“Monks, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called 'Perfectly Enlightened' because of disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and liberation through non-clinging regarding form. Monks, a monk liberated by wisdom is also called 'liberated by wisdom' because of disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and liberation through non-clinging regarding form.

Monks, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called 'Perfectly Enlightened' because of disenchantment... regarding feeling... regarding perception... regarding volitional formations... regarding consciousness. Monks, a monk liberated by wisdom is also called 'liberated by wisdom' because of disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and liberation through non-clinging regarding consciousness.

Monks, among them, what is the distinction, what is the excellence, what is the difference between the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the monk liberated by wisdom? Venerable Sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root...

Monks, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the originator of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path...”
132:
Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is the proclaimer of the Noble Path that was undeclared, the knower of the Noble Path, the one who has realized the Noble Path, and the one skilled in the Noble Path. Bhikkhus, now the disciples dwell following the path, becoming possessed of it afterwards. Bhikkhus, this is the distinction, the specific intent, and the difference between the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, and a bhikkhu liberated by wisdom.

## This is a sutta pertaining to the state of one beyond training (Asekkhabhāgiya).

Among those suttas, which sutta pertains both to defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya) and to cultivation (Vāsanābhāgiya)?

'Rain soddens what is covered; it does not sodden what is open. Therefore, open what is covered; thus the rain will not sodden it.'

In the passage, 'Rain soddens what is covered,' it refers to defilement because it describes the state of being sodden by rain for one who has a covered house. In the passage, 'It does not sodden what is open,' it refers to cultivation because it describes the state of not being sodden by rain for one who has an open house. In the passage, 'Therefore, open what is covered; thus the rain will not sodden it,' it refers to both defilement and cultivation because it describes the opening of the cover and the state of not being sodden. This is a sutta that pertains both to defilement and to cultivation.

'Great King, these four types of persons are found existing in the world. Which four? One who is in darkness and bound for darkness; one who is in darkness and bound for light; one who is in light and bound for darkness; and one who is in light and bound for light.' Among these four, the person who is in light and bound for darkness and the person who is in darkness and bound for darkness pertain to the category of defilement. The person who is in darkness and bound for light and the person who is in light and bound for light pertain to the category of cultivation. This is a sutta that pertains both to defilement and to cultivation.

Among those suttas, which sutta pertains both to defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya) and to penetration (Nibbedhabhāgiya)?

'The wise do not say that a bond made of iron, wood, or grass is a strong bond. Attachment and longing for jeweled earrings, children, and wives are the real bonds.'

This refers to defilement.

'The wise say that this bond of defilement is strong, which pulls one down, is seemingly loose yet hard to release. Having cut even this strong bond of defilement, the wise wander forth, without longing, having abandoned sensual pleasures.'
133:
This refers to penetration (Nibbedha). This sutta pertains both to defilement and to penetration.

“Bhikkhus, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has an underlying tendency towards: this becomes an object for the stationing of consciousness. When there is an object, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is stationed and grows, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there arise future birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Bhikkhus, if one does not intend and does not plan, but an underlying tendency still remains: this becomes an object for the stationing of consciousness. When there is an object, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is stationed and grows, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there arise future birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering, unmixed with happiness.” This refers to defilement.

“Bhikkhus, when one does not intend, does not plan, and has no underlying tendency: this does not become an object for the stationing of consciousness. When there is no object, there is no support for consciousness. When consciousness is not stationed and does not grow, there is no production of renewed existence in the future. When there is no production of renewed existence in the future, future birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering, unmixed with happiness.” This refers to penetration. This sutta pertains both to defilement and to penetration.

Among those suttas, which sutta pertains both to defilement (Saṃkilesabhāgiya) and to the state of one beyond training (Asekkhabhāgiya)?

“Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling is accustomed to saying, ‘The ocean, the ocean.’ Bhikkhus, in the discipline of the Noble Ones, that is not the ocean; that is a great mass of water, a great expanse of water. Bhikkhus, the eye is the ocean for a man; its tide consists of forms. This refers to defilement.”
134:
Monks, the monk who can withstand that surge consisting of forms is said to have crossed the ocean of the eye, with its waves, whirlpools, sharks, and demons. Having crossed and reached the other shore, that Brahmin stands on dry land. This is the Asekha (one beyond training).

Monks, the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... Monks, the mind is a man's ocean; its surge consists of mental objects. This is Saṃkilesa (defilement).

Monks, the monk who can withstand that surge consisting of mental objects is said to have crossed the ocean of the mind, with its waves, whirlpools, sharks, and demons. Having crossed and reached the other shore, that Brahmin stands on dry land. This is the Asekha. The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:

'He who has crossed this ocean with its sharks and demons,
With its waves, whirlpools, and dangers, so difficult to cross,
He is called a knower of the end of the path (vedantagū), one who has lived the holy life,
One who has reached the end of the world, one who has gone to the further shore.'

This is the Asekha. This sutta is one that pertains to both Saṃkilesa and Asekha.

Monks, there are these six fish-hooks in the world for the misfortune, harm, and destruction of beings. What are the six? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them, monks, this monk is called one who has swallowed Māra's hook, who has met with misfortune and ruin, and who can be dealt with by the Evil One according to his wish.

Monks, there are sounds cognizable by the ear... odors cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tangibles cognizable by the body... mental objects cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them, monks, this monk is called one who has swallowed Māra's hook, who has met with misfortune and ruin, and who can be dealt with by the Evil One according to his wish. This is Saṃkilesa.
135:
Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a monk does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, monks, this monk is called one who has not swallowed Māra's hook, who has broken the hook, who has utterly destroyed the hook, who has not met with misfortune or ruin, and who is not one to be dealt with by the Evil One according to his wish.

Monks, there are sounds cognizable by the ear... and mental objects cognizable by the mind. If a monk does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, monks, this monk is called one who has not swallowed Māra's hook, who has broken the hook, who has utterly destroyed the hook, who has not met with misfortune or ruin, and who is not one to be dealt with by the Evil One according to his wish. This is the Asekha (Arahant). This sutta is one that pertains to both Saṃkilesa and Asekha.

Among those suttas, which is the sutta that pertains to Saṃkilesa, Nibbedha (penetration), and Asekha?

This world is afflicted by heat, overwhelmed by contact; it calls suffering 'self'. In whatever way it conceives [of things], it turns out otherwise than that.

Becoming otherwise, the world is attached to existence, overwhelmed by existence, and delights only in existence. That which it delights in is fear; that of which it is afraid is suffering. This is Saṃkilesa.

'This holy life is lived for the complete abandoning of existence.' This is Nibbedha.

'Whatever ascetics or brahmins say that liberation from existence is by means of existence, I say that none of them are liberated from existence. Or whatever ascetics or brahmins say that escape from existence is by means of non-existence (vibhava), I say that none of them have escaped from existence. For this suffering arises dependent on acquisitions (upadhi).' This is Saṃkilesa.
136:
“With the destruction of all clinging, there is no arising of suffering.” This teaching is nibbedha (penetration).

“Look at this world: many beings, overwhelmed by ignorance, are attached to what has come to be and delight in what has come to be; they are not released from existence. Whatever existences there are, in every way and everywhere, all those existences are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.” This teaching is saṃkilesa (defilement).

“Thus, for one who sees this existence as it really is with right wisdom, craving for existence is abandoned, and one does not delight in non-existence. With the destruction of cravings in every way, the remainderless fading away and cessation is Nibbāna.” This teaching is nibbedha (penetration).

“For that bhikkhu who is quenched, there is no further existence because of non-clinging. Having conquered the five Māras and won the battle, that such a one (tādī) has transcended all existences.” This teaching is asekha (the one beyond training/arahant). This sutta pertains to the side of defilement, the side of penetration, and the side of the one beyond training.

“Monks, there are these four persons. Which four? One who goes with the stream (anusotagāmī), one who goes against the stream (paṭisotagāmī), one who is steady in self (ṭhitatto), and the brahmin (arahant) who has crossed over, reached the far shore, and stands on dry land.” Among those four, the person who goes with the stream stands on the side of defilement. Among those four, the person who goes against the stream and the person who is steady in self stand on the side of penetration. Among those four, the brahmin who has crossed over, reached the far shore, and stands on dry land is an asekha. This sutta pertains to the side of defilement, the side of penetration, and the side of the one beyond training.

Among those suttas, which sutta pertains to the side of defilement, the side of habitual tendencies (vāsanā), and the side of penetration?

There are six types of persons born in various ways. There is a person who, being dark and born into a dark class, produces dark unwholesome states. There is a person who, being dark and born into a dark class, produces bright wholesome states. There is a person who, being dark and born into a dark class, attains Nibbāna which is clearly seen, having results that are neither dark nor bright.
137:
There is a person who, being bright and born into a bright class, produces dark unwholesome states. There is a person who, being bright and born into a bright class, produces bright wholesome states. There is a person who, being bright and born into a bright class, attains Nibbāna which is clearly seen, having results that are neither dark nor bright. Among these four persons, the person who is dark, born into a dark class, and produces dark unwholesome states, and the person who is bright, born into a bright class, but produces dark unwholesome states—these two persons stand on the side of defilement. Among those four, the person who is dark, born into a dark class, but produces bright wholesome states, and the person who is bright, born into a bright class, and produces bright wholesome states—these two persons stand on the side of habitual tendencies (vāsanā). Among those four, the person who is dark, born into a dark class, but attains Nibbāna which is clearly seen, having results that are neither dark nor bright, and the person who is bright, born into a bright class, and attains Nibbāna which is clearly seen, having results that are neither dark nor bright—these two persons stand on the side of penetration. This is a sutta that pertains to the side of defilement, the side of habitual tendencies, and the side of penetration.

Monks, there are these four kinds of kamma. Which four? There is dark kamma with dark results. There is bright kamma with bright results. There is dark-and-bright kamma with dark-and-bright results. There is kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright results, which is supreme among kammas, especially excellent, and leads to the destruction of kamma. Among these four kinds of kamma, dark kamma with dark results and dark-and-bright kamma with dark-and-bright results are called defilement. Bright kamma with bright results is called habitual tendency (vāsanā). Kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright results, which is supreme among kammas, especially excellent, and leads to the destruction of kamma, is called penetration. This is a sutta that pertains to the side of defilement, the side of habitual tendencies, and the side of penetration.

Among those suttas, which sutta pertains to both the side of habitual tendencies and the side of penetration?

“Having attained the human state, (discerning) the two tasks—the duty and the non-duty—one should perform the good deeds of the right duty, or the abandoning of the fetters,” so it was said.
138:
"Meritorious deeds that are only good tasks should be performed"—this is vāsanā. "Or, the abandoning of fetters should be performed"—this is nibbedha.

"Having performed meritorious deeds, those who have done merit go from a happy state to a happy state. Through the abandoning of fetters, they are released from aging and death."

"Having performed meritorious deeds, those who have done merit go from a happy state to a happy state"—this is vāsanā. "Through the abandoning of fetters, they are released from aging and death"—this is nibbedha. This sutta is one that partakes in both vāsanā (vāsanābhāgiya) and nibbedha (nibbedhabhāgiya).

"Monks, there are these two kinds of efforts (padhāna). Which two? One who gives robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick to those who have gone forth from home to homelessness. And one who (strives for) Nibbāna—the relinquishment of all acquisitions (upadhi), the destruction of craving, dispassion, and cessation—for those who have gone forth from home to homelessness." Among these two, giving robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick to those who have gone forth from home to homelessness is vāsanā. Nibbāna—the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, and cessation—for those who have gone forth from home to homelessness is nibbedha. This sutta is one that partakes in both vāsanā and nibbedha.

Among those suttas, a sutta partaking in the defilement of craving (taṇhā-saṃkilesabhāgiya) should be shown by way of the group of cravings alone, through the three cravings: sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). Or else, it should be shown by whatever object one is attached to. The detail of that craving consists of the thirty-six nets of craving (taṇhā-vicarita).

Among those suttas, a sutta partaking in the defilement of views (diṭṭhi-saṃkilesabhāgiya) should be shown by way of the group of views alone, through annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) and eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi). Or else, it should be shown by whatever object one adheres to by the power of views, thinking, "This alone is the truth, everything else is empty." The detail of those views consists of the sixty-two types of views.

Among those suttas, a sutta partaking in the defilement of misconduct (duccarita-saṃkilesabhāgiya) should be shown by way of volition (cetanā), by mental action (cetasika-kamma), and by the three types of misconduct: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. The detail of that misconduct consists of the ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha).
139:
Among those suttas, a sutta partaking in the purification of craving (taṇhā-vodānabhāgiya) should be shown by way of serenity (samatha). A sutta partaking in the purification of views (diṭṭhi-vodānabhāgiya) should be shown by way of insight (vipassanā). A sutta partaking in the purification of misconduct (duccarita-vodānabhāgiya) should be shown by way of good conduct (sucarita). There are three unwholesome roots. Why is this so? It is because of the arising of saṃsāra. In saṃsāra thus arisen, bodily misconduct, bodily good conduct, verbal misconduct, verbal good conduct, mental misconduct, and mental good conduct occur. This sutta, which states that "by the result of this unlovely kamma, this mark of a fool (bāla-lakkhaṇa) arises," is a sutta partaking in defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya).

This sutta, which states that "by the result of this lovely kamma, this mark of a Great Man (mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa) arises," is a sutta partaking in vāsanā (vāsanābhāgiya).

Among those suttas, a sutta partaking in defilement should be shown by way of the four planes of defilement: the plane of latent tendencies (anusaya-bhūmi), the plane of obsessions (pariyuṭṭhāna-bhūmi), the plane of fetters (saṃyojana-bhūmi), and the plane of clinging (upādāna-bhūmi). For one with unabandoned latent tendencies, obsession arises; one overcome by obsession is bound by fetters; one bound by fetters clings; with clinging as condition, existence (bhava) comes to be; with existence as condition, birth (jāti) comes to be; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. Through these four planes of defilement, all defilements reach inclusion and convergence. This is a sutta partaking in defilement.

A sutta partaking in vāsanā should be shown by way of the three good conducts. A sutta partaking in penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya) should be shown by way of the four truths. A sutta partaking in the state of a non-learner (asekkhabhāgiya) should be shown by way of the three things: the qualities of a Buddha (Buddha-dhamma), the qualities of a Paccekabuddha (Paccekabuddha-dhamma), and the plane of a disciple (sāvaka-bhūmi). It should be shown in the domain of one who meditates (jhāyi-visaya).

Among those root terms, what are the eighteen root terms (mūlapada)? They are: the mundane (lokiya), the supramundane (lokuttara), and both the mundane and supramundane; the person-based (sattādhiṭṭhāna), the Dhamma-based (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), and both the person-based and Dhamma-based; knowledge (ñāṇa), the knowable (ñeyya), and both knowledge and the knowable; vision (dassana), development (bhāvanā), and both vision and development; own words (sakavacana), others' words (paravacana), and both own words and others' words; the answerable (vissajjanīya), the unanswerable (avissajjanīya), and both the answerable and unanswerable; kamma, result (vipāka), and both kamma and result; the wholesome (kusala), the unwholesome (akusala), and both the wholesome and unwholesome; the permitted (anuññāta), the prohibited (paṭikkhitta), and both the permitted and prohibited; and praise (thava).
140:
Among those (eighteen discourses), which is the mundane discourse?

An evil deed committed does not immediately curdle like fresh milk; it follows the fool, smoldering like fire covered by ashes, waiting to bring its result.

## This is mundane.

"Monks, there are these four wrong courses... (and so on) ... Just as the moon wanes in the dark fortnight, so the fame of one who follows such wrong courses wanes." This is mundane.

"Monks, there are these eight worldly conditions. Which eight? Gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, happiness and pain. Monks, these are the eight worldly conditions." This is mundane.

Among those, which is the supramundane discourse?

Whose senses are stilled, like horses well-tamed by a charioteer; for such a one, free from pride and without taints (āsavas), even the gods envy that stable one.

## This is supramundane.

"Monks, there are these five supramundane faculties. Which five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Monks, these are the five supramundane faculties." This is supramundane.

Among those, which is the discourse that is both mundane and supramundane?

The two verses beginning with "Having obtained the human state, two things: duty and non-duty." The portion containing "good duties and meritorious deeds" and "having performed meritorious deeds, those who have done merit go from heaven to heaven" is the mundane discourse.

The portion containing "the complete abandoning of fetters" and "through the abandoning of fetters, they are liberated from aging and death" is the supramundane discourse. This is the discourse that is both mundane and supramundane.
141:
"Monks, when there is the nutriment of consciousness, there is the descent of name-and-form. When there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the occurrence of renewed existence. When there is the occurrence of renewed existence, there is birth. When there is birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. Monks, suppose there were a great tree; its roots going downwards and its roots going sideward all draw up the sap. Monks, thus that great tree, having that sap as its nutriment and that sap as its sustenance, would stand for a long time. In the same way, monks, when there is the nutriment of consciousness, there is the descent of name-and-form... (all) ... Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering." This is mundane.

"Monks, when there is no nutriment of consciousness, there is no descent of name-and-form. When there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no occurrence of renewed existence. When there is no occurrence of renewed existence, there is no birth. When there is no birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Monks, suppose there were a great tree, and a man were to come with a hoe and a basket. He would cut the tree at its root, dig it up, and pull out the roots, even the fine ones like the roots of usīra grass. He would cut the tree into pieces, split the pieces, and reduce them to splinters. He would dry the splinters in the wind and sun, burn them with fire, and reduce them to ashes. He would then winnow the ashes in a strong wind or let them be carried away by a swift-flowing river. Monks, thus that great tree would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. In the same way, monks, when there is no nutriment of consciousness, there is no descent of name-and-form... (all) ... Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering." This is supramundane. This is both mundane and supramundane.
142:
Among those (teachings), what is the teaching based on beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna)?

"Having traversed all directions with the mind, one finds no one dearer than oneself in any place. In this way, for each individual, their own self is dear. Therefore, one who loves oneself should not harm others."

## This is the teaching based on beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna).

"All beings that have been and all those that will be, all these beings will go, abandoning the body. Knowing this, the wise person, being ardent, should practice the holy life."

## This is the teaching based on beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna).

"Monks, a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta) endowed with seven qualities should not be abandoned for as long as one lives, even if one is excluded, sent away, or treated harshly by the neck. What are the seven? He is dear, respected, and praiseworthy; he is a counselor and patient in speech; he speaks deep discourse and does not urge one to what is wrong. Monks, a noble friend endowed with these seven qualities should not be abandoned for as long as one lives." The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:

"Dear, respected, and praiseworthy, a counselor and patient in speech,
Speaker of deep discourse, and one who does not urge one to what is wrong;
That friend should be associated with by one desiring a friend, even for as long as one lives."

## This is the teaching based on beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna).

Among those (teachings), what is the teaching based on phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna)?

"Whatever sensual happiness there is in the world, and whatever divine happiness there is in heaven,
These are not worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of the destruction of craving (taṇhakkhaya)."

## This is the teaching based on phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna).
143:
"Nibbāna taught by the Fully Enlightened One is truly very happy. In that Nibbāna, suffering ceases. It is sorrowless, stainless, and secure."

## This is the teaching based on phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna).

Among those (suttas), what is both the teaching based on beings and the teaching based on phenomena?

"Having killed craving which is like a mother, and conceit which is like a father; and having killed the two kings of the warrior caste, namely the two views of eternalism and nihilism; and having destroyed the kingdom together with its followers, namely the twelve bases (āyatana) along with the delight and lust that are like a tax-collecting clerk." This is the teaching based on phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna).

"The Arahant (Brahmana) who is free from suffering goes (to Nibbāna)." This is the teaching based on beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna). This is both the teaching based on beings and the teaching based on phenomena.

"Monks, there are these four bases of power (iddhipāda). What are the four? The base of power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; the base of power endowed with concentration due to energy... mind... investigation and volitional formations of striving." This is the teaching based on phenomena (dhammādhiṭṭhāna).

"That person places the mind well in the body, and places the body well in the mind. Having entered upon the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness in the body, he dwells therein." This is the teaching based on beings (sattādhiṭṭhāna). This is both the teaching based on beings and the teaching based on phenomena.

Among those (suttas), what is knowledge (ñāṇa)?

"That supramundane knowledge which exists, by which one is called 'Omniscient'; for that knowledge there is no decline, and it proceeds at all times."

## This is knowledge (ñāṇa).

"Wisdom is indeed supreme in the world, that which leads to Nibbāna. By that wisdom, one truly knows Nibbāna, which is the end of birth and death."

## This is knowledge (ñāṇa).

Among those (suttas), what is the knowable (ñeyya)?

"Dhotaka, I shall proclaim to you the peace (Nibbāna), which is to be realized in this very life without traditional hearsay. Knowing which, and wandering mindfully, one may cross over the craving that clings to the world."
144:
"O Blessed One, knowing that Nibbāna and practicing with mindfulness, one can cross over the craving that clings to the world; I, the Buddha, greatly delight in that supreme peace."

"Dhotaka, whatever you cognize—above (the future), below (the past), and across the middle (the present)—knowing this as an attachment in the world, do not create craving for existence or non-existence."

## This is the knowable (ñeyya).

"Monks, it is because of not understanding and not penetrating the Four Noble Truths that both you and I have run and wandered for such a long time in this Saṃsāra. ... Monks, this Noble Truth of Suffering has been understood and penetrated. The Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering has been understood and penetrated. The Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering has been understood and penetrated. The Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering has been understood and penetrated. Craving for existence has been cut off; the cord of existence (bhavanetti) is exhausted; now there is no more renewed existence." The Blessed One said this. Having spoken this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this verse:

"Because of not seeing the Four Noble Truths as they really are,
We have wandered for a long time in various births.
These truths have now been seen; the cord of existence is uprooted;
The root of suffering is cut; now there is no more renewed existence."

## This is the knowable (ñeyya).

Among those twenty-eight suttas, what is both knowledge and the knowable (ñāṇañca ñeyyañca)? "Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent." This is the knowable (ñeyya).

The noble disciple who knows and sees thus, sees "Form is impermanent," sees "Feeling is impermanent," and sees perception, formations, and consciousness as "impermanent." This is knowledge (ñāṇa).

"That noble disciple is liberated from form, liberated from feeling, liberated from perception, liberated from formations, liberated from consciousness, and liberated from suffering," I say. This is both knowledge and the knowable (ñāṇañca ñeyyañca).
145:
“All formations are impermanent”—this is what is to be known (ñeyya). “When one sees with wisdom”—this is knowledge (ñāṇa). “Then one becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification”—this is both knowledge and what is to be known.

“All formations are suffering”—this is what is to be known (ñeyya). “When one sees with wisdom”—this is knowledge (ñāṇa). “Then one becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification”—this is both knowledge and what is to be known.

“All phenomena are non-self”—this is what is to be known (ñeyya). “When one sees with wisdom”—this is knowledge (ñāṇa). “Then one becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification”—this is both knowledge and what is to be known.

“Soṇa, whatever recluses or brahmins, regarding the impermanent, suffering, and subject-to-change form, perceive it as ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’—what else is this but a failure to see things as they really are? Regarding impermanent feeling... (pe) ... impermanent perception... (pe) ... impermanent formations... (pe) ... regarding the impermanent, suffering, and subject-to-change consciousness, they perceive it as ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’—what else is this but a failure to see things as they really are?”—this is what is to be known.

“Soṇa, whatever recluses or brahmins, regarding the impermanent, suffering, and subject-to-change form, do not perceive it as ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’—what else is this but seeing things as they really are? Regarding impermanent feeling... (pe) ... impermanent perception... (pe) ... impermanent formations... (pe) ... regarding the impermanent, suffering, and subject-to-change consciousness, they do not perceive it as ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’—what else is this but seeing things as they really are?”—this is knowledge.

## This is both knowledge and what is to be known.

Among those discourses, what is vision (dassana)?

“Those who clearly understand the Noble Truths, well-taught by the One of profound wisdom,
Even if they should be greatly negligent, they do not take up an eighth existence.”

## This is called vision (dassana).
146:
“Just as a stone pillar firmly planted in the earth is unshakable by the winds from the four directions, so too, I say, is the superior person who sees the Noble Truths with penetration.”

## This is vision (dassana).

“Monks, a noble disciple who possesses the four factors of stream-entry may, if he wishes, declare of himself: ‘I am finished with hell, finished with the animal realm, finished with the sphere of hungry ghosts, finished with the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my destination. Having wandered and roamed among devas and humans for seven times at most, I shall make an end of suffering.’ What are the four? Here, monks, the noble disciple’s faith in the Tathāgata is settled, established, grown, and takes root; it is unshakable by any recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world. Indeed, he has reached certainty in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise.’ That is to say, the destruction of intoxication... (pe) ... cessation, Nibbāna. Furthermore, he is liked, pleasing, dear, and charming to his fellow practitioners, both lay and ordained. Furthermore, he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, unblemished, unspotted, unsullied, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and leading to concentration. A noble disciple possessed of these four factors of stream-entry may, if he wishes, declare of himself: ‘I am finished with hell, finished with the animal realm, finished with the sphere of hungry ghosts, finished with the plane of misery, the bad destination, and the nether world. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my destination. Having wandered and roamed among devas and humans for seven times at most, I shall make an end of suffering.’”

## This is vision (dassana).
147:
Among those twenty-eight discourses, what is the discourse on development (bhāvanā)?

'He whose faculties [such as faith] are well-developed, internally and externally in the whole world, having penetrated this world and the next, he awaits his time, developed and well-tamed.'

## Ayaṃ bhāvanā.

'Monks, there are these four factors of Dhamma (dhammapada). Which four? Non-covetousness is a factor of Dhamma, non-ill will is a factor of Dhamma, right mindfulness is a factor of Dhamma, and right concentration is a factor of Dhamma. Monks, these are the four factors of Dhamma.'

## Ayaṃ bhāvanā.

Among those discourses, what is the discourse that is both vision (dassana) and development (bhāvanā)?

'One should cut the five [lower fetters] and abandon the five [upper fetters].' This passage is called the discourse on vision. 'One should further develop the five [faculties]. A monk who has transcended the five attachments [lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and wrong view] is called one who has crossed the flood.' This passage is called the discourse on development. This is the discourse that is both vision and development.

'Monks, there are these three faculties (indriya). Which three? The faculty of "I shall know the unknown" (anaññātaññassāmītindriya), the faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya), and the faculty of one who has known (aññātāvindriya). Monks, what is the faculty of "I shall know the unknown"? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the realization of the Noble Truth of Suffering which has not yet been realized; for the realization of the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering... the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering... the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering which has not yet been realized. Monks, this is called the faculty of "I shall know the unknown".' This is the discourse on vision.

'Monks, what is the faculty of final knowledge? Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; "This is the cessation of suffering"... "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering". Monks, this is called the faculty of final knowledge.'

'Monks, what is the faculty of one who has known? Here, monks, with the destruction of the taints, a monk enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge in this very life. He understands: "Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done"...'
148:
He understands clearly: 'There is no further work to be done for the sake of these sixteen tasks of the Path.' Monks, this is called the faculty of one who has known. This is the discourse on development. This discourse is called both the discourse on vision and the discourse on development.

Among those twenty-eight discourses, what is the discourse on own words (sakavacana)?

'To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the good, to purify one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.'

## This is the discourse on own words.

'Monks, there are these three characteristics of a fool, signs of a fool, and behaviors of a fool, by which others recognize a fool as a fool. Which three? Monks, a fool is one who thinks bad thoughts [such as covetousness], speaks bad words [such as falsehood], and does bad deeds [such as killing]. Monks, these are the three characteristics, signs, and behaviors of a fool.'

'Monks, there are these three characteristics of a wise person, signs of a wise person, and behaviors of a wise person, by which others recognize a wise person as a wise person. Which three? Monks, a wise person is one who thinks well-conceived thoughts [such as non-covetousness], speaks well-spoken words, and does well-performed deeds [such as abstaining from killing]. Monks, these are the three characteristics, signs, and behaviors of a wise person.'

## This is the discourse on own words.

Among those twenty-eight discourses, what is the discourse on others' words (paravacana)?

'There is nothing as extensive as the earth, there is no depth equal to the abyss (pātāla), there is nothing as high as Mount Meru, and there is no man like a Universal Monarch (cakkavatti).'

## This is the discourse on others' words.
149:
"Lord of Devas, Sakka, let there be victory through well-spoken words," said Vepacitti the Asura. "Vepacitti, let there be victory through well-spoken words," said Sakka. "Vepacitti, speak a verse," said Sakka. Monks, then Vepacitti, Lord of Asuras, recited this verse:

"Fools would break out even more if there were no one to restrain them. Therefore, the wise should restrain the fool with heavy punishment."

Monks, when the verse was spoken by Vepacitti, Lord of Asuras, the Asuras rejoiced, while the Devas remained silent. Then Vepacitti, Lord of Asuras, said to Sakka, Lord of Devas, "Sakka, speak a verse." Monks, when this was said, Sakka, Lord of Devas, recited this verse:

"I consider this alone to be the restraint of a fool: when one knows the other is angry, one remains mindful and calm."

Monks, when the verse was spoken by Sakka, Lord of Devas, the Devas rejoiced, while the Asuras remained silent. Then Sakka, Lord of Devas, said to Vepacitti, Lord of Asuras, "Vepacitti, speak a verse." Monks, when this was said, Vepacitti, Lord of Asuras, recited this verse:

"Vāsava, I see only this fault in patience: when the fool thinks, 'This one endures me out of fear,' the witless one oppresses even more, like a bull over a fleeing creature."

Monks, when the verse was spoken by Vepacitti, Lord of Asuras, the Asuras rejoiced, while the Devas remained silent. Then Vepacitti, Lord of Asuras, said to Sakka, Lord of Devas, "Sakka, speak a verse." Monks, when this was said, Sakka, Lord of Devas, recited these verses:

"Whether the fool thinks 'He endures me out of fear' or not, among all goals, one's own goal is supreme; there is no goal higher than patience.

He who, being strong, endures the weak—that they call the highest patience; for the weak must always endure.

They call that strength 'no strength' which is the strength of a fool. For one who is strong and guarded by Dhamma, there is no opponent."
150:
"He who gets angry back at one who is angry is worse because of that. He who does not get angry back at one who is angry wins a battle hard to win.

He practices for the benefit of both—his own and the other's—who, knowing the other is angry, remains mindful and calm.

People who are unskilled in the Dhamma think of him as a 'fool' even as he heals the welfare of both himself and the other."

"Monks, when these verses were spoken by Sakka, Lord of Devas, the Devas rejoiced, while the Asuras remained silent." This is Paravacana (the words of others).

In this context, what are Sakavacana and Paravacana?

Both the benefit obtained now and the benefit to be obtained in the future are overwhelmed by passion and so forth for one who follows the example of those who are afflicted and full of defilements. Those who take the training as the essence and are established in virtue, conduct, livelihood, the holy life, and service as the core—this is one extreme. Those who have such a doctrine and view that "there is no fault in sensual pleasures"—this is the second extreme. Both these extremes increase the cemetery and increase wrong views. Not fully understanding these two extremes, some shrink back (through craving for existence) and some overreach (through the view of annihilation). This is Paravacana.

Those who, having fully understood these two extremes, do not stand in them through craving or views, and do not conceive themselves through them—for them, there is no cycle of suffering to be described. This is Sakavacana. This inspired utterance is both Sakavacana and Paravacana.

King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, while I was in seclusion and solitude, this thought arose in my mind: 'To whom is the self dear, and to whom is the self not dear?' Then, Venerable Sir, it occurred to me: 'Those who practice misconduct by body, speech, and mind—to them the self is not dear. Even though they might say, "The self is dear to us," yet the self is not dear to them. Why is that? Because what an enemy would do to an enemy, that they do to themselves; therefore, the self is not dear to them. But those who practice good conduct by body, speech, and mind—to them the self is dear. Even though they might say, "The self is not dear to us," yet the self is dear to them. Why is that? Because what a loved one would do to a loved one, that they do to themselves; therefore, the self is dear to them.'"

"So it is, Great King! So it is, Great King! So it is, Great King. Those who practice misconduct by body, speech, and mind—to them the self is not dear. Even though they might say, 'The self is dear to us,' yet the self is not dear to them. Why is that? Great King, what an enemy would do to an enemy, that they do to themselves..."
151:
...should do. That very thing they do to themselves. Therefore, their self is dear to them.

“So it is, Great King! So it is, Great King! Great King, those who practice misconduct by body, speech, and mind, for them the self is not dear. Even if they were to say, ‘Our self is dear to us,’ yet their self is not dear to them. For what reason? Great King, what an enemy would do to an enemy, that they do to themselves. Therefore, their self is not dear to them.

Great King, those who practice good conduct by body, speech, and mind, for them the self is dear. Even if they were to say, ‘Our self is not dear to us,’ yet their self is dear to them. For what reason? Great King, what a dear one would do for a dear one, that they do to themselves. Therefore, their self is dear to them.” Thus the Blessed One spoke... the Teacher said:

“If one knows oneself to be dear, one should not bind oneself to evil.
For happiness is not easily gained by one who does evil deeds.
When one is oppressed by the Ender [Death] and abandons this human existence,
What then is one’s own? What does one take when one goes?
What follows one like a shadow that never leaves?
Both the merit and the evil that a mortal performs here,
That indeed is one’s own; that one takes when one goes.
That follows one like a shadow that never leaves.
Therefore, one should do what is good, accumulating for the future life.
Merits are the support for beings in the world beyond.”

This sutta is paravacana (the words of another). The anugīti (subsequent verse) is sakavacana (one’s own words). This sutta is called both sakavacana and paravacana.

Among those six suttas, what is the visajjanīya (that which is to be answered)?
When questions are asked: these five aggregates should be known with higher knowledge; this truth of suffering should be fully understood; this truth of origin should be abandoned; this truth of the path should be developed; this truth of cessation should be realized. These wholesome and unwholesome states, thus grasped, bring about this result.
152:
Of those wholesome and unwholesome states thus grasped, this is the benefit; thus, this is the visajjanīya. One should point out with certainty the exalted nature of the Buddha: “The Blessed One is exalted,” the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, and the good practice of the Saṅgha. One should point out with certainty: “All conditioned things are impermanent,” “All conditioned things are suffering,” “All phenomena are non-self.” Or whatever other sutta is of such a nature. This is the visajjanīya.

Among them, what is the avisajjanīya (that which is not to be answered)?

“O Trainer of men, whatever the Blessed One desires,
